reaudit: Week 13–14, 50 consecutive episodes.
close_loop: Present at ED, acute medicine and microbiology governance; embed the order set default.
evidence: [1975] Surgery, blood culture use: adherence 58.7% → 65% (departmental presentation only)
[8087] Acute medicine, coagulation screens: inappropriate tests 34–39% → 10–20% (condition-specific electronic order sets)
[5681] General wards, sepsis care: small improvements only (guidance, education and monthly feedback)
pitfalls: Second set delays antibiotics → state that both sets can be taken in one draw, as SMI S 12 allows, and antibiotics must not wait.
Lab counts bottles, not sets → agree how the LIMS shows a set before cycle 1.
Contamination may rise with more sets → track contamination as a balancing measure.
Order set change needs IT time → start with a printed two-label pack.
pearls: Pair with the contamination audit; both use the same LIMS extract.
Recruit an ED sepsis nurse lead.
Show single-set cases later labelled 'possible contaminant' to explain why two sets matter.
effort: ~15 min per 10 episodes from LIMS and notes

question: What proportion of blood culture bottles are loaded onto the analyser within 4 hours of collection?
why: Delayed loading slows detection and can miss some organisms, especially where samples travel to a hub lab. The library has no audit of collection-to-loading time.

standard.source: UK SMI S 12: Sepsis and systemic or disseminated infections (UKHSA, issue 1.1, April 2025), section 5.4 optimal transport and storage conditions
standard.wording: Specimens should be transported and processed as soon as possible. Inoculated bottles should be loaded onto automated blood culture analyser (or incubated in the case of non-automated analysers) without delay and ideally within a maximum of 4 hours from time of collection.

pass: Analyser loading time is 4 hours or less after the collection time on the request.
population: All blood culture bottles from the hospital (ED, wards, ICU). Exclude bottles with no collection time recorded (count them separately).
sample: All bottles over 1 week (usually 300+), from the LIMS and analyser log.
data_source: Request collection time (EPR/ICE label); LIMS receipt time; analyser loading log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Place a blood culture analyser module (or 24-hour loading point) at the site with the longest delays, or add a timed courier run for blood cultures overnight.
reaudit: Week 13–14, all bottles over 1 week.
close_loop: Present at the pathology network board and microbiology governance; embed the loading point or courier schedule and add the measure to the lab KPI set.
evidence: [6344] Microbiology, positive blood cultures: 50% had a Gram stain within 2 hours of flagging (prospective audit, no re-audit)
[7895] Acute medicine, urine samples: sample errors fell by 50% (easier collection and labelling)
[3976] Haematology clinic: waiting-time standard met only after point-of-care testing replaced sample transport
pitfalls: Collection time missing or defaulted to label print time → report missing times separately and fix the label workflow.
Hub-and-spoke labs blame transport → split delays into collection-to-receipt and receipt-to-load.
Capital cost of a new module → start with courier timing, which is cheaper.
Seasonal volume changes → re-audit in the same season if possible.
pearls: Recruit the microbiology laboratory manager; they own the analyser log.
Plot delays by hour of collection; the night peak is usually obvious.
Use the same week-day pattern in both cycles.
effort: ~1 hour in total from a LIMS and analyser extract

question: What proportion of adults with an incidental lung nodule of 5 mm or more on CT have follow-up arranged in line with BTS guidance?
why: Incidental nodules on CT done for other reasons are often lost when the patient leaves the requesting team. Library audits of incidental findings cover gallbladder polyps [2604] [2780], not lung nodules.

standard.source: BTS quality standards for the investigation and management of pulmonary nodules (BMJ Open Resp Res 2018), quality statement 4
standard.wording: People with pulmonary nodules confirmed on CT are offered discharge, further surveillance, further workup or treatment according to BTS Guidelines

pass: Within 4 weeks of the report, a surveillance CT is requested at the BTS interval or the patient is referred to the nodule/lung clinic, as matches the nodule size and risk.
population: Adults with a new solid or subsolid lung nodule of 5 mm or more (or 80 mm³ or more) reported on CT done for another reason (ED, inpatient, outpatient). Exclude known cancer under follow-up, lung screening programme patients and palliative patients.
sample: 40 consecutive reports over the last 3 months.
data_source: RIS free-text search for 'nodule'; RIS for follow-up CT requests; EPR for nodule clinic referrals and letters.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Use a standard nodule code in the report that auto-refers the case to the lung nodule MDT list, so follow-up does not depend on the requesting team.
reaudit: Week 13–14, next 40 consecutive nodule reports.
close_loop: Present at radiology and respiratory governance; embed the coded auto-referral and the nodule clinic's tracking list.
evidence: [2604] Primary care, gallbladder polyps: 41.6% lost to follow-up → 100% returned to surveillance (recall invitations)
[9431] Acute medicine, follow-up imaging after pneumonia: 22/42 → 37/50 had repeat imaging (emails, posters, leaflets)
[2780] Surgery, gallbladder polyp surveillance: 17% of pathways followed guidance (no re-audit)
pitfalls: Free-text search misses nodules → search several terms and check a sample of chest CTs by hand.
Reports do not state size → ask radiologists to use the BTS size bands in the code.
Respiratory team fears extra workload → show that most small nodules are discharged by the MDT, not seen in clinic.
Follow-up requested but never done → record whether the CT happened as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the lung nodule MDT lead and a chest radiologist.
Fix the size cut-offs to the BTS guideline in both cycles.
Give the nodule nurse the tracking list; it survives trainee rotation.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from RIS and EPR

question: What proportion of inpatients with an eGFR below 30 who receive iodine-based contrast have a documented decision about intravenous volume expansion?
why: Inpatients with severe kidney disease have the highest risk of contrast-associated kidney injury. National audits found poor risk assessment [7543] [6487]; no closed-loop audit of the prevention step is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG148 Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management, rec 1.2.8 (2019, updated October 2024)
standard.wording: For inpatients having iodine-based contrast media, consider intravenous volume expansion with either isotonic sodium bicarbonate or 0.9% sodium chloride if they are at particularly high risk, for example, if: they have an eGFR less than 30 ml/min/1.73 m2; they have had a renal transplant; a large volume of contrast medium is being used (for example, higher than the standard diagnostic dose or repeat administration within 24 hours); intra-arterial administration of contrast medium with first-pass renal exposure is being used. [2019]

pass: IV volume expansion is prescribed around the scan, or the notes record a reason not to give it (e.g. fluid overload, emergency scan).
population: Adult inpatients with an eGFR below 30 (latest before the scan) having contrast-enhanced CT or angiography. Exclude patients on dialysis.
sample: 40 consecutive scans over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: RIS contrast scans linked to LIMS eGFR; EPMA for fluids; EPR for documented decisions.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an 'eGFR under 30: IV fluids plan (give / not giving because...)' prompt to the RIS vetting screen, visible to the vetting radiologist and the ward.
reaudit: Week 13–14, next 40 consecutive scans.
close_loop: Present at radiology and renal governance; embed the vetting prompt and a ward order-set line for pre-scan fluids.
evidence: [7543] UK national contrast audit: 41% of inpatients had the recommended risk assessment (no re-audit)
[6487] RCR national audit: poor compliance; clinically significant post-contrast AKI in 0.4% of inpatients (no re-audit)
[6038] Hospital-wide AKI care: all measures met 3.7% → 8.4% of patient-days (care bundle with education)
pitfalls: Emergency scans cannot wait for fluids → accept a documented 'not given: emergency' as a pass.
Clinicians argue the evidence is weak → NICE says 'consider', so the pass is a documented decision, not fluid itself.
eGFR from months earlier → use the latest eGFR before the scan and state this rule in advance.
Heart failure patients → record the reason; do not push fluids.
pearls: Recruit a renal registrar and a CT vetting radiologist.
Report AKI after scans as a secondary measure; it keeps the audit balanced.
Keep the prompt short; a one-line pick list is used, a paragraph is not.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from RIS, LIMS and EPMA

question: What proportion of inpatient and ED MRI requests have the referrer's MRI safety screening questions fully completed?
why: Pacemakers, metal fragments and other implants missed at referral cause cancellations and serious incidents. No audit of referrer MRI safety screening is in the library.

standard.source: MHRA Safety guidelines for magnetic resonance imaging equipment in clinical use (version 5.0, July 2026), section 5.3.4 screening prior to examination, figure 5 stage 1
standard.wording: Referrer completes targeted MRI screening questions as part of the MRI referral, designed to highlight any potential contraindications to MRI.

pass: Every targeted MRI safety question on the request (e.g. pacemaker or other implant, metal fragments, previous surgery, pregnancy) is answered, none left blank or 'unknown' without a plan.
population: MRI requests for adult inpatients and ED patients. Exclude requests made by radiologists.
sample: 50 consecutive requests over 2 weeks.
data_source: RIS/ICE MRI request form; MRI department log of delays or cancellations for safety queries.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the MRI safety questions mandatory fields on the electronic MRI request, with 'unknown' allowed only when a named person is chasing the information.
reaudit: Week 13–14, next 50 consecutive requests.
close_loop: Present at the MR safety committee and radiology governance; embed the mandatory fields and report monthly via the MR safety expert.
evidence: [7133] Theatres, WHO checklist: Sign In compliance 55% → 99% (wall-mounted redesigned checklist)
[7271] ED intubation checklist: use 16.7% → 84% (prompts at the point of use)
[9433] ED renal colic: STONE score recorded 5.3% → 78.9% (mandatory prompts in ICE/iRefer requests)
pitfalls: Mandatory fields invite ticking 'no' without asking → compare the request answers with the radiographer's full screen.
Unconscious patients cannot answer → allow 'unknown: collateral being sought' and record who is chasing.
IT change is slow → use a required free-text line as an interim.
MRI staff and referrers blame each other → present the data jointly with the MR safety expert.
pearls: Recruit the MR safety expert and a senior MRI radiographer.
Measure delays caused by safety queries; they show the cost.
Keep the question list identical in both cycles.
effort: ~15 min per 10 requests from RIS

question: Is the median dose-length product of adult CT head scans for suspected stroke at or below the national diagnostic reference level of 790 mGy cm?
why: CT head for stroke is one of the highest-volume CT examinations, so small excess doses add up. Library dose audits cover CT KUB, CTPA and colonography [9422] [5555] [7163]; none covers stroke CT head against the current national level.

standard.source: IR(ME)R 2017 regulation 12(3)(c) and UKHSA National Diagnostic Reference Levels (updated 11 December 2025), table 1 adult CT
standard.wording: (3) Without prejudice to paragraphs (1) and (2), the operator must select equipment and methods to ensure that for each exposure the dose of ionising radiation to the individual undergoing the exposure is as low as reasonably practicable and consistent with the intended diagnostic or therapeutic purpose and in doing so must have regard, in particular to— ... (c) adherence to such diagnostic reference levels for radiodiagnostic examinations falling within regulation 3(a), (b), (e) and (f) as the employer may have established, as set out in the employer’s procedures. UKHSA table 1: Head, Acute stroke, All sequences, CTDIvol 47 mGy, DLP 790 mGy cm, adopted 2022.

pass: Department level: median DLP ≤790 mGy cm per scanner. Patient level: DLP ≤790 mGy cm for the whole examination.
population: Adults having non-contrast CT head for suspected acute stroke. Exclude CT angiography and perfusion sequences done in the same visit, and repeat scans for movement (count those separately).
sample: 50 consecutive examinations per scanner over 2 weeks.
data_source: RIS or dose-monitoring software (DLP, CTDIvol, scanner, protocol); PACS dose sheet if no software.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Review the stroke CT head protocol with the medical physics expert (tube current modulation, scan length, iterative reconstruction) and lock the optimised protocol on every scanner.
target: Median ≤790 mGy cm on every scanner
reaudit: Week 13–14, 50 consecutive examinations per scanner.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee; embed the protocol, update local DRLs and add the median to the annual IR(ME)R audit programme.
evidence: [6899] Radiology, CT dose audits: median DLP reduced by up to 43% (scanner exposure control optimised)
[9422] Urology/radiology, CT KUB: scans starting above T10 48% → 21.9% (new protocol)
[7585] Radiology, CT brain lens exclusion: 0% → 14.5% (radiographer re-education only)
pitfalls: Mixing stroke and trauma protocols → filter by clinical indication, not protocol name alone.
Repeat series inflate DLP → record them separately so the protocol is judged fairly.
One scanner drives the result → report per scanner.
Re-education alone gives small gains → change the protocol, not only behaviour.
pearls: Recruit the medical physics expert first; they can pull dose data quickly.
Use the NDRL version adopted in 2022 in both cycles.
Check image quality with a neuroradiologist after any protocol change.
effort: ~30 min in total from dose-monitoring software

question: What proportion of CT aortograms for suspected acute aortic dissection from the ED are ECG-gated?
why: Non-gated scans blur the aortic root and can miss or mimic type A dissection, a condition with high mortality and frequent delay [2947]. No audit of CT aortogram protocol is in the library.

standard.source: RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Thoracic Aortic Dissection in the Emergency Department (March 2025), introduction
standard.wording: The diagnostic modality of choice is CT Aortogram (CTA) which has high diagnostic accuracy in discriminating the various components of TAD. Initial non-contrast acquisition should form part of the scanning protocol for its value in assessment of intramural haematoma. ... Arterial phase acquisition should routinely be performed with ECG synchronisation (ECG-gated scan) with the aim of producing motion-free images of the aortic root.

pass: The arterial phase is ECG-gated (prospective or retrospective) as recorded in the scan protocol or DICOM series description.
population: Adults having CT aortogram from the ED for suspected acute aortic dissection or acute aortic syndrome, in and out of hours.
sample: 40 consecutive scans over the last 3 months.
data_source: RIS protocol field and PACS series descriptions; report for motion artefact comment.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Set a single 'CT aorta – suspected dissection' protocol on every scanner that is ECG-gated by default, with gating leads stocked in the CT room.
reaudit: Week 13–14, next 40 consecutive scans.
close_loop: Present at radiology and ED governance and the regional aortic network; embed the default protocol and out-of-hours radiographer training record.
evidence: [2947] UK type A aortic dissection: delays in diagnosis or transfer in 47.3%, initial misdiagnosis in 15.6% (national audit, no re-audit)
[5555] Radiology, CTPA: excess scan length 39.1 → 19.5 mm (protocol change with extra topogram)
[9422] Radiology, CT KUB: scans starting above T10 48% → 21.9% (new protocol)
pitfalls: Out-of-hours radiographers unfamiliar with gating → include night scans and give them a one-page set-up card.
Fast or irregular heart rates → record the reason when gating is not possible and accept it as a documented exception.
Series names vary by scanner → agree how gating is identified with the CT superintendent before cycle 1.
Small numbers → pool 3 months.
pearls: Recruit a cardiothoracic or vascular radiologist and the CT superintendent.
Report motion artefact as a secondary measure; it shows why gating matters.
Make the gated protocol the default so it survives staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 scans from RIS and PACS

question: What proportion of blood gas analyser tests in the ED are run under an operator ID with in-date recorded competence?
why: Shared or expired log-ins hide untrained users and wrong results on devices used for time-critical decisions. The library has one POCT governance survey [5563] and no audit of operator competence.

standard.source: MHRA Management and use of IVD point of care test devices (updated 14 July 2026), section 4.2 training
standard.wording: Only staff whose training and competence has been established and recorded should be permitted to carry out POCT. They should also receive continued support and regular updates.

pass: The test was run under a personal operator ID that is on the POCT training register with an in-date competence on the test date.
population: All patient tests on ED blood gas analysers. Exclude quality control runs.
sample: All patient tests over 1 week (usually several hundred), from middleware.
data_source: POCT middleware operator log; POCT training register; staff rota for shared IDs.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Remove all shared operator IDs and switch on middleware lock-out for expired competence, with a 30-day reminder email to the user.
reaudit: Week 13–14, all patient tests over 1 week.
close_loop: Present at the POCT committee and ED governance; embed the lock-out and report monthly to the POCT committee.
evidence: [5563] Irish hospitals, POCT governance: only a quarter had POCT committees (survey, no re-audit)
[7258] ED point-of-care ultrasound: 0% → up to 90% stored on PACS (network link and electronic requests)
[3976] Haematology clinic: waiting-time standard met after POCT by trained nurse specialists
pitfalls: Lock-out blocks a doctor during an emergency → keep a short-term emergency ID that is audited weekly.
Training capacity cannot meet demand → agree extra training sessions with the POCT team before the lock-out date.
Doctors rotating in without training → add POCT training to ED induction.
Middleware data unfamiliar to clinicians → ask the POCT coordinator to run the extract.
pearls: Recruit the POCT coordinator; they own the register and middleware.
Announce the lock-out date early and publish weekly counts of expired users.
Keep the same analysers in both cycles.
effort: ~30 min in total from middleware and register

question: What proportion of urine pregnancy tests done in the ED have a complete point-of-care test record in the patient notes?
why: Pregnancy tests guide imaging, drugs and surgery, and a faulty batch can only be recalled if batch and patient are recorded. Library audits measure whether a test is done [7712] [6008], not whether it is traceable.

standard.source: MHRA Management and use of IVD point of care test devices (updated 14 July 2026), section 4.10 record keeping
standard.wording: It is imperative to keep accurate records of patient results from POCT devices. These records should include: date; device type; batch numbers; result; operator identity; patient identity

pass: The patient record shows all six items: date, test type, batch number, result, tester identity and patient identity.
population: Patients aged 12–55 who had a urine pregnancy test in the ED. Exclude tests sent to the laboratory.
sample: 50 consecutive tests over 2 weeks.
data_source: ED EPR or paper record; ED pregnancy test register if one exists.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a structured 'urine pregnancy test' entry in the ED EPR with required fields for result, batch number and tester, and move testing to one area with the kits.
reaudit: Week 13–14, 50 consecutive tests.
close_loop: Present at the POCT committee and ED governance; embed the structured entry and consider a connected reader for pregnancy tests.
evidence: [7712] General surgery, pregnancy testing in abdominal pain: 41.8% → 80% (education, posters, nursing huddle)
[6008] Surgical admissions, pregnancy status documented: 30% → 75% (prompt in the clerking document)
[2745] Paediatric abdominal pain: documented pregnancy test in 13.3% (no re-audit)
pitfalls: Tests done but not documented → count only what is in the record; say so in advance.
Batch number seen as bureaucracy → share the MHRA recall case study.
Kits in several places → put them in one place next to the EPR terminal.
Paper and electronic records mixed → check both in cycle 1 and cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit an ED senior nurse and the POCT coordinator.
Use the same age band and exclusion rules in both cycles.
Stick the batch number label on the kit box to make copying easy.
effort: ~15 min per 10 tests from ED records

question: What proportion of repeat liver function test requests on adult inpatients are made less than 72 hours after the previous one?
why: Daily routine liver tests add cost, blood loss and lab workload without changing care. Library audits show reductions are possible [8036] [8087]; none uses the RCPath minimum retesting interval as the standard.

standard.source: RCPath G147 National minimum retesting intervals in pathology (version 2, March 2021), B-L2 liver, acute inpatient setting
standard.wording: B-L2 Acute inpatient setting — Testing at 72-hour intervals in acute setting (apart from those in L4). B-L4 Acute poisoning (e.g. paracetamol), TPN, liver unit, acute liver injury and ITU patients — May require more frequent monitoring.

pass: The repeat LFT is 72 hours or more after the previous LFT, or the patient is in a B-L4 group.
population: Adult inpatients on medical and surgical wards with a repeat LFT. Exclude ICU, liver unit, TPN, acute poisoning and acute liver injury patients (B-L4).
sample: 100 consecutive repeat LFT requests over 1 week (from the LIMS).
data_source: LIMS request history by patient; EPR for B-L4 exclusions.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a minimum retesting interval rule in the electronic order system: a repeat LFT within 72 hours shows the last result and needs a reason from a pick-list.
target: ≥80% of repeat requests at 72 hours or more (or an exception)
reaudit: Week 13–14, 100 consecutive repeat requests.
close_loop: Present at the laboratory users' group and medical governance; embed the order rule and report monthly LFT volumes.
evidence: [8036] District general hospital, LFTs: inappropriate tests 28.0% → 18.4% (education-led PDSA cycles)
[8087] Acute medicine, coagulation screens: inappropriate 34–39% → 10–20% (order sets and a digital indication prompt)
[6456] Paediatric ICU, LFTs: sustained fall in daily LFTs (request form and nurse champions)
pitfalls: LFTs bundled in a 'daily bloods' order set → change the order set as well as the rule.
Hard blocks anger clinicians → use a soft stop with a reason, not a block.
Exception groups not flagged in the LIMS → check exclusions against the EPR for a sample.
Gains fade after rotation → keep the rule, not only teaching.
pearls: Recruit the duty biochemist and a digital clinical safety officer.
Show the cost and carbon of avoidable tests per month.
Report by ward; it makes the change local.
effort: ~30 min in total from a LIMS extract plus exclusion checks

question: What proportion of ED blood samples for urea and electrolytes are reported as haemolysed?
why: Haemolysis gives false high potassium, forces repeat blood tests and delays decisions in the ED. Library sample rejection audits cover transfusion [7693] and INR [1718]; none covers ED haemolysis.

standard.source: Local standard
standard.wording: No more than 5% of ED urea and electrolyte samples should be reported as haemolysed (haemolysis index above the laboratory's potassium reporting limit).

pass: The sample is not flagged as haemolysed above the potassium reporting limit.
population: All ED urea and electrolyte samples from adults. Exclude samples taken in resuscitation during cardiac arrest.
sample: All ED samples over 1 week (from the LIMS), with a notes review of 50 haemolysed samples for collection method.
data_source: LIMS haemolysis index flags by location; ED notes for collection method, device and collector.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Stock and default to vacuum tube collection through a needle or butterfly (no syringe transfer), and send ED samples by pneumatic tube at the lower speed setting agreed with the lab.
reaudit: Week 13–14, all ED samples over 1 week.
close_loop: Present at ED and pathology users' governance; embed the stock change and monthly haemolysis rate feedback by ED area.
evidence: [1718] Orthopaedics, INR samples: rejection 16.5% → 11.1% (education and stocking short-tubing collection devices)
[7693] UK transfusion samples: rejection 2.99% → 4.4% between national audits (no single intervention)
[7895] Acute medicine, urine samples: sample errors fell by 50% (easier collection and labelling)
pitfalls: Lab changes the haemolysis threshold between cycles → fix the threshold before cycle 1.
Collection method rarely documented → use a short 2-week sticker on the request to capture it.
Pneumatic tube settings are outside ED control → involve estates and the lab early.
Staff feel blamed → report by area, not by person.
pearls: Recruit the lab quality manager and an ED nurse educator.
Measure delay to a valid potassium; it shows the patient impact.
Feed back the rate monthly on the ED safety board.
effort: ~30 min from a LIMS extract plus 15 min per 10 notes

question: What proportion of unexpected cancers found in routine surgical specimens have a documented action by the requesting team within 14 days of the report?
why: Unexpected cancers in appendix, gallbladder and other routine specimens are easily missed after discharge. One library audit found only half of appendix reports reviewed within 15 days [7670]; no audit targets unexpected malignancy across specialties.

standard.source: RCPath G133 Best practice recommendations: communication of unexpected findings, urgent reports, delayed reports and the use of alert systems in diagnostic cellular pathology (version 2, February 2026), sections 2 and 4
standard.wording: Service users sending specimens should have systems in place to ensure that all histopathology reports are read by someone who is suitably trained and qualified to read and interpret them correctly, in the context of the patient’s clinical details. ... In participating in the use of a coding or alert system, pathologists and their employing authorities should make it clear that it is the responsibility of the requesting clinician to have systems in place to ensure timely reading and acting upon of a laboratory report.

pass: Within 14 days of report authorisation the notes show an action: MDT referral, clinic appointment, or letter to patient and GP with a plan.
population: Adults whose routine surgical specimen (e.g. appendix, gallbladder, hernia sac, uterus, prostate chips, skin excised as benign) shows a malignant or pre-malignant neoplasm not suspected before surgery. Exclude specimens sent as suspected cancer.
sample: 40 consecutive cases over the last 6–12 months (SNOMED search).
data_source: LIMS SNOMED codes for malignancy by specimen type; EPR, MDT lists and clinic letters for the action.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Pathologists add an 'unexpected malignancy' alert code that places the case on the relevant MDT list automatically and sends a copy to the MDT coordinator.
reaudit: Week 13–14, next consecutive cases (pool 3 months if fewer than 20).
close_loop: Present at cellular pathology and surgical governance; embed the alert code and MDT auto-listing in the LIMS.
evidence: [7670] General surgery, appendix histology: reviewed within 15 days 49.5% → 77.6%; communication documented 16% at baseline (agreed protocol)
[2818] Surgery, perianal abscess cultures: only 6% reviewed at baseline (education and guideline)
[8427] Breast histopathology: 0/10 → 10/10 reports complete (reporting proforma)
pitfalls: Small numbers per month → use a 6–12 month retrospective window for cycle 1.
Pre-malignant lesions debated → list the included diagnoses with a pathologist before cycle 1.
Surgeon on leave when report arrives → auto-listing to the MDT removes the single point of failure.
Letters sent but no plan → count only actions that state what happens next.
pearls: Recruit a consultant histopathologist and an MDT coordinator.
Include specialties beyond general surgery; gynaecology and urology specimens are often forgotten.
Track the time to MDT discussion as a secondary measure.
effort: ~20 min per 10 cases from LIMS and EPR

question: What proportion of adult ward inpatients with a NEWS2 score of 5 or more have their next full set of observations recorded within 1 hour?
why: Missed or late repeat observations after a raised score are a leading theme in deterioration incidents. Library audits of NEWS2 monitoring come mainly from old age psychiatry [3352][3458] and electronic dashboards [7443]; no closed-loop audit of the 1-hour repeat on acute adult wards has been published in the library.

standard.source: Royal College of Physicians, NEWS2 Chart 4: Clinical response to the NEWS trigger thresholds (2017)
standard.wording: Total 5 or more — Urgent response threshold — Frequency of monitoring: Minimum 1 hourly

pass: The next complete NEWS2 set (all seven parameters) is timed within 60 minutes of the first score of 5 or more.
population: Adults on acute medical and surgical wards with a first NEWS2 score of 5 or more during the audit period. Exclude patients on end-of-life care with an agreed plan to stop routine observations, and patients in critical care, theatre or recovery.
sample: 40 consecutive episodes of a first NEWS2 score of 5 or more across 3–4 wards over the last 4 weeks (one episode per patient).
data_source: Electronic observations system (e.g. Nervecentre, VitalPAC) trigger report for cases and timings; notes for exclusions.

question: What proportion of adult ward inpatients at high risk from sepsis (suspected infection and NEWS2 of 7 or more) have NEWS2 recalculated within 30 minutes?
why: NICE NG253 sets a 30-minute re-score for high-risk sepsis so that non-response triggers senior and critical care input. Library sepsis audits measure time to antibiotics [6876][6435]; none measures the 30-minute re-score after ward deterioration.

standard.source: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.5 (2024; guideline published 2025, updated 2026)
standard.wording: Recalculate the NEWS2 score and re-evaluate risk of sepsis periodically, in line with the AoMRC statement on the initial antimicrobial treatment of sepsis (2022): every 30 minutes, for those at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis

pass: A complete NEWS2 is recorded within 30 minutes of the first qualifying score of 7 or more.
population: Adults (16 or over) on inpatient wards with suspected or confirmed infection and a first NEWS2 of 7 or more on ward deterioration. Exclude patients on end-of-life care and those moved to critical care within 30 minutes.
sample: 30–40 consecutive episodes over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Electronic observations system for NEWS2 of 7 or more; notes or sepsis screening tool to confirm suspected infection; observation timestamps.

question: What proportion of adult inpatients started on intravenous antibiotics for suspected sepsis have blood cultures taken before the first dose?
why: Cultures taken after antibiotics often grow nothing, which blocks later narrowing of treatment. The one closed-loop blood culture audit in the library rose only from 58.7% to 65% after a presentation [1975].

standard.source: NICE NG253 rec 1.8.1 (2016, amended 2024; guideline published 2025, updated 2026)
standard.wording: For people in hospital who have suspected infections: start looking for the source of infection (see the section on finding and controlling the source of infection) take microbiological and blood samples before giving an antimicrobial.

pass: Blood culture collection time is earlier than or the same as the first antibiotic administration time.
population: Adults (16 or over) in ED or on wards given a first dose of IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis. Exclude patients who had antibiotics before arrival and those transferred on antibiotics from another hospital.
sample: 40 consecutive adults over the last 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Electronic prescribing (first dose time); laboratory system (blood culture collection time); sepsis screening tool for cases.

Pair with the pharmacy antibiotic report to find cases fast.
Keep the grab bag checklist owned by the ward sister, not the audit team.

question: What proportion of adult ward inpatients at medium risk from sepsis (suspected infection and NEWS2 of 5 or 6) who are given antibiotics receive the first dose within 3 hours?
why: NICE now allows a deferral of up to 3 hours at medium risk, but the 3 hours is a maximum, not a target. Library audits of sepsis timing use the 1-hour standard [6876][2656]; none measures the 3-hour limit for medium risk.

standard.source: NICE NG253 rec 1.8.17 (2024; guideline published 2025, updated 2026)
standard.wording: For people at medium risk of severe illness or death from sepsis, a clinician with core competencies in the care of acutely ill patients (FY2 level or above) should consider: deferring administration of a broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment for up to 3 hours after calculating the person's first NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration and using this time to gather information for a more specific diagnosis (see recommendations on finding and controlling the source of infection and choice of antibiotic therapy) discussing with a senior clinical decision maker. Once a decision is made to give antibiotics, do not delay administration any further.

pass: First antibiotic dose given within 3 hours of the first NEWS2 of 5 or 6 with suspected infection.
population: Adults (16 or over) on inpatient wards with suspected infection and a first NEWS2 of 5 or 6 on ward deterioration who were given antibiotics for that episode. Exclude those already on antibiotics for the same infection and those whose score rose to 7 or more before a decision.
sample: 40 consecutive episodes over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Electronic observations system for time zero; electronic prescribing for administration time; notes for suspected infection.

question: What proportion of inpatients aged 65 or over with a postural drop in blood pressure have a documented medication review within 48 hours of the reading?
why: Library audits of lying and standing blood pressure mostly measure whether it is done [1685][1596][1168]. Acting on an abnormal result is rarely measured; one project found medication review in 0% at baseline [1824].

standard.wording: Ensure that the person's individual risk factors identified in the comprehensive falls assessment are promptly addressed with appropriate interventions to reduce their risk of falls. These interventions can be offered in the same service or involve an appropriate referral.

pass: Within 48 hours of the reading, the notes record a review of blood-pressure-lowering and other falls-risk medicines, with each stopped, reduced or kept with a reason.
population: Inpatients aged 65 or over with a recorded postural drop (systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more, or symptoms on standing). Exclude patients in the last days of life.
sample: 40 consecutive patients with a postural drop over the last 2–3 months on care of older people and acute medical wards.
data_source: Observation charts or EPR for lying and standing readings; medical notes and drug chart for the review.

question: What proportion of inpatients who fall have a documented check for fracture and spinal injury before they are moved from the floor?
why: Moving a patient with a hip or spinal fracture without checks causes avoidable harm. The National Audit of Inpatient Falls found checks before moving in 69% rising to only 77% over five years [1169]. The library holds audits of post-fall medical review [1171][6153] but not of the pre-move check on its own.

standard.source: NICE QS86 statement 4 (2015, updated 2025)
standard.wording: People who fall during a hospital stay are checked for signs or symptoms of fracture and potential for spinal injury before they are moved. [2015]

pass: Nursing post-fall record states that the patient was checked for signs of fracture and spinal injury before being moved.
population: All adult inpatient falls reported on the incident system. Exclude falls where the patient got up alone before staff arrived (record the number).
sample: 40 consecutive reported inpatient falls over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Incident reporting system (Datix or equivalent) for cases; nursing post-fall record and medical notes for the check.

Put the checklist in the post-fall grab folder on each ward.

question: What proportion of inpatients who hit their head in a fall have neurological observations recorded half-hourly for the first 2 hours?
why: Missed deterioration after an inpatient head strike is a recurring serious incident, especially in people on anticoagulants. The library audit of post-fall reviews focused on CT decisions [1171]; no audit of the early observation schedule after an inpatient head injury has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG232 rec 1.9.11 (2003, current guideline 2023); applied to inpatients by the local post-fall protocol
standard.wording: Carry out and record observations on a half-hourly basis until there is a GCS score of 15. Observations for people with a GCS score of 15 should start after the initial assessment in the emergency department and the minimum frequency should be: half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly. [2003]

pass: Four recorded neurological observation sets (GCS, pupils, limb movements) in the first 2 hours after the fall, none more than 40 minutes apart.
population: Adult inpatients with a witnessed head strike or an unwitnessed fall where head injury cannot be excluded. Exclude patients on end-of-life care.
sample: 30–40 consecutive falls with head strike or unwitnessed falls over the last 3 months.
data_source: Incident system for cases; neurological observation chart or electronic observations system for timings.

question: What proportion of adults at high risk of pressure ulcers who cannot reposition themselves are repositioned at least every 4 hours?
why: Missed turns are the most direct cause of hospital-acquired pressure ulcers. The library holds audits of risk scoring [5876] and EPR frameworks [7760] but no closed-loop audit of the 4-hour repositioning interval on repositioning charts.

standard.wording: Encourage adults who have been assessed as being at high risk of developing a pressure ulcer to change their position frequently and at least every 4 hours. sample: 40 patients on 3–4 wards: one 24-hour period each, over 2 weeks.
data_source: Repositioning (SSKIN) charts in EPR or paper; risk assessment for eligibility.

question: What proportion of inpatients with an indwelling urinary catheter have a documented reason for it that is still valid on the audit day?
why: Catheter-associated urinary infection rises with every day a catheter stays in. Library catheter audits focus on insertion records in ED [6829][2278]; the ongoing need on the ward is rarely measured.

standard.source: NICE CG139 rec 1.2.2.2 (2003, guideline updated 2017)
standard.wording: The patient's clinical need for catheterisation should be reviewed regularly and the urinary catheter removed as soon as possible. [2003]

pass: The notes or catheter care plan record an indication from an agreed list (e.g. retention, hourly output monitoring in unstable patients, sacral wound healing, end-of-life comfort, urology plan), and that indication still applies on the audit day.
population: All adult inpatients with an indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheter on the audit day. Exclude long-term catheters managed in the community with a documented plan.
sample: 40 catheterised patients across medical and surgical wards on 2 audit days (point prevalence).
data_source: Ward walk-round to identify catheters; catheter care plan or passport and medical notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a daily 'catheter still needed?' question to the nursing care rounds in the EPR, with a nurse-led removal protocol when no valid indication is ticked.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: same wards, 2 audit days, 40 patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the infection prevention committee. If it works, keep the daily question and the nurse-led removal protocol, and report catheter days on the infection dashboard.
evidence: [8178] neurosurgery: indwelling catheter use 25.6% → 11%; TWOC within 24 h 3% → 93% (removal pathway)
[6829] ED: catheter insertion documented 8% → 30% (single intervention)
[2278] urology ED: little change after a documentation campaign (fix that fails)
pitfalls: Doctors and nurses disagree on what counts as valid → agree the indication list with urology and infection prevention before cycle 1.
Nurses worry about removing catheters without a doctor → the protocol must name who can remove.
Point prevalence misses short catheters → run two audit days a week apart.
Retention after removal worries staff → include a bladder scan step in the protocol.
pearls: Recruit the continence nurse and an infection prevention nurse.
A ward walk-round finds catheters faster than the EPR.
Use the catheter passport if the trust already has one.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients on a ward walk-round

question: What proportion of adults with an indwelling urinary catheter and suspected urinary infection are diagnosed without using a urine dipstick?
why: Dipsticks are almost always positive in catheterised patients and drive unneeded antibiotics. No audit of dipstick use in catheterised inpatients has been published in the library; the nearest entries address catheter care and UTI prescribing [6140][8178].

standard.source: NICE QS90 statement 2 (2015, updated 2023)
standard.wording: Adults with indwelling urinary catheters do not have dipstick testing to diagnose urinary tract infections (UTIs). [2015, updated 2023]

pass: No urine dipstick result is recorded or cited in the decision to diagnose or treat the suspected UTI.
population: Adult inpatients with an indwelling catheter who had a urine sample sent or antibiotics started for suspected UTI. Exclude patients with intermittent self-catheterisation.
sample: 40 consecutive episodes over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Laboratory catheter urine sample list for cases; nursing observations for dipstick results; notes and e-prescribing.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Fever, loin pain, delirium, rigors etc.

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a hard stop to the EPR urinalysis entry for patients flagged as catheterised ('Dipstick not valid with a catheter: send culture if symptomatic'), and remove dipsticks from the catheter trolley.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive episodes, same template.
close_loop: Present at the antimicrobial stewardship and infection prevention committees. If it works, keep the EPR stop and add it to nursing induction.
evidence: [6140] acute medical unit UTI prescribing: compliance with local policy 100% and stop dates 100% at re-audit (CQUIN audit)
[8178] neurosurgery: CAUTI rate 94% → 45.5% (catheter removal pathway)
[5393] catheter care audit (nearest related entry)
pitfalls: Dipsticks done but not written down → ask nurses on the audit wards and record 'unknown' honestly.
Doctors worry about missing sepsis → the fix sends a culture; it does not stop treatment.
Catheter status not flagged in the EPR → the fix needs a catheter flag first.
Result improves only on the pilot ward → roll out the EPR stop trust-wide once shown to work.
pearls: Recruit an antimicrobial pharmacist and the continence nurse.
Pull cases from the lab 'catheter specimen' list.
Record antibiotic starts; the saving makes the case to managers.
effort: ~20 min per 10 episodes from lab list and EPR

question: What proportion of peripheral cannulas in place on adult wards have been used in the previous 24 hours?
why: Idle cannulas cause phlebitis and Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection. Library cannula audits look at insertion date and care bundles [4746][9478]; the idle cannula rate itself is rarely the measure.

standard.source: NICE QS61 statement 5 (2014)
standard.wording: People who need a vascular access device have their risk of infection minimised by the completion of specified procedures necessary for the safe insertion and maintenance of the device and its removal as soon as it is no longer needed.

pass: The cannula has been used for an IV drug, fluid or blood product in the previous 24 hours, or a documented reason to keep it (e.g. high risk of deterioration) is recorded.
population: All peripheral cannulas in adult inpatients on medical and surgical wards on the audit day. Exclude critical care and patients on end-of-life care with a comfort plan.
sample: 40–50 cannulas across 4 wards on 2 audit days (point prevalence).
data_source: Ward walk-round; cannula care record (VIP chart); drug chart and fluid chart for use in last 24 hours.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a daily 'cannula needed?' prompt to the VIP score entry in the EPR, with nurse-led removal if unused for 24 hours and no reason recorded.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: same wards, 2 audit days, same template.
close_loop: Present at the infection prevention committee and vascular access group. If it works, keep the prompt and report idle cannula rate with the Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia data.
evidence: [9478] peripheral cannula bundle: compliance 54% → 82% (weekly feedback on care bundle)
[7792] cannula bacteraemia: incidence down 54.5% (daily review of cannula need, feedback, new dressings and care plans)
[4746] insertion date: 13.8% of cannulas in place over 72 hours (single audit)
pitfalls: Doctors keep cannulas 'just in case' → allow a documented reason; the aim is conscious decisions.
Oral switch not done, so cannula looks used → note IV antibiotics that could have been switched as a context finding.
Point prevalence misses short stays → use two days a week apart.
Nurses unsure they may remove cannulas → confirm the trust policy allows nurse-led removal.
pearls: Recruit the infection prevention nurse; they may already run a cannula audit.
Do the walk-round at mid-morning after drug rounds.
Show the number of idle cannula days per month; it is a striking figure.
effort: ~10 min per 10 cannulas on a ward walk-round

question: What proportion of adult ward inpatients receiving oxygen have it signed for on the drug chart at every drug round?
why: Signing oxygen at each drug round is how staff check the patient is within target. In the library, signing at drug rounds rose only from 0% to 18% after a new chart [6130]; audits otherwise measure the prescription itself [8052][7745].

standard.source: British Thoracic Society guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings, summary of recommendations (2017), section 4
standard.wording: Oxygen should be prescribed and a signature should be entered on the drug chart on each drug round.

pass: Oxygen signed (or electronically recorded as administered, with device and flow) at every drug round in the previous 24 hours.
population: Adult inpatients receiving supplemental oxygen on medical and surgical wards on the audit day. Exclude critical care, theatre recovery and patients on home oxygen self-managed.
sample: 40 patients across 4–5 wards on 2 audit days (point prevalence).
data_source: Drug chart or e-prescribing administration record; bedside check of device and flow.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make oxygen a scheduled administration on e-prescribing at each drug round (or a pre-printed oxygen box on the paper chart) so it appears on the nurse's medicines round list.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: same wards, 2 audit days, 40 patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety group and respiratory directorate. If it works, keep the scheduled administration and add oxygen signing to the medicines safety dashboard.
evidence: [6130] ward oxygen use: signed at drug rounds 0% → 18%; valid prescription 55% → 94% (new oxygen chart, alert stickers, education)
[7745] surgical inpatients: oxygen prescribed 18% → 54.8% (QI project)
[5035] acute medicine: oxygen prescribed 0% → 49% (nurse-facilitated reminder)
pitfalls: Oxygen treated as 'not a drug' by staff → show the BTS wording at ward huddles.
E-prescribing lists oxygen as 'as required', so it never appears on the round → change it to scheduled with the pharmacy system team.
Patients who stopped oxygen mid-day confuse counts → count only rounds while on oxygen.
Gains fade after the audit → build it into the system, not a poster.
pearls: Recruit a respiratory nurse specialist and the e-prescribing pharmacist.
Collect device and target range as context; they show the wider picture.
Audit on two different weekdays.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients at the bedside and drug chart

question: What proportion of DNACPR decisions made in hospital record a discussion with the patient or those close to them, or the reason no discussion took place?
why: Failures to discuss DNACPR decisions have led to legal challenges and national reviews. Library DNACPR audits mostly measure form completion [1798][2039]; the discussion item on its own is rarely measured.

standard.source: BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN, Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation, 3rd edition (1st revision) 2016, section 15
standard.wording: Good documentation includes the following, on the CPR decision form or in the main health record or in some cases both: … details of any discussions about the decision with the patient, with those close to them, and (for a person who does not have capacity) with any person with authority to make decisions on their behalf and/ or with an IMCA • where no discussions have taken place the reasons for this

pass: The form or notes record who the decision was discussed with and when, or state a specific reason why no discussion took place (e.g. patient lacks capacity and no family reachable, with a plan to contact them).
population: New DNACPR decisions (or ReSPECT forms with a CPR recommendation of 'not for CPR') made for adult inpatients. Exclude decisions made in the community and brought in.
sample: 40 consecutive new decisions over the last 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Electronic DNACPR/ReSPECT register or resuscitation team list; forms and medical notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make 'discussed with' and 'reason not discussed' mandatory fields that must be completed before an electronic DNACPR or ReSPECT form can be signed.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive new decisions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the resuscitation committee and end-of-life care group. If it works, keep the mandatory fields and include this item in the resuscitation team's regular DNACPR audit.
evidence: [7508] DNACPR QI: clearer documentation of discussions and of reasons conversations had not happened (form redesign and teaching)
[8001] geriatric medicine: DNACPR documentation 55% → 73% (treatment escalation plan QI)
[2039] acute surgery: escalation status 42% → 46.6% (re-audit)
pitfalls: Discussions happen but are written in a different part of the notes → check both the form and the notes.
Decisions made at night with family unreachable → a clear reason and plan counts as a pass.
Clinicians feel their judgement is being questioned → audit the record, not the decision.
Mandatory fields filled with 'N/A' → spot-check 5 forms for meaningful content.
pearls: Recruit the resuscitation officer; they hold the register.
Involve a palliative care consultant in presenting the results.
Share one anonymised good example with every audited team.
effort: ~15 min per 10 forms from the register and notes

question: What proportion of DNACPR decisions made by a doctor other than the responsible consultant are endorsed by that consultant within 24 hours?
why: Decisions made out of hours by junior doctors need prompt senior review. Library treatment escalation audits found consultant involvement of 12% rising to 27% [8001]; no closed-loop audit of endorsement timing has been published in the library.

standard.source: BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN, Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation, 3rd edition (1st revision) 2016, section 15
standard.wording: if that is not the senior responsible clinician, the name and position of the senior responsible clinician, who should review and if appropriate endorse the decision at the earliest opportunity

pass: Consultant endorsement (signature or documented review) dated within 24 hours of the decision (local operational limit for 'at the earliest opportunity').
population: New inpatient DNACPR decisions made by a clinician who is not the responsible consultant. Exclude decisions reversed within 24 hours.
sample: 40 consecutive qualifying decisions over the last 1–2 months.
data_source: DNACPR/ReSPECT register; forms and notes for endorsement signature and time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add unendorsed DNACPR decisions to the daily post-take and board-round list generated by the EPR, so the consultant sees and signs them on the next ward round.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 qualifying decisions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the resuscitation committee and medical directorate governance. If it works, keep the board-round list and add endorsement time to the regular DNACPR audit.
evidence: [8001] geriatric medicine: consultant involvement 12% → 27% (treatment escalation plan QI)
[1798] DNACPR form quality: sustained gains in most of 7 standards (form redesign)
[3800] old age psychiatry: resuscitation decisions 4% → 40% (re-audit)
pitfalls: Weekend decisions wait until Monday → report weekday and weekend separately; agree 24 hours includes weekends.
Endorsement recorded only as a signature without a date → count undated signatures as fail and fix the form.
Consultants feel second-guessed → frame it as protecting junior colleagues.
ReSPECT and DNACPR forms coexist → include both and record which.
pearls: Recruit an acute medicine consultant as sponsor.
The resuscitation officer's register makes case-finding quick.
Present decisions changed at review; they show why endorsement matters.
effort: ~15 min per 10 forms from the register and notes

question: What proportion of infants who are not independently mobile and attend the emergency department with a bruise have a safeguarding assessment by a paediatrician before discharge?
why: Bruising in a baby who cannot move independently is a sentinel injury before serious abuse. No audit of this pathway has been published in the library; the nearest entries address safeguarding recording and burns checklists [5947][4091].

standard.source: NICE CG89 rec 1.1.2 (2009, updated 2025)
standard.wording: Suspect child maltreatment if there is bruising or petechiae (tiny red or purple spots) that are not caused by a medical condition (for example, a causative coagulation disorder) and if the explanation for the bruising is unsuitable. Examples include: bruising in a child who is not independently mobile

pass: A paediatrician's safeguarding assessment (history, full skin examination and documented outcome, including social care check or referral) is recorded before the infant leaves the ED or paediatric unit.
population: Infants who are not independently mobile (usually under 6 months, or older infants not yet crawling or cruising) attending ED with any bruise, whether or not it is the reason for attendance. Exclude bruises from documented birth injury or a known bleeding disorder under specialist care.
sample: All qualifying attendances over the last 6 months (expect 20–40 in a district general hospital).
data_source: ED system search for age under 12 months with 'bruise' in triage or diagnosis codes; ED and paediatric notes; social care referral records.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'mobile? bruise?' question to ED triage for children under 12 months that auto-refers any bruise in a non-mobile infant to the paediatric registrar.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 onward: all qualifying attendances for the next 3 months, same template.
close_loop: Present at the hospital safeguarding committee and paediatric and ED governance. If it works, keep the triage question and add the pathway to ED and paediatric induction.
evidence: [4091] preschool burns: referral for further opinion 0% → 3%, checklist completed in 97% of notes where used (NAI checklist)
[5947] primary care: maltreatment-related coding up 1.4-fold (simple coding strategy)
[6983] safeguarding training audit: new training did not improve reporting (fix that fails)
pitfalls: Small numbers → use a 6-month window and report every case, not just a percentage.
Bruise mentioned only in the examination, not triage → search free text as well as codes.
Mobility not recorded → record 'not recorded' as its own category; it is a finding.
Parents' distress makes staff reluctant to refer → the triage rule removes individual judgement.
pearls: Recruit the named doctor for safeguarding children as co-lead.
Ask the ED IT lead for a free-text search of 'bruise' in under-1s.
Use the local safeguarding partnership bruising protocol for the referral steps.
effort: ~30 min per 10 attendances from ED and paediatric notes

question: What proportion of adults with suspected neutropenic sepsis receive their first dose of intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of arrival at hospital?
why: Neutropenic sepsis kills quickly and delay is the main modifiable factor. The library holds two closed loops, with baselines of 15% and well below target [6435][8112]; most units have never re-measured after their first project.

standard.source: NICE CG151 rec 1.4.1.1 (2012, updated 2024)
standard.wording: Treat suspected neutropenic sepsis as an acute medical emergency and offer empiric antibiotic therapy immediately.

pass: First dose of intravenous empiric antibiotic given (administration time on the drug chart or EPR) within 60 minutes of the arrival time, or of the time the patient became unwell if already an inpatient. The 60-minute limit is the audit's measure of 'immediately'.
population: Adults (18+) who had systemic anticancer treatment in the last 6 weeks and presented with fever or were unwell and were treated as suspected neutropenic sepsis. Exclude patients whose antibiotics were started before arrival and those on end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive episodes over the last 3–4 months (ED, acute medical unit, oncology/haematology wards and assessment unit).
data_source: Acute oncology or chemotherapy helpline log and ED system for cases; ED arrival time from the ED system; antibiotic administration time from the drug chart or EPR; neutrophil count from the results system.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
ED or assessment unit arrival, or time of deterioration for inpatients
e.g. no cannula, waiting for bloods, not triaged as sepsis

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Introduce a patient group direction so the triage or assessment-unit nurse gives the first dose of piperacillin with tazobactam without waiting for a doctor or a neutrophil count.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive episodes, same template and same settings.
close_loop: Present at the cancer services and ED governance meetings with the acute oncology lead. If it works, keep the PGD, add door-to-needle time to the acute oncology monthly dashboard and include PGD sign-off in ED nurse induction.
evidence: [6435] oncology, UK: antibiotics within 60 min 15% → 95% (care pathway plus PGD for nurse-led first dose)
[8112] acute medicine, UK: antibiotics within 1 hour reached only 60% after training and several initiatives
[6356] acute medicine: Sepsis Six management 1% → 67% (trust protocol and teamwork)
pitfalls: Arrival time and administration time sit in different systems → agree before cycle 1 which timestamp counts, and use administration time only.
Patients who were never neutropenic get excluded later, changing the denominator → include all treated as suspected neutropenic sepsis and report confirmed cases separately.
ED nurses may object to a PGD they have not been trained on → agree the PGD with pharmacy and the ED nurse educator before launch.
Gains fade when the audit team rotates → hand the dashboard to the acute oncology nurse team.
pearls: Recruit the acute oncology nurse; they already see most of these patients within 24 hours.
Stock piperacillin with tazobactam in the ED resus cupboard so the dose is not delayed by pharmacy.
Ask the chemotherapy unit to give patients an alert card to show at triage.
Report median minutes as well as the percentage so small improvements are visible.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from ED system and EPR

question: What proportion of adults treated for suspected neutropenic sepsis receive no aminoglycoside in their initial empiric antibiotic regimen, unless a reason is documented?
why: Adding gentamicin adds kidney and hearing toxicity with no survival benefit, yet many local sepsis protocols still pair it with other agents. No audit of aminoglycoside use in neutropenic sepsis has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG151 rec 1.4.3.2 (2012, updated 2024)
standard.wording: Do not offer an aminoglycoside, either as monotherapy or in dual therapy, for the initial empiric treatment of suspected neutropenic sepsis unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications.

pass: No aminoglycoside prescribed in the first 24 hours of empiric treatment, or an aminoglycoside given with a patient-specific or microbiological reason written in the notes (e.g. penicillin allergy regimen, known resistant organism, septic shock per local policy).
population: Adults (18+) receiving anticancer treatment who were started on intravenous empiric antibiotics for suspected neutropenic sepsis. Exclude patients already on antibiotics for another infection.
sample: 40 consecutive episodes over the last 3–4 months.
data_source: Acute oncology log or ED coding for cases; drug chart or EPR for antibiotics in the first 24 hours; medical notes for the documented reason; allergy record.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
All agents given in the first 24 hours

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Remove gentamicin from the neutropenic sepsis antibiotic order set and the sepsis page of the local antimicrobial app, leaving piperacillin with tazobactam alone as the default with a separate penicillin-allergy option.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive episodes, same template.
close_loop: Present at the antimicrobial stewardship committee with the oncology pharmacist. If it works, keep the order set and add aminoglycoside use to the stewardship quarterly report.
evidence: [7660] regional oncology centre: correct peri-procedural antibiotics 93% → 96% (teaching and guideline access)
[2465] general surgery: antibiotic stop/review date 56% → 61.1% (email and posters only)
[6661] ENT: guideline change moved empirical drops to the agreed choice in 24 of 25 cases
pitfalls: Local policy may still recommend gentamicin for shock or allergy → agree the local exceptions with microbiology before cycle 1 and count them as passes.
ED sepsis protocols override the oncology guideline → change the ED sepsis page at the same time.
Small numbers if few patients get gentamicin → report the count as well as the percentage.
Microbiologists may object without local resistance data → bring the latest bacteraemia sensitivity report to the meeting.
pearls: Recruit the oncology or antimicrobial pharmacist; they can check every new episode within 24 hours.
Check the penicillin-allergy regimen at the same time so the fix does not leave a gap.
Share one-page results with ED and acute medicine, where most first doses are prescribed.
Build the order set so the default is the correct regimen with one click.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPR

question: What proportion of adults with confirmed neutropenic sepsis have a validated risk score (such as MASCC) documented within 24 hours of presentation?
why: Without a risk score, low-risk patients cannot be stepped down to oral or outpatient treatment and stay in hospital longer. The one audit in the library found 61.1% were low risk by MASCC but did not measure scoring or close the loop [7845].

standard.source: NICE CG151 rec 1.5.1.1 (2012, updated 2024)
standard.wording: A healthcare professional with competence in managing complications of anticancer treatment should assess the patient's risk of septic complications within 24 hours of presentation to secondary or tertiary care, basing the risk assessment on presentation features and using a validated risk scoring system.

pass: A named validated score (MASCC or CISNE) with its total written in the notes or EPR within 24 hours of arrival.
population: Adults (18+) receiving anticancer treatment with confirmed neutropenic sepsis (neutrophils 0.5×10⁹/L or lower plus fever or signs of sepsis). Exclude patients on end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive confirmed episodes over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: Acute oncology log for cases; medical and acute oncology notes or EPR for the score and time; results system for neutrophil count.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory MASCC score field to the acute oncology assessment form in the EPR, completed at the first acute oncology review.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive confirmed episodes, same template.
close_loop: Present at the cancer services governance meeting. If it works, keep the form field and report the proportion of low-risk patients switched to oral antibiotics as the next measure.
evidence: [7845] UK cancer centre: 61.1% of admissions were low risk by MASCC; median stay 6 v 8 days (no loop)
[2712] general surgery: severity score in acute pancreatitis 10% → 80% (printed score added to clerking)
[6435] oncology: care pathway with ward documentation took first-dose antibiotic timing from 15% to 95%
pitfalls: Scores written by the medical team before neutrophils are known → count only scores recorded after the count is available.
Weekend admissions without acute oncology cover → record day of admission and report weekends separately.
Staff tick 'low risk' without a number → a pass needs the named score and its total.
The field is added but nobody acts on it → track step-down to oral antibiotics in the re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the acute oncology nurse specialist to own the field.
Print the MASCC score on the back of the neutropenic sepsis pathway so it is scored at the bedside.
Agree with consultants before cycle 1 which score counts as validated.
Link the score to a one-line step-down plan so it has a purpose.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPR

question: What proportion of adults starting a new course of chemotherapy have documented written and verbal information on neutropenic sepsis and the 24-hour oncology helpline before cycle 1?
why: Patients who do not know the warning signs or the helpline number arrive late with sepsis. No audit of pre-treatment neutropenic sepsis information has been published in the library; the nearest oncology information audit is from 2003 [4328].

standard.source: NICE CG151 rec 1.1.1.1 (2012, updated 2024)
standard.wording: Provide patients having anticancer treatment and their carers with written and oral information, both before starting and throughout their anticancer treatment, on: neutropenic sepsis; how and when to contact 24-hour specialist oncology advice; how and when to seek emergency care.

pass: The pre-treatment consultation, consent form or chemotherapy nurse assessment records that neutropenic sepsis was explained, a written leaflet or alert card with the 24-hour helpline number was given, and this was dated before the first dose.
population: Adults (18+) starting a new line of intravenous or oral chemotherapy. Exclude patients who only receive hormone therapy.
sample: 40 consecutive new starts over the last 2 months.
data_source: Chemotherapy e-prescribing system (e.g. ChemoCare) for new starts; consent form and chemotherapy pre-assessment record for information given; date of first dose from the prescribing system.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion: all three before first dose

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a required 'neutropenic sepsis information and alert card given' tick box, with date, to the chemotherapy pre-assessment template that must be completed before cycle 1 is released.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new starts, same template.
close_loop: Present at the chemotherapy unit and cancer services meeting. If it works, keep the tick box and audit a sample each quarter with the chemotherapy nurse lead.
evidence: [4328] oncology: standardised nurse-led written chemotherapy information improved reported patient information
[2609] urology: patient leaflet given 30% → 80% (email to consultants and registrars)
[8056] ED early-pregnancy bleeding: leaflet provision 19% → 81% (leaflet access and reminders)
pitfalls: Information is given but written in a place you do not search → list every document type before cycle 1 (consent form, nurse assessment, clinic letter).
Oral chemotherapy started in clinic by a different team → include oral starts and record the team.
Nurses object to another tick box → replace a free-text field rather than adding a new page.
Leaflet stock runs out → ask the unit manager to keep alert cards with the consent packs.
pearls: Recruit the chemotherapy nurse lead; they run pre-assessment.
Use the UKONS or local alert card so the helpline number is always the same.
Check oral chemotherapy clinics as well; they are often missed.
Ask two patients at the re-audit to show you their card; it makes the result real for staff.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from chemotherapy records

question: What proportion of adults starting rituximab for a haematological cancer have hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody results available before the first dose?
why: Hepatitis B reactivation after rituximab can cause fatal liver failure, and prophylaxis is only possible if serology is known before treatment. The library has one rituximab pre-infusion checklist audit (43.5% → 93.75%) but none in haematology [7550].

standard.source: NICE CG165 rec 1.5.48 (2013, updated 2017)
standard.wording: In people who are HBsAg negative and anti-HBc positive (regardless of anti-HBs status) and are starting rituximab or other B cell-depleting therapies: offer prophylaxis with lamivudine; start prophylaxis before beginning immunosuppressive therapy and continue for a minimum of 6 months after stopping immunosuppressive therapy.

pass: Both HBsAg and anti-HBc results reported on the results system before the date of the first rituximab dose.

question: What proportion of adults starting fluorouracil or capecitabine have a DPD deficiency test result documented before the first dose?
why: People with DPD deficiency can die from standard doses of fluoropyrimidines, which are among the most used cancer drugs. No audit of pre-treatment DPD testing has been published in the library.

standard.source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2020
standard.wording: Patients with complete or partial dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency are at increased risk of severe and fatal toxicity during treatment with these medicines. All patients should be tested for DPD deficiency before initiation to minimise the risk of these reactions.

pass: A DPYD genotype (or DPD phenotype) result is on the results system or in the notes, dated before the first dose of intravenous fluorouracil or capecitabine.
population: Adults (18+) starting intravenous fluorouracil or oral capecitabine for any cancer. Exclude topical fluorouracil and patients previously treated with a fluoropyrimidine.
sample: 40 consecutive new starts over the last 3 months.
data_source: Chemotherapy e-prescribing system for new starts and first-dose date; genetics or pathology results system for DPYD result and report date; prescription for dose adjustment.

reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new starts, same template.
close_loop: Present at the chemotherapy/SACT safety group. If it works, keep the hard stop and add DPYD turnaround time to the SACT dashboard.

question: What proportion of adults given a non-urgent red cell transfusion on medical or haematology wards have a documented discussion of the reason, risks and alternatives before the transfusion starts?
why: The national audit found consent documented in only 43% of notes, and only 38% of patients recalled hearing about risks [6543]. The library has surgical consent audits but no closed loop in medical patients.

standard.source: NICE NG24 recs 1.14.2 and 1.14.3 (2015, updated 2026)
standard.wording: Provide verbal and written information to people who may have or who have had a transfusion, and their family members or carers (as appropriate), explaining: the reason for the transfusion; the risks and benefits; the transfusion process; any transfusion needs specific to them; any alternatives that are available, and how they might reduce their need for a transfusion; that they are no longer eligible to donate blood; that they are encouraged to ask questions. [2015] Document discussions in the patient's notes. [2015]

pass: Before the first unit is started, the notes or EPR record the reason for transfusion, the risks discussed and any alternatives discussed (or a note that the patient lacked capacity and a best-interests decision was made).
population: Adults (18+) on medical, elderly care or haematology wards given a planned (non-emergency) red cell transfusion. Exclude major haemorrhage and patients on a chronic transfusion programme with a signed long-term consent.
sample: 40 consecutive transfusion episodes over the last 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Blood bank issue list for cases; medical notes, EPR or transfusion prescription for the consent record and time; transfusion record for start time.

reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive episodes on the same wards, same template.
close_loop: Present at the hospital transfusion committee with the transfusion practitioner. If it works, roll the consent section out to surgical wards and add it to the annual transfusion audit programme.

[2584] general surgery: transfusion risk on consent 0% → 71.4% (EIDO leaflets and induction teaching)

Out-of-hours transfusions have poorer documentation → report in-hours and out-of-hours separately.
Juniors say it takes too long → keep the section to four tick boxes and one free-text line.
Patients without capacity are counted as fails → accept a documented best-interests decision.
