Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is later removed in an IT update → confirm it remains mandatory at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus/immunisation lead nurse as the audit lead, combining with the hepatitis B/C testing audit for efficiency.
Agree the accelerated vaccination schedule and handover process for short stays with the pharmacy and community hepatitis service before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report vaccination offer rates at the health and justice partnership board to keep this prioritised after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record
pass: The reception health record documents that hepatitis B vaccination was offered, with the outcome recorded (accepted and first dose given, declined, or already fully vaccinated).

question: What proportion of people entering prison who report injecting drug use in the last month have their injection sites checked and are referred to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management?
why: Injecting drug use carries specific risks (site infection, overdose, blood-borne virus transmission) that require a physical check and a clear referral pathway distinct from simply recording drug use history. No audit in corpus of injection site checking and referral completion at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.4 (table 1, item 14) (2016)
standard.wording: If the person has used intravenous drugs, check them for injection sites. Refer them to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management and they need immediate support.

population: All new receptions reporting intravenous drug use in the last month over the audit period. Exclude people already actively engaged with the prison substance misuse service from a very recent previous custodial episode.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting intravenous drug use over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
data_source: First-stage assessment record, substance misuse service referral log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'injection sites checked' field to the first-stage assessment template for anyone reporting intravenous drug use, with a direct one-click referral to substance misuse services built in.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception records and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison substance misuse governance meeting; if the mandatory field and one-click referral work, embed them as the standard reception pathway for reported intravenous drug use.
evidence: No audit in corpus of injection site checking and referral completion at prison reception for people reporting intravenous drug use.
pitfalls: Disclosure of intravenous drug use may be incomplete due to stigma or fear of consequences → train staff in a non-judgemental, harm-reduction approach to improve disclosure.
Physical examination for injection sites requires appropriate privacy and consent → confirm the examination process respects dignity and consent before cycle 1.
Injection site infections may need urgent same-day medical review, not just a substance misuse referral → ensure the pathway includes an option for urgent medical assessment.
Substance misuse service capacity may limit rapid referral response → report referral-to-seen time as a secondary measure.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is bypassed under reception time pressure → monitor compliance at re-audit, not just presence of the field.
pearls: Recruit the prison substance misuse lead nurse and reception team jointly.
Agree the examination and consent process with the clinical lead before cycle 1.
Use the same reporting definition (intravenous drug use in the last month) at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report results at the substance misuse governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the reception record and referral log
pass: For a person reporting intravenous drug use in the last month, the record shows injection sites were physically checked, and, where there were concerns about immediate clinical management, a referral to substance misuse services was made at, or immediately after, first-stage assessment.

question: What proportion of adults with hypertension aged 80 and over on antihypertensive treatment have a clinic blood pressure below 150/90 mmHg at their most recent reading?
why: Older patients have a different, less strict blood pressure target that accounts for the balance of benefit and harm from tighter control, but this age-specific target is not always distinguished from the under-80 target in routine practice audits. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets the NG136 clinic BP target for adults aged 80 and over.

standard.source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.21 (2019, amended 2022)
standard.wording: For adults with hypertension aged 80 and over, reduce clinic blood pressure to below 150/90 mmHg and ensure that it is maintained below that level. Use clinical judgement for people with frailty or multimorbidity.

population: Adults aged 80 and over on the practice hypertension register, on one or more antihypertensive medicines for at least 3 months, with a clinic BP reading in the last 12 months. Exclude patients with type 1 diabetes or severe CKD, who have a different NG136 table 2 target.
sample: 40 consecutive patients aged 80 and over from the hypertension register, or all if fewer.
data_source: Practice hypertension register, GP clinical system BP readings, frailty coding.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an age- and frailty-aware target display to the hypertension review template so clinicians see the correct NG136 target (under-80, 80-and-over, or individualised for frailty) automatically rather than applying a single blanket target.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/frailty meeting; if the age-aware target display improves appropriate target-setting, keep it live for all hypertension reviews.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of NG136 clinic blood pressure target achievement in adults aged 80 and over.
pitfalls: Applying the under-80 target to older patients can lead to inappropriate over-treatment and falls risk → make sure the template clearly separates the two age-based targets.
Frailty coding is often incomplete, making it hard to identify who needs an individualised target → improve frailty coding as part of this audit, not as an afterthought.
Postural hypotension should be checked in this age group per NG136 1.4.16 → include a postural BP check alongside the target assessment.
A single high reading may not reflect true control → use the most recent recorded reading but flag for re-check rather than treating one value as definitive.
Improvement may fade if the age-aware display is not maintained after an EPR update → confirm it remains accurate at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's frailty or elderly care lead GP to champion the age-aware target display.
Agree the frailty definition and individualised target-setting process with the whole team before cycle 1.
Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report target-achievement rates at the QOF/frailty meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the hypertension register and BP readings
pass: The most recent clinic blood pressure reading in the last 12 months is below 150/90 mmHg, or, for patients with frailty or multimorbidity, a documented clinical judgement is recorded explaining a different individualised target.

question: What proportion of stable patients with atrial fibrillation taking warfarin have their time in therapeutic range discussed, with the option of switching to a direct-acting oral anticoagulant, at their most recent routine anticoagulation review?
why: Patients remaining on warfarin despite poor anticoagulation control may benefit from switching to a DOAC, but this discussion depends on time in therapeutic range being calculated and reviewed, which is easy to omit from a routine INR check. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets this specific NG196 recommendation on warfarin review and switching.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.6.6 (2021)
standard.wording: For adults with atrial fibrillation who are already taking a vitamin K antagonist and are stable, continue with their current medication and discuss the option of switching treatment at their next routine appointment, taking into account the person's time in therapeutic range.

population: Adults with atrial fibrillation on warfarin under the practice's or anticoagulation clinic's routine review, with a review in the last 12 months. Exclude patients with a mechanical heart valve or other indication requiring warfarin specifically.
sample: 40 consecutive warfarin patients with a routine review in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: Anticoagulation clinic or practice warfarin register, INR monitoring records, consultation notes.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic time-in-therapeutic-range calculation to the anticoagulation review template, with a mandatory 'DOAC switch discussed: yes/outcome' field that cannot be left blank at routine review.
reaudit: At 6 months, same warfarin register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's anticoagulation/QOF meeting; if the mandatory field improves discussion rates, keep it live for every routine warfarin review.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of NG196 warfarin review and DOAC-switch discussion completion.
pitfalls: Time in therapeutic range calculation requires several recent INR results and a recognised method (for example, Rosendaal) → agree the calculation method and data source with the anticoagulation service before cycle 1.

Patients who are genuinely well controlled and prefer warfarin should still have the discussion documented, even if the outcome is to continue warfarin → audit that the discussion happened, not just the outcome.
Anticoagulation monitoring may be run by a community service outside the GP record → confirm data-sharing arrangements before starting.
Some patients have valid reasons to avoid a DOAC (for example, renal function, cost of monitoring not relevant) → record these clearly rather than treating as non-compliance.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is skipped when reviews are done quickly → spot-check consultation quality at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's anticoagulation lead GP or pharmacist, or the community anticoagulation service, to champion the mandatory field.
Agree the time-in-therapeutic-range calculation method before cycle 1 so results are comparable.
Use the same warfarin register extraction method at re-audit.
Report discussion completion rates at the anticoagulation/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the warfarin register and consultation notes
pass: At the most recent routine anticoagulation review, the patient's time in therapeutic range is calculated (or estimated from recent INR results) and a documented discussion of the option to switch to a DOAC has taken place, regardless of the outcome of that discussion.

question: What proportion of patients on the asthma register who have been dispensed 6 or more short-acting beta agonist (SABA) inhalers in the last 12 months have a documented clinical review of the reasons for overuse?
why: Heavy SABA use is a marker of poor asthma control and increased risk of a fatal or near-fatal attack, but a high dispensing count can go unnoticed if no one reviews repeat prescribing data specifically for this pattern. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets clinical review triggered by SABA over-use volume (as opposed to switching the default prescribing pathway, covered elsewhere in the library).

standard.source: NICE NG245 Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and management (BTS/NICE/SIGN), rec 1.6.1 (2024)
standard.wording: Take into account and try to address the possible reasons for uncontrolled asthma before starting or adjusting medicines for asthma in adults, young people and children. These may include: alternative diagnoses or comorbidities; suboptimal adherence; suboptimal inhaler technique; smoking (active or passive), including vaping using e-cigarettes; occupational or environmental exposures.

population: Patients aged 12 and over on the asthma register dispensed 6 or more SABA inhalers in the last 12 months, identified from the prescribing system. Exclude patients under specialist severe asthma service review with their own monitoring pathway.
sample: 40 consecutive patients meeting the SABA over-use threshold over the last 6 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Prescribing dispensing data, asthma register, consultation templates.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Run a monthly practice search flagging patients reaching the 6-SABA-inhaler threshold, generating an automatic task for a respiratory review appointment.
reaudit: At 6 months, same prescribing search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's respiratory/QOF meeting; if the monthly search prompts timely review, add it to the standing list of prescribing safety searches.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of clinical review triggered by SABA over-use volume, distinct from prescribing-default switch audits already in the library.
pitfalls: Dispensing data may lag behind actual use if patients stockpile inhalers → use dispensing counts as a prompt for review, not a precise measure of use.
Patients may obtain inhalers from more than one source (for example, online pharmacy) → note this as a limitation when interpreting results.
A review may happen but not address all relevant factors → audit the content of the review, not just its occurrence.
Some patients with legitimately severe asthma may need frequent SABA under specialist guidance → exclude those under active severe asthma service review.
Improvement may fade if the monthly search stops running after a system change → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory lead nurse or pharmacist to run the monthly search and lead reviews.
Agree the 6-inhaler threshold and review template content with the team before cycle 1.
Use the same prescribing search method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report over-use flags and review completion at the respiratory/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after staff rotate.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prescribing search and consultation templates
pass: A patient dispensed 6 or more SABA inhalers in the last 12 months has a documented clinical review addressing possible reasons for overuse (inhaler technique, adherence, alternative diagnoses, smoking/vaping, triggers) within 8 weeks of reaching that threshold.

question: What proportion of adults with a new diagnosis of chronic kidney disease have their GFR and ACR category jointly recorded and used to state their risk of adverse outcomes in the record?
why: NICE's CKD classification combines GFR and ACR categories into a single risk grid, but practices commonly record the two results without translating them into the combined risk category that should guide monitoring frequency and referral. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets whether the combined GFR/ACR risk classification (as opposed to the individual test results) is documented.

standard.source: NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, rec 1.2.1 (2014)
standard.wording: Classify CKD in adults using a combination of GFR and ACR categories (as described in table 1). Be aware that: increased ACR is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes; decreased GFR is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes; increased ACR and decreased GFR in combination multiply the risk of adverse outcomes.

population: Adults with a coded diagnosis of CKD (stage 3a or above, or stage 1-2 with proteinuria) with a GFR and ACR result in the last 12 months. Exclude patients under active nephrology follow-up whose classification is documented in specialist correspondence rather than the GP record.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the CKD register, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: CKD register, GP clinical system, laboratory results, annual review template.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic GFR/ACR risk-grid calculator to the CKD annual review template that displays the combined NICE risk category as soon as both results are entered, rather than requiring manual look-up of table 1.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/long-term conditions meeting; if the automatic calculator improves documentation, keep it as the default CKD annual review tool.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of combined GFR/ACR risk classification documentation under NG203 rec 1.2.1.
pitfalls: GFR and ACR results may be recorded on different dates and never brought together in one place → the calculator should pull the most recent value of each, regardless of date, and flag if either is more than 12 months old.
Staff may record the individual numeric results without translating them into the categorical grid → make the categorical output, not just the raw numbers, the audited item.
Patients under nephrology may have their classification documented only in hospital letters → check for this before counting as a gap in the GP record.
A single ACR result in category A2/A3 needs confirmation before acting on it clinically, per NICE → note this distinction in staff training so classification and clinical action are not conflated.
Improvement may fade if the calculator is not maintained after an EPR template change → confirm it remains functional at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's CKD lead nurse or clinical pharmacist to champion the automatic calculator.
Agree the calculator's exact grid values with NICE table 1 before building it, to avoid errors.
Use the same CKD register definition at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report documentation rates at the QOF/long-term conditions meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the CKD register and laboratory results
pass: The record documents both the GFR category (G1-G5) and ACR category (A1-A3) together, with the combined NICE risk category (low, moderate, high or very high) stated, at the time of diagnosis or most recent annual review.

question: What proportion of patients on shared-care DMARD monitoring have their individual risk factors for toxicity (renal function, age, alcohol use, interacting medicines) reviewed at least annually, with monitoring frequency adjusted accordingly?
why: DMARD shared care guidance expects monitoring frequency to be individualised to risk, not applied as a single fixed interval for everyone, but an annual risk review distinct from the routine blood test cycle is easy to omit. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets the annual DMARD toxicity risk review as a discrete step separate from routine blood monitoring.

standard.source: British Society for Rheumatology shared care guidance for DMARD monitoring (as summarised by NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service)
standard.wording: Risk factors for DMARD toxicity should be reviewed at least annually, adjusting the frequency of monitoring according to the level of risk identified. A shared care protocol should be agreed upon delineating the responsibilities of each party.

population: Patients on the practice's shared-care DMARD register on treatment for 12 months or more. Exclude patients within their first year of treatment, who follow a different, more frequent initial monitoring schedule.
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the shared-care DMARD register on treatment for over 12 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Shared-care DMARD register, GP consultation and annual review templates, laboratory results.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a dedicated 'annual DMARD risk review' template, separate from the routine blood monitoring recall, that prompts the reviewing clinician to check renal trend, age, alcohol use and new interacting prescriptions once a year for every shared-care DMARD patient.
reaudit: At 12 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's medicines optimisation/QOF meeting; if the dedicated template improves completion, keep it as a standing annual task alongside routine monitoring.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of the annual DMARD toxicity risk review as a discrete step from routine blood monitoring.
pitfalls: Routine blood monitoring can be mistaken for the full annual risk review, when it only covers some of the required factors → keep the two as clearly separate template items.

Interacting medicines (for example, trimethoprim prescribed by an out-of-hours service) may not trigger an alert if prescribed outside the practice → include a manual interaction check as part of the annual review.
Alcohol intake may be under-reported → use a standard, non-judgemental question as part of the review.
Shared care responsibilities between specialist and GP may be unclear for who leads the annual risk review → confirm this explicitly in the shared care agreement before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade if the annual review template is not linked to a recall system → build in an automatic annual reminder.
pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the annual risk review process.
Agree with the rheumatology or gastroenterology shared care team which factors and thresholds to use before cycle 1.
Use the same DMARD register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report annual review completion at the medicines optimisation meeting to sustain the process after staff rotate.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the DMARD register and consultation templates
pass: A documented annual review of individual toxicity risk factors (renal function trend, age, alcohol intake, interacting medicines such as trimethoprim or NSAIDs) is recorded, with the monitoring interval confirmed as appropriate or adjusted as a result.

question: What proportion of ambulance-to-emergency-department patient handovers are completed within 15 minutes of the ambulance arriving?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance handover timing has been published in the library, despite this being the single most reported pre-hospital patient-safety problem in England.

standard.source: AACE, Hospital Handovers (webpage, accessed 2026)
standard.wording: The nationally defined target for hospitals included in the NHS Standard Contract states that all handovers between ambulance and A&E must take place within 15 minutes, with none waiting more than 30 minutes.

population: Inclusion: all adult and paediatric patients brought to the ED by a NHS ambulance over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients brought by non-emergency patient transport service, self-presenting or brought by police/other agency
sample: 50 consecutive ambulance arrivals over 2 weeks, using the ambulance service's own arrival timestamp and the ED's handover-accepted timestamp
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record (arrival time) matched to the ED tracking system (handover-accepted or 'patient in department' time)

template.note: number of patients in the department at the time of arrival, if available

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a rapid 'streaming and handover' nurse and a cohorting bay so incoming ambulances are met at the door, with a visible countdown clock at the ambulance entrance and an internal professional standard escalation when handover passes 30 minutes.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months using the same 2-week sampling window and template
close_loop: Present at the joint ED-ambulance trust liaison meeting; if the streaming nurse role works, make it a permanent rostered post and add handover time to the trust's monthly urgent and emergency care dashboard
evidence: No closed-loop audit of ambulance-to-ED handover timing is in the library; nearest related entries concern ED waiting times and flow
pitfalls: Ambulance and ED clocks are not synchronised → agree a single timestamp source before cycle 1
Small numbers on quiet shifts hide the true delay → sample across day, evening and night shifts
Definition of 'handover accepted' drifts between cycles → lock the definition (first ED clinician contact) in writing with the ambulance trust liaison
Ambulance and nursing staff see this as blame-shifting → present it jointly as a shared flow problem, not a performance league table
Gains fade once the streaming nurse post is not backfilled on leave → build it into the establishment, not a rota extra
pearls: Recruit the ambulance trust liaison officer as a co-presenter before cycle 1
Agree the timestamp definitions with both organisations in writing before data collection starts
Display live handover times on the department screen so staff see the effect of the change in real time
Link the audit to the trust's existing corridor-care or ambulance-queue safety huddle so it does not need a new meeting
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the ambulance and ED electronic records
pass: Ambulance clock-stop (patient accepted by an ED clinician) is within 15 minutes of the ambulance's arrival time recorded on the ambulance electronic patient record

question: What proportion of ambulance pre-alert calls for adult major trauma patients record all the core information items required by the trauma network?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-alert content quality has been published in the library; incomplete pre-alerts delay trauma team assembly and equipment preparation.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: service delivery, rec 1.8.1 (2016)
standard.wording: Record the following in patients with major trauma in pre-hospital settings: ... the ambulance call sign, name of the person taking the call and time of call.

population: Inclusion: all adult patients brought in as a pre-alerted trauma call over a 4-week period. Exclusion: patients arriving unannounced with trauma subsequently identified
sample: 40 consecutive pre-alerted adult trauma calls over 4 weeks
data_source: Trauma call proforma/EPR trauma page compared against the recorded ambulance radio pre-alert message (call recording or written pre-alert sheet)
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the free-text pre-alert radio message with a structured ATMIST (age, time, mechanism, injuries, signs, treatment) proforma shared with the ambulance trust, printed automatically as a trauma call sheet when the pre-alert is logged.
target: ≥90% of pre-alerts complete on all items
reaudit: Re-audit at 4 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the joint trauma network governance meeting with the ambulance trust; embed the ATMIST proforma in both the ambulance despatch system and the ED trauma call sheet if it improves completeness
evidence: ONA-024 and ONA-026 (pelvic fracture care) show ambulance-to-hospital information sharing already matters in this network; no audit of pre-alert content completeness itself is in the library
pitfalls: Radio recordings are hard to retrieve after a few days → agree a retrieval process with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small sample if trauma calls are infrequent → extend the collection window to 6 weeks in a lower-volume unit
Definitions of 'given' vary between reviewers → agree a one-page scoring key before starting
Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the trust's trauma desk lead in designing the proforma
Improvement fades once new crews rotate in → add ATMIST training to ambulance trust induction
pearls: Get sign-off from the trauma network's clinical lead before starting, since the change affects the ambulance trust too
Use existing trauma network governance meetings to close the loop rather than creating a new forum
Pilot the ATMIST proforma on one ambulance station before a wider rollout
Keep the same reviewer for both cycles to reduce scoring drift
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from the trauma proforma and call recordings
pass: The recorded pre-alert (written or on the trauma call proforma) contains mechanism of injury, injuries found, vital signs, treatment given, estimated time of arrival, and the ambulance call sign/name of caller/time of call

question: What proportion of pre-alerted major trauma patients have a trauma team leader and team ready to receive the handover before the patient arrives?
why: No closed-loop audit of trauma team readiness at handover has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: service delivery, recs 1.8.4 and 1.8.5 (2016)
standard.wording: A senior nurse or trauma team leader in the emergency department should receive the pre-alert information and determine the level of trauma team response according to agreed and written local guidelines. The trauma team leader should be easily identifiable to receive the handover and the trauma team ready to receive the information.

population: Inclusion: all pre-alerted adult and paediatric trauma calls over 4 weeks. Exclusion: unannounced trauma arrivals
sample: 40 consecutive pre-alerted trauma calls over 4 weeks
data_source: Trauma call log/EPR trauma page and direct observation or debrief sheet completed by the trauma team leader
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a mandatory trauma team leader tabard and a pre-arrival checklist (bay, airway trolley, blood products requested, team roles assigned) signed off by the TTL before the patient arrives, triggered automatically by the pre-alert bleep.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance meeting; if the checklist works, add it as a mandatory step in the trauma call bleep system
evidence: No audit of trauma team readiness at handover is in the library; ONA-024/ONA-026 show related pelvic-trauma pathway gaps
pitfalls: Readiness is hard to verify retrospectively → use direct observation for at least half the sample
Staff may complete the checklist after the event to look compliant → timestamp the checklist electronically
Small numbers if major trauma calls are rare → extend the collection window
Rota gaps mean no consultant TTL is available out of hours → escalate staffing gaps found by the audit to rota planning
Improvement fades once the tabard goes missing → keep a spare stock in the resus room
pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator to help design and pilot the checklist
Agree with nursing and ED consultant leads before cycle 1 who owns team readiness
Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the audit tool the same across cycles so the readiness rate is directly comparable
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the trauma log and direct observation
pass: A named trauma team leader is recorded as having received the pre-alert, and the trauma bay/team is documented as ready (equipment checked, team present) before the patient's arrival

question: What proportion of adults with major trauma needing pre-hospital rapid sequence induction have it started within 45 minutes of the initial 999 call?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-hospital RSI timing has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.2.3 (2016)
standard.wording: Aim to perform RSI as soon as possible and within 45 minutes of the initial call to the emergency services, preferably at the scene of the incident.

population: Inclusion: adults with major trauma who cannot maintain their own airway and/or ventilation and who receive pre-hospital RSI by a critical care team. Exclusion: RSI performed in hospital only
sample: 20 consecutive pre-hospital RSIs over 3 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance/critical care paramedic or HEMS patient report form, cross-checked against the 999 call log time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Feed back individual case timelines to the regional critical care/HEMS desk at the monthly trauma governance meeting, with a standard 'time to RSI' field added to the electronic patient report form so delays are flagged automatically.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the regional trauma network's pre-hospital governance meeting; if the ePR field works, ask the ambulance trust to make it a standard audit field
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital RSI timing is in the library; ONA-026 (pelvic fracture TXA timing) shows the same network already audits pre-hospital time-critical interventions
pitfalls: 999 call time and drug administration time are recorded on different systems → agree the linkage method with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small numbers because pre-hospital RSI is rare → pool data across a longer period or across the regional network
Case-mix varies (rural versus urban scenes) → record scene location type to interpret outliers
Crews may feel individually blamed for system delays → present aggregated, anonymised timelines only
Improvement is not sustained after staff turnover on the critical care desk → build the RSI-time review into the desk's standard handover
pearls: Agree data-sharing with the ambulance/critical care service before starting, since most of the data sits outside the hospital
Recruit the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead as co-owner of the audit
Use the existing trauma governance meeting to close the loop
Keep case numbers pooled across the network if a single trust's volume is too small to interpret alone
effort: ~30 min per case from the ambulance/HEMS patient report form
pass: Time from the initial 999 call to RSI drug administration (scene or en route) is 45 minutes or less

question: What proportion of adults with active pre-hospital haemorrhage who receive intravenous fluid are given crystalloid only when blood components are not available?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-hospital fluid choice in active bleeding has been published in the library; inappropriate crystalloid use can worsen coagulopathy.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.5.22 (2016)
standard.wording: In pre-hospital settings only use crystalloids to replace fluid volume in patients with active bleeding if blood components are not available.

population: Inclusion: adults with active bleeding from trauma who receive any IV fluid pre-hospital. Exclusion: patients with no fluid given, or fluid given only after blood products started
sample: 30 consecutive pre-hospital trauma patients with active bleeding who received IV fluid, over 3 months
data_source: Ambulance/HEMS patient report form fluid administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'blood available: yes/no, reason for crystalloid' field to the ambulance/HEMS electronic patient report form fluid section, and reinforce the crystalloid-avoidance message in the trauma network's annual pre-hospital update training.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the regional trauma network pre-hospital governance meeting; embed the mandatory field in the ambulance ePR if it improves practice
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital fluid choice in active bleeding is in the library; ONA-026 (pelvic fracture TXA) is the nearest related pre-hospital trauma audit
pitfalls: Free-text fluid records make coding inconsistent → agree a coding key with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Blood component availability varies by crew type, confounding comparisons → record crew type for every case
Small numbers if pre-hospital blood is well established locally → pool across the network
Crews may see this as second-guessing a scene decision → frame feedback as system learning, not individual performance
Gains fade if new crews are not told about the change → add to annual mandatory pre-hospital training
pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's clinical governance lead from the start
Use the trauma network's existing pre-hospital blood programme meeting to close the loop
Keep the same fluid-choice coding key for both cycles
Share results with crews as a learning bulletin, not a performance table
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the ambulance/HEMS patient report form
pass: Crystalloid is given to a bleeding trauma patient only when the ambulance/HEMS crew records that blood components were not carried or not available at the time

question: What proportion of adults with a head injury and a GCS of 12 or less, and no suspected extracranial bleeding, receive tranexamic acid within 2 hours of injury?
why: No closed-loop audit of tranexamic acid timing in isolated head injury has been published in the library; the nearest related entries concern TXA in pelvic fracture.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.17 (2023)
standard.wording: For people with a head injury and a GCS score of 12 or less who are not thought to have active extracranial bleeding, consider: a 2 g intravenous bolus injection of tranexamic acid for people 16 and over ... Give the tranexamic acid as soon as possible within 2 hours of the injury, in the pre-hospital or hospital setting and before imaging.

population: Inclusion: adults with GCS 12 or less after head injury and no suspected extracranial bleeding, seen pre-hospital or in ED within 2 hours of injury. Exclusion: known contraindication documented at triage (e.g. injury time unknown, >2 hours ago)
sample: 30 consecutive eligible adults over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form and ED trauma clerking, cross-checked against the recorded time of injury and time of TXA administration
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add TXA as a default prompt on both the ambulance head injury pathway card and the ED trauma order set whenever GCS 12 or less is entered without a bleeding flag, with the 2-hour deadline shown on the prompt.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance meeting; if the prompt works, add it to both the ambulance clinical decision support tool and the ED EPR trauma order set permanently
evidence: ONA-026 (pelvic fracture TXA within 1 hour) shows a closed-loop audit of TXA timing already works in this network for a different injury; no equivalent audit exists for isolated head injury
pitfalls: Time of injury is often uncertain → exclude or flag cases with an estimated rather than witnessed injury time
Ambulance and ED records are on separate systems → agree a single audit form covering both before cycle 1
Small numbers in a district general hospital → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Clinicians may worry about giving TXA before imaging excludes a contraindication → reinforce the NICE wording ('before imaging') in training
Gains fade if the prompt is switched off during a system upgrade → check it after any EPR update
pearls: Agree with the ambulance trust which record system will supply the injury-time and TXA-time fields before starting
Recruit a trauma nurse coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid
Present pooled ambulance and hospital data together so both services see the whole pathway
Keep the same eligibility criteria (GCS ≤12, no extracranial bleeding) across cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and ED records
pass: TXA 2 g IV bolus is given, or a documented reason for not giving it is recorded, within 2 hours of injury

question: What proportion of ambulance patient report forms for head-injured children and adults record a Glasgow Coma Scale score using the correct adult or paediatric version?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance GCS recording accuracy has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.15 (2003)
standard.wording: Ambulance crews and paramedics should be fully trained in the use of the adult and paediatric versions of the GCS and its derived score.

population: Inclusion: all patients conveyed by ambulance after a head injury over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients with no ambulance patient report form available
sample: 40 consecutive ambulance-conveyed head injury patients over 2 weeks
data_source: Ambulance patient report form handed over with the patient, or the ambulance trust's electronic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Feed back examples of incomplete or wrong-version GCS recording to the ambulance trust's clinical education team for inclusion in the next mandatory update training cycle, and add a hard-stop prompt for the paediatric GCS version in the electronic patient report form for patients under 5.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present jointly to the ED and ambulance trust clinical governance leads; if the electronic prompt reduces errors, keep it as a permanent build
evidence: No audit of ambulance GCS recording accuracy is in the library; ONA-163 shows the same trauma network already audits documentation quality for head injury in children
pitfalls: Ambulance and hospital notes may be scored differently by different reviewers → use one trained reviewer for the whole audit
Paediatric cases are infrequent, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period for the under-5 subgroup
Ambulance crews may feel individually singled out → report results in aggregate only
Definitions of 'correct version' can be disputed at the 5-year-old boundary → agree the cut-off with the ambulance trust in advance
Improvement is not sustained after a change of electronic patient record supplier → re-check the prompt after any system change
pearls: Agree access to ambulance patient report forms with the ambulance trust's information governance team before starting
Involve the ambulance trust's clinical education lead in interpreting results
Use existing joint governance meetings rather than creating a new one
Keep the same scoring key across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ambulance patient report form
pass: A GCS score (eye, verbal, motor and total) is recorded on the ambulance patient report form, using the paediatric GCS for children under 5 and the standard GCS for everyone else

question: When ambulance crews identify a safeguarding concern in a patient with a head injury, what proportion of cases have this documented and verbally handed over to the emergency department?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance-to-ED safeguarding handover has been published in the library, despite this being an explicit training requirement.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.16 (2003, amended 2014)
standard.wording: Ambulance crews and paramedics should be trained in the safeguarding of people under 16 and people 16 and over who are vulnerable. They should document and verbally inform emergency department staff of any safeguarding concerns.

population: Inclusion: all patients arriving with a head injury by ambulance whose patient report form flags a safeguarding concern (non-accidental injury suspicion, vulnerable adult, self-neglect, frequent falls in a vulnerable adult) over 3 months. Exclusion: no safeguarding flag on the ambulance form
sample: 20 consecutive flagged cases over 3 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form safeguarding section, matched to the ED clerking/triage note and the trust safeguarding referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'ambulance safeguarding flag received: yes/no, action taken' field to the ED triage template, so a flagged case cannot be booked in without an ED safeguarding decision being recorded.
target: 100% of flagged cases have a documented ED safeguarding decision
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the trust safeguarding committee jointly with the ambulance trust designated safeguarding lead; if the mandatory field works, keep it permanently in the triage template
evidence: No audit of ambulance-to-ED safeguarding handover for head injury is in the library; NNA-089 (adolescent mental health assessment) shows the same department already audits vulnerable-patient pathway gaps
pitfalls: Safeguarding flags on ambulance forms are often free text and easy to miss at triage → make the field mandatory rather than free text
Small numbers given expected low case volume → extend the collection period to 6 months
Information governance restrictions on accessing ambulance safeguarding data → agree data-sharing with the ambulance trust's safeguarding lead first
Staff may under-report to avoid extra paperwork → make the field quick (drop-down, not free text)
Loop closure stalls if the safeguarding committee meets infrequently → agree a fixed re-audit slot on the agenda in advance
pearls: Involve both trusts' safeguarding leads from the outset, since this is a cross-organisational pathway
Use the existing safeguarding committee to close the loop rather than a new meeting
Keep the case definition (types of flag counted) identical across cycles
Share anonymised case learning, not identifiable feedback, with individual crews
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and ED records
pass: Where the ambulance patient report form records a safeguarding concern, the ED clerking or triage note documents that the concern was verbally handed over and an ED safeguarding action was taken (referral, discussion with named nurse, or documented reason not to act)

question: What proportion of adults with suspected acute stroke conveyed by ambulance are admitted directly to a specialist acute stroke unit without first going to a general emergency department bay?
why: No closed-loop audit of direct ambulance-to-stroke-unit conveyance has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, rec 1.3.1 (2008)
standard.wording: Admit everyone with suspected stroke directly to a specialist acute stroke unit after initial assessment, from either the community, the emergency department, or outpatient clinics.

population: Inclusion: adults brought by ambulance with a positive pre-hospital stroke screen (e.g. FAST-positive) over a 4-week period. Exclusion: stroke diagnosed after arrival with no pre-hospital stroke screen documented
sample: 30 consecutive FAST-positive ambulance conveyances over 4 weeks
data_source: Ambulance patient report form (FAST screen result and pre-alert), ED tracking system (bed location) and stroke unit admission log

options: General ED bay then stroke unit
General ED bay only, not admitted to stroke unit

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a direct-conveyance protocol with the ambulance trust so a FAST-positive pre-alert triggers the stroke unit bed to be held and the patient taken straight there (bypassing the general ED cubicle) unless immediate resuscitation is needed.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the stroke network's operational delivery network meeting with ambulance trust representation; embed the direct-conveyance protocol in the ambulance dispatch system if it improves the rate
evidence: NNA-119/NNA-120 (TIA aspirin and CT decision-making) show this network already audits stroke and TIA pathway steps in the ED; no audit of ambulance-to-stroke-unit direct conveyance is in the library
pitfalls: Bed availability on the stroke unit may block direct conveyance regardless of the pathway → record bed availability as a separate field
Small numbers in a unit without a hyperacute stroke service → adjust the pathway definition to the local model of care
FAST-positive pre-alerts may be over- or under-called → cross check against the final stroke/TIA/stroke-mimic diagnosis
ED staff may resist bypassing initial ED assessment → involve ED consultants in agreeing exceptions (e.g. unstable airway) in advance
Gains fade if the stroke unit's bed-holding process is not maintained → review bed-holding capacity at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the direct-conveyance protocol jointly with ambulance, ED and stroke medicine before cycle 1
Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Track bed availability as a confounder so failures to bypass are not all attributed to the pathway
Keep the FAST-positive definition identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and stroke unit records
pass: The patient's first inpatient bed after ambulance arrival is the acute/hyperacute stroke unit, or a documented reason is recorded for going elsewhere (for example, needing immediate resuscitation)

question: What proportion of adults with an ambulance-diagnosed ST-elevation myocardial infarction receive a 300 mg aspirin loading dose before hospital arrival?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-hospital aspirin administration in STEMI has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes, rec 1.1.4 (2010)
standard.wording: Offer people with acute STEMI a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence that they are allergic to it.

population: Inclusion: adults with a pre-hospital 12-lead ECG diagnosis of STEMI conveyed by ambulance over 3 months. Exclusion: cardiac arrest before aspirin could be given
sample: 30 consecutive ambulance-diagnosed STEMI patients over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form medication record, cross-checked with the cardiac catheter laboratory admission proforma
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Feed back cases where aspirin was omitted or delayed to the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead, and add a mandatory 'aspirin given: dose/time or reason not given' field to the ambulance STEMI pathway record.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the cardiac network's primary PCI governance meeting with ambulance trust representation; embed the mandatory field permanently if compliance improves
evidence: NNA-384 (angiography timing in NSTEMI) shows this network already audits ACS pathway timings in hospital; no audit of pre-hospital aspirin administration in STEMI is in the library
pitfalls: Patients who self-medicate with aspirin before the ambulance arrives may be miscounted → record 'already taken' as a separate category
Small numbers of pre-hospital STEMI diagnoses in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network
Allergy documentation is sometimes missing rather than a true contraindication → distinguish 'documented allergy' from 'not recorded'
Crews may feel blamed for a system-level cath lab bottleneck → keep the audit focused on the aspirin step only
Gains fade if the mandatory field is removed in a system update → recheck after any ambulance ePR change
pearls: Agree data access with the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead before starting
Use the cardiac network's existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the STEMI diagnosis definition (ambulance 12-lead ECG criteria) identical across cycles
Share results as a learning bulletin for crews, not a named performance table
effort: ~15 min per case from the ambulance patient report form
pass: 300 mg aspirin is given by the ambulance crew (or already taken and confirmed) before hospital arrival, or a documented allergy/contraindication is recorded

question: What proportion of adults who achieve return of spontaneous circulation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest have their oxygen saturation titrated to 94-98% by the time of ED handover?
why: No closed-loop audit of post-ROSC oxygen titration during ambulance transfer has been published in the library, despite hyperoxaemia and hypoxaemia both being harmful after cardiac arrest.

standard.source: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023)
standard.wording: After ROSC, once SpO2 can be measured reliably or arterial blood gas values are obtained, titrate the inspired oxygen to achieve an arterial oxygen saturation of 94-98% ... Avoid hypoxaemia ... Avoid hyperoxaemia following ROSC.

population: Inclusion: adults with sustained ROSC after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest conveyed by ambulance over 6 months. Exclusion: death before ED arrival, re-arrest during transfer with no further ROSC
sample: 20 consecutive ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form observations chart, cross-checked with the ED resuscitation room record at handover
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'post-ROSC oxygen target 94-98%' prompt to the ambulance cardiac arrest care bundle card and the post-ROSC section of the electronic patient report form, so oxygen is actively titrated down once saturations are reliably measured.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the cardiac arrest network's post-resuscitation care governance meeting with the ambulance trust; embed the prompt permanently in the ambulance care bundle card if it improves the target rate
evidence: No audit of post-ROSC oxygen titration during ambulance transfer is in the library; the nearest related entries concern oxygen prescribing with target saturations in the ED
pitfalls: Pulse oximetry can be unreliable in a cold, shut-down post-arrest patient → record whether the SpO2 reading was judged reliable
Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → extend the collection period or pool with a neighbouring ambulance sector
Crews may keep FiO2 high out of caution → reinforce the harm of hyperoxaemia in training, not just hypoxaemia
Definitions of 'reliable SpO2' vary → agree a working definition with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Gains fade without refresher training after the initial rollout → add to the annual post-resuscitation care update
pearls: Link the audit to the trust's existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes review meeting
Recruit a resuscitation officer from both the ambulance trust and the ED as joint audit leads
Keep the SpO2 target and 'reliable reading' definitions identical for both cycles
Feed results back through the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest governance process, which already exists
effort: ~15 min per case from ambulance and ED resuscitation records
pass: The last recorded SpO2 before ED handover is 94-98%, or a documented reason for a different target is recorded (for example, known chronic respiratory disease with a lower target)

question: What proportion of adults with return of spontaneous circulation after cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause are transported directly to a hospital with 24/7 primary PCI capability?
why: No closed-loop audit of direct conveyance to a cardiac arrest/heart attack centre after ROSC has been published in the library.

standard.source: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023)
standard.wording: Adult patients with a cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac aetiology should be transported directly to a hospital with 24/7 coronary angiography capability.

population: Inclusion: adults with sustained ROSC after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest thought to be of cardiac cause, over 6 months. Exclusion: cardiac arrest with an obvious non-cardiac cause (trauma, drowning, hanging)
sample: 20 consecutive eligible ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form destination decision record and receiving hospital's cardiac arrest centre admission log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a documented destination-decision algorithm with the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest desk so presumed-cardiac ROSC cases bypass the nearest general ED and go directly to the network's 24/7 PCI centre unless airway or scene factors prevent it.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the out-of-hospital cardiac arrest network governance meeting with ambulance trust representation; if the destination algorithm reduces onward transfers, adopt it as standard ambulance dispatch policy
evidence: No audit of direct post-ROSC conveyance to a PCI centre is in the library; NNA-384 (angiography timing in NSTEMI) shows the same network already audits related cardiac pathway timings
pitfalls: Presumed cardiac cause is a judgement call and can be coded inconsistently → agree the coding criteria with ambulance clinicians before cycle 1
Rural areas may have long transfer times to the PCI centre → record transfer distance as a confounder
Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → pool data across the network if a single ambulance sector is too small
Onward inter-hospital transfers add delay and risk if the algorithm is not followed → track onward transfers as a secondary outcome
Improvement is not sustained if the algorithm is not built into ambulance dispatch software → make it a system default rather than a memory-based decision
pearls: Agree the destination algorithm jointly between the ambulance trust and the cardiac network before starting
Use the existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 'presumed cardiac cause' definition identical across both cycles
Track time from ROSC to cath lab as well as destination choice, since it is the outcome that matters clinically
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and cardiac network records
pass: The patient is taken directly to a 24/7 primary PCI centre, or a documented reason for going elsewhere is recorded (for example, airway instability requiring the nearest ED)

question: What proportion of adults with return of spontaneous circulation who remain comatose have active fever prevention (temperature kept below 37.7°C) documented for the first 72 hours?
why: No closed-loop audit of post-ROSC temperature control has been published in the library.

standard.source: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023)
standard.wording: Continuously monitor the core temperature in patients who remain comatose after ROSC. Actively prevent fever (defined as a temperature > 37.7°C) for at least 72 h in post-cardiac arrest patients who remain comatose.

population: Inclusion: adults admitted to critical care remaining comatose after ROSC, over 6 months. Exclusion: death or awakening within 24 hours of admission
sample: 20 consecutive comatose post-ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Critical care observation chart (continuous temperature trend) and drug chart (antipyretic administration)
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'post-ROSC fever prevention (target <37.7°C for 72 hours)' order set to the critical care admission bundle, with a nurse-initiated antipyretic protocol that fires automatically when temperature crosses the threshold.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the critical care and resuscitation joint governance meeting; embed the order set permanently in the critical care EPR if it improves compliance
evidence: No audit of post-ROSC fever prevention is in the library; the nearest related entries concern general post-resuscitation and post-arrest ED care
pitfalls: Continuous core temperature monitoring devices are not always available → record the monitoring method used (core probe, bladder, tympanic)
Small numbers because comatose ROSC admissions are infrequent → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Staff may treat fever reactively rather than proactively → make the order set nurse-initiated so no medical review delay is needed
Definitions of 'active prevention' vary between units → agree what counts (paracetamol, cooling blanket, ice packs) before cycle 1
Gains fade after critical care nursing rotation → include in critical care induction training
pearls: Recruit the critical care outreach or resuscitation officer team to help identify eligible cases prospectively
Use an existing critical care mortality and morbidity or resuscitation governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 37.7°C threshold and monitoring definitions identical across cycles
Track antipyretic administration alongside temperature trend, not temperature alone
effort: ~20 min per case from the critical care observation and drug chart
pass: Core temperature is continuously monitored and stays below 37.7°C throughout the first 72 hours, or an active fever-prevention intervention (antipyretic, cooling device) is documented whenever it rises above that threshold

question: What proportion of adults aged 65 and over attended by an ambulance after a fall, but not conveyed to hospital, are referred for a comprehensive falls assessment?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance non-conveyance falls referral has been published in the library; NNA-083 audits ED-discharged fall patients but not those never brought to hospital at all.

standard.source: NICE NG249 Falls: assessment and prevention in older people and in people 50 and over at higher risk, rec 1.1.3 (2025)
standard.wording: Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and comprehensive falls management ... for people who ... have fallen and cannot get up without help, or ... have had 2 or more falls in the last 12 months.

population: Inclusion: adults aged 65 and over attended by ambulance after a fall and not conveyed to hospital, over a 4-week period. Exclusion: falls with an injury requiring conveyance
sample: 30 consecutive non-conveyed fall attendances over 4 weeks
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record 'not conveyed' outcome and referral field, cross-checked with the community falls service referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'falls service referral: yes/no, reason' field to the ambulance non-conveyance falls pathway, with a direct electronic referral route to the local falls service built into the ambulance ePR.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust and community falls service governance meetings; embed the electronic referral route permanently if it increases uptake
evidence: NNA-083 (ED-discharged fall patients referred for falls assessment) shows this pathway gap already exists at the ED end; no audit of ambulance non-conveyance falls referral is in the library
pitfalls: Non-conveyed falls attendances are not always well documented → agree a minimum dataset with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Falls services vary in how they accept ambulance referrals → confirm the referral route works before auditing uptake
Small numbers if 'not conveyed' coding is inconsistent → review ambulance coding practice first
Ambulance crews under time pressure may skip the referral step → make it a single click in the ePR rather than a phone call
Gains fade if the falls service cannot cope with increased referrals → agree capacity with the falls service before scaling up
pearls: Involve the community falls service lead and the ambulance trust's falls lead together from the start
Use the trust's existing falls prevention steering group to close the loop
Keep the NG249 referral criteria identical across both cycles
Track whether referrals are actually acted on by the falls service, not just made
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from ambulance and falls service records
pass: A referral to a community falls service (or GP with a falls-specific request) is made and documented at the time of the ambulance 'see and treat, not conveyed' episode for a patient meeting the assessment criteria

question: What proportion of ED patients on a time-critical medication (Parkinson's, insulin, anti-epileptic, immunosuppressant, or long-term steroid) receive their next scheduled dose at the usual time while waiting in the department?
why: No closed-loop audit of time-critical medication administration during ED waits has been published in the library, despite an RCEM national safety flash on this exact risk.

standard.source: RCEM Safety Flash: Time Critical Medication (November 2023)
standard.wording: All patients should have time critical medications prescribed and administered at their usual time whilst in the ED.

population: Inclusion: adults identified at triage as taking a time-critical medication (movement disorder, immunomodulator, diabetes, steroid, epilepsy, anticoagulant) with a dose due during their ED stay, over 4 weeks. Exclusion: patients discharged before the next dose was due
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 4 weeks
data_source: ED triage record (time-critical medication flag), drug chart/EPMA administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Display the UKCPA patient-facing poster at reception/triage so patients can flag their own time-critical medicines, add a mandatory 'time-critical medication' triage field that creates a timed EPMA task, and confirm ED pharmacy cover for medicines availability.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting; if the triage flag and pharmacy cover improve compliance, keep both permanently and report results to the trust medication safety group
evidence: No audit of time-critical medication timing in the ED is in the library; NNA-135 (haloperidol ECG before dosing) shows the same department already audits time-critical prescribing safety
pitfalls: Patients may not know or disclose that a medicine is time-critical → use the UKCPA poster to prompt disclosure
Triage staff may not recognise all time-critical drug classes → use the MISSED mnemonic (movement, immunomodulators, sugar, steroids, epilepsy, DOACs) in training
Small numbers if flagging is inconsistent → audit the flagging rate itself as a secondary measure
ED pharmacy may not have 24/7 cover → record time of day to see if out-of-hours delays predominate
Improvement fades once the initial safety flash awareness fades → repeat the poster and training at 6-monthly intervals
pearls: Display the RCEM/UKCPA poster at triage before starting data collection
Recruit the ED pharmacist as a co-lead, since medicines availability is part of the standard
Use the trust medication safety group, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the same list of time-critical drug classes (the MISSED categories) across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from triage and EPMA records
pass: The patient's time-critical medication due while in the ED is prescribed and administered within 30 minutes of its usual time, or a documented clinical reason for delay/omission is recorded

question: What proportion of adults on long-term steroid therapy who present with signs of possible adrenal crisis receive hydrocortisone promptly?
why: No closed-loop audit of prompt steroid replacement in possible adrenal crisis has been published in the library, despite an RCEM national safety flash on missed steroid-dependency risk.

standard.source: RCEM Safety Flash: Cortico-Steroid Dependency (December 2023)
standard.wording: Patients on long term steroid therapy (by any route) are at risk of an adrenal crisis if they miss their medication or have intercurrent illness/injury. ... Start steroids promptly in patients at risk of an adrenal crisis. ... Severe intercurrent illness ... Hydrocortisone 100mg IM or IV.

population: Inclusion: adults with documented long-term steroid dependency (Addison's disease, hypopituitarism, or long-term glucocorticoid therapy of any route) presenting with a severe intercurrent illness over 6 months. Exclusion: steroid-dependent patients presenting for an unrelated minor problem with no signs of illness
sample: 20 consecutive eligible presentations over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: ED triage note (steroid card/medic alert bracelet, drug history) and drug chart/EPMA administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'steroid card/medic alert seen: yes/no' question to the ED triage template, stock pre-drawn hydrocortisone 100 mg in the resus room drug cupboard, and add an adrenal crisis order set to the ED EPR.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting; if pre-stocking and the order set improve time to treatment, keep both permanently and add to ED induction
evidence: No audit of prompt hydrocortisone administration in adrenal crisis is in the library; the nearest related entries concern sepsis care bundle compliance
pitfalls: Adrenal crisis presentations are non-specific and easily missed → use the RCEM safety flash's red-flag list (nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, syncope, unexplained fever, long-lie) as the case-finding filter
Small numbers given expected low volume → extend the collection period to 12 months if needed
Steroid cards are not always carried → also check EPR medication history and GP summary care record
Hydrocortisone may not be immediately available on the resus trolley → confirm stock location with pharmacy before cycle 1
Gains fade once the safety flash is no longer fresh in staff minds → repeat awareness training at 6-monthly intervals
pearls: Display the NHS Steroid Emergency Card image at triage as a visual prompt
Recruit an ED pharmacist to confirm hydrocortisone stocking before starting
Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the case-finding red-flag list identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from triage and drug chart records
pass: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV is given within 30 minutes of triage/first assessment in a steroid-dependent patient with severe intercurrent illness (persistent vomiting, acute trauma, sepsis or surgery)

question: What proportion of children under 16 with a suspected sepsis red flag identified by an ambulance crew have a sepsis pre-alert call made to the receiving emergency department?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance sepsis pre-alerting for children has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG254 Suspected sepsis in under 16s: recognition, diagnosis and early management, rec 1.7.3 (2025)
standard.wording: Treat the risk of sepsis as an emergency and refer immediately for emergency medical care by the most appropriate means of transport (usually 999 ambulance) if a child or young person with suspected sepsis meets any high risk criteria in table 3.

population: Inclusion: children under 16 conveyed by ambulance with a documented NICE high-risk sepsis criterion, over 6 months. Exclusion: children brought by ambulance for an unrelated reason with sepsis diagnosed only after arrival
sample: 20 consecutive eligible children over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form (high-risk criterion documented) and ED pre-alert log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a paediatric sepsis red-flag prompt to the ambulance clinical decision-support tool that triggers a structured pre-alert message, and set the ED to open the paediatric sepsis order set automatically when a sepsis pre-alert is received.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust and paediatric emergency governance meeting; embed the automatic order-set trigger permanently if it reduces time to antibiotics
evidence: NNA-077 (paediatric sepsis antibiotics within 1 hour in the ED) shows this pathway already has a hospital-side gap; no audit of the ambulance pre-alert step for paediatric sepsis is in the library
pitfalls: High-risk criteria may not be explicitly documented by ambulance crews → agree a checklist with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small numbers given expected low paediatric sepsis volume → pool across a longer period or with a neighbouring trust
Pre-alert calls may mention 'unwell child' without naming sepsis specifically → record whether the word 'sepsis' or 'high risk' was used
Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the paediatric-trained ambulance clinical lead in the design
Gains fade once the decision-support prompt is switched off in an update → recheck after any ambulance system change
pearls: Link the audit to the existing paediatric sepsis quality improvement work already running in the ED
Recruit a paediatric emergency nurse and the ambulance trust's paediatric lead as joint owners
Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting to close the loop
Track time to antibiotics as the outcome that ultimately matters, alongside the process measure of pre-alerting
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and ED records
pass: A structured pre-alert call is made to the receiving ED before arrival, stating that a high-risk sepsis criterion has been identified

question: What proportion of patients cared for in a corridor or other non-designated clinical space in the ED have a full set of observations recorded at least hourly?
why: No closed-loop audit of observation frequency for patients in corridor care has been published in the library; RCEM has raised corridor care as a rising national patient-safety concern.

standard.source: Local standard, based on NICE CG50 Acutely ill patients in hospital, rec 1.3 (2007) principle of physiological track-and-trigger monitoring for all acutely unwell patients regardless of location
standard.wording: Physiological observations should be monitored at least every 12 hours, unless a decision has been made at a senior level to increase or decrease this frequency for an individual patient.

population: Inclusion: all adults cared for in a corridor, ambulance queue or other non-designated ED space for more than 1 hour, over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients in a designated cubicle or bay throughout their stay
sample: 40 consecutive corridor-care episodes over 2 weeks
data_source: ED nursing observation chart (paper or electronic), matched to the location log showing time spent in a non-designated space

template.note: one per hour in corridor care

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Name a corridor-care safety nurse on each shift with explicit responsibility for hourly observations and NEWS2 escalation, and flag every corridor-care patient on the electronic tracking board with a visible observation-due countdown.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting and trust corridor-care/overcrowding escalation group; make the named safety nurse role permanent on busy shifts if it improves compliance
evidence: No audit of observation frequency for corridor-cared patients is in the library; the nearest related entries concern ED waiting times and flow
pitfalls: Corridor-care time is not always logged separately from cubicle time → agree a location-logging method before cycle 1
Staff may under-document during periods of extreme pressure, the exact time this audit targets → use direct spot-checks as well as retrospective chart review
Numbers vary hugely by day-of-week surge → sample across several different pressure levels
Staff may see this as adding more paperwork during an already unsafe situation → pair the audit with the safety-nurse role, not extra forms
Improvement is not sustained if the role is dropped once escalation pressure eases → keep it as a standing response to a defined occupancy trigger
pearls: Agree with senior nursing and medical leads what counts as 'corridor care' before starting
Use the trust's existing overcrowding/escalation policy meeting to close the loop
Track NEWS2 escalation, not just observation frequency, as the outcome that matters
Keep the same location-logging method for both cycles
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the nursing observation chart and tracking board log
pass: A full set of observations (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, temperature, consciousness level) is recorded at least hourly for every hour spent in a corridor or non-designated space, or a documented senior decision sets a different frequency

question: What proportion of adults aged 65 and over attending the ED have a Clinical Frailty Scale score recorded at triage?
why: No closed-loop audit of Clinical Frailty Scale recording at ED triage has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.4.2 (2023) and BGS Silver Book II principle that frailty assessment should start at first contact
standard.wording: Consider that older people, or people who are frail, may have a lower threshold for CT scanning after a head injury because of an increased risk of both traumatic intracranial lesions and pre-existing neurological conditions that complicate assessment.

population: Inclusion: all patients aged 65 and over attending the ED over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients who die or leave before triage is completed
sample: 50 consecutive patients aged 65 and over over 2 weeks
data_source: ED triage record/EPR frailty field
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the Clinical Frailty Scale a mandatory field in the ED triage screen for every patient aged 65 and over (cannot complete triage without it), with an automatic prompt to refer to the frailty/same-day emergency care team when the score is 5 or more.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED and frailty service joint governance meeting; keep the mandatory triage field permanently if referral rates and recording improve
