evidence: NNA-341 (medication review in severe frailty) and NNA-083 (falls referral after head injury) show this trust already tracks frailty-related gaps; no audit of CFS recording at ED triage itself is in the library
pitfalls: CFS scoring needs a collateral history, which is not always available at triage → allow a 'provisional score, confirm later' option
Staff may not be trained in CFS scoring → provide a laminated CFS reference card at every triage desk
Small numbers if attendance data is not filtered correctly by age → double-check the age filter before sampling
Recording a score without acting on it (no referral) undermines the point → audit the referral step as well as the recording step
Gains fade after new starters join triage → add CFS training to ED induction
pearls: Involve the frailty/geriatric medicine team in designing the referral trigger before cycle 1
Use existing frailty service governance meetings to close the loop
Keep the referral threshold (CFS ≥5) identical across both cycles
Display CFS reference cards at every triage station, not just centrally
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ED triage record
pass: A Clinical Frailty Scale score (1-9) is recorded on the triage assessment for every patient aged 65 and over

question: What proportion of adults with acute severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or ECG changes) in the ED receive calcium gluconate or calcium chloride within 15 minutes of the result being available?
why: No closed-loop audit of time to cardio-protective calcium administration in severe hyperkalaemia has been published in the library.

standard.source: UK Kidney Association, Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults clinical practice guideline (2023)
standard.wording: IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride should be given immediately to patients with severe hyperkalaemia (serum potassium ≥6.5 mmol/L) and/or ECG changes consistent with hyperkalaemia.

population: Inclusion: adults in the ED with a venous or arterial potassium of 6.5 mmol/L or above, or ECG changes of hyperkalaemia, over 3 months. Exclusion: cardiac arrest before treatment could be given
sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: ED point-of-care/laboratory result timestamp and drug chart/EPMA administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a hyperkalaemia order set in the ED EPR that fires automatically when a potassium result of 6.5 mmol/L or above is filed, pre-selecting calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% with a one-click prescribe-and-administer pathway.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting; if the automatic order set improves compliance, keep it permanently and share with acute medicine for ward-based hyperkalaemia
evidence: No audit of time to calcium administration in severe hyperkalaemia is in the library; the nearest related entries concern sepsis care bundle compliance for similarly time-critical treatment
pitfalls: Point-of-care and laboratory potassium results may be recorded on different systems → agree a single result-timestamp source before cycle 1
Small numbers given expected low volume of severe hyperkalaemia → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
ECG-change cases without an extreme potassium value are easy to miss in a lab-based search → also screen ED ECGs reported as hyperkalaemic pattern
Nursing may wait for medical review before giving calcium → confirm local policy allows nurse-initiated calcium via a patient group direction or protocol
Gains fade if the automatic order set is switched off in a system update → recheck after any EPR change
pearls: Agree the case-finding method (lab result search plus ECG report search) with the laboratory and ED IT teams before starting
Recruit an ED pharmacist to help design the order set
Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the 6.5 mmol/L and 15-minute definitions identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from laboratory, ECG and drug chart records
pass: Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride is given within 15 minutes of the potassium result being available (or of ECG changes being recognised) for patients meeting the severe hyperkalaemia definition

question: What proportion of adults presenting to the ED with suspected carbon monoxide poisoning have a carboxyhaemoglobin level measured before treatment decisions are made?
why: No closed-loop audit of carboxyhaemoglobin testing in suspected carbon monoxide poisoning has been published in the library.

standard.source: UK Health Security Agency, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Diagnosis and Management (Public Health England/UKHSA toxicological guidance, 2021)
standard.wording: Carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) concentration should be measured as soon as possible after exposure, either from an arterial or venous blood sample analysed by co-oximetry, to confirm the diagnosis and guide management.

population: Inclusion: adults presenting to the ED with a history or suspicion of carbon monoxide exposure over 6 months. Exclusion: incidental low-level exposure with no symptoms and no suspicion raised by staff
sample: 20 consecutive suspected carbon monoxide poisoning presentations over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: ED clerking note and blood gas/co-oximetry result
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'suspected carbon monoxide exposure' order set to the ED EPR that automatically requests a co-oximetry blood gas and prompts a fire and rescue service/Gas Safe notification and hyperbaric referral consideration.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting and share findings with the local fire and rescue service liaison; embed the order set permanently if it improves testing rates
evidence: No audit of carboxyhaemoglobin testing in suspected carbon monoxide poisoning is in the library; the nearest related entries concern general poisoning and overdose pathways
pitfalls: Mild or vague presentations (headache, flu-like symptoms) may not trigger suspicion → add a seasonal awareness campaign (winter heating season) alongside the audit
Small numbers given expected low local volume → extend the collection period to 12 months
Co-oximetry may not be available on every blood gas analyser → confirm equipment availability before cycle 1
Household/multiple casualties may not all be flagged to the same audit → cross-check ambulance dispatch data for clustered presentations
Gains fade outside the winter season when suspicion is lower → repeat awareness training before each heating season
pearls: Recruit ED toxicology/poisons information (TOXBASE) contacts as a resource, not a data source, when designing the order set
Use the ED patient safety meeting to close the loop
Keep the same case-finding method (clerking note search for 'carbon monoxide' or 'CO poisoning') across both cycles
Coordinate with the fire and rescue service so household safety checks follow confirmed cases
effort: ~20 min per case from ED clerking and blood gas records
pass: A carboxyhaemoglobin level by co-oximetry is documented before a management decision (oxygen therapy duration, hyperbaric oxygen referral, discharge) is made

question: What proportion of children discharged from the ED after a first anaphylaxis episode leave with two adrenaline auto-injectors and a written action plan?
why: No closed-loop audit of complete anaphylaxis discharge equipment for children has been published in the library; NNA-188 audits the specialist allergy referral step but not the auto-injector and action plan themselves.

standard.source: NICE NG258 Assessment and referral after emergency treatment for anaphylaxis, rec 1.1.15 (2026)
standard.wording: Before a person is discharged from hospital after emergency treatment for a suspected or confirmed anaphylactic reaction: provide them (or their family members or carers as appropriate) with 2 adrenaline auto-injectors as an interim measure ... and a written anaphylaxis action plan.

population: Inclusion: children under 16 discharged from the ED after treatment for suspected or confirmed anaphylaxis, over 3 months. Exclusion: children admitted to a ward or PICU rather than discharged from the ED
sample: 20 consecutive eligible discharges over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: ED discharge summary/EPR anaphylaxis discharge bundle
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a mandatory anaphylaxis discharge bundle in the ED EPR that cannot be completed without ticking 'two auto-injectors supplied/confirmed', 'action plan given' and 'training given', with the auto-injectors and action plan template stocked in every paediatric bay.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the paediatric emergency governance meeting; keep the mandatory bundle permanently if compliance improves and report to the paediatric allergy service
evidence: NNA-188 (paediatric allergy service referral before discharge) shows this discharge pathway is already partly audited; no audit of the auto-injector and action plan completeness itself is in the library
pitfalls: Families may already own auto-injectors, making 'supplied' an incomplete measure → record 'supplied or confirmed in-date and carried' as the combined pass criterion
Written action plans are sometimes given verbally only → audit for a physical or electronic copy actually handed over, not just advice given
Small numbers if paediatric anaphylaxis presentations are infrequent → extend the collection period to 6 months
Stock shortages of auto-injector trainer devices can limit training → confirm trainer-device stock with pharmacy before cycle 1
Gains fade if new staff are not shown the mandatory bundle → add to paediatric ED induction
pearls: Recruit the paediatric allergy service to help design the action-plan template
Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the discharge bundle definition identical across both cycles
Stock auto-injectors and action plans directly in paediatric bays to remove a barrier to completion
effort: ~15 min per case from the ED discharge record
pass: The discharge record confirms 2 adrenaline auto-injectors were supplied (or already owned and confirmed in date) and a written anaphylaxis action plan was given, with training on use documented

question: What proportion of adults with a suspected ureteric colic who have significant pain in the ED receive their first dose of analgesia within 20 minutes of arrival?
why: No closed-loop audit of time to first analgesia specifically in renal colic has been published in the library; the corpus's 8 existing time-to-analgesia audits do not target this patient group.

standard.source: NICE NG118 Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management, rec 1.2.1 (2019)
standard.wording: Offer people with suspected renal colic a choice of NSAID, paracetamol or opioid if NSAIDs are contraindicated or not giving sufficient pain relief, as first-line treatment for pain relief.

population: Inclusion: adults triaged with suspected ureteric/renal colic and a documented pain score of 4 or more, over 4 weeks. Exclusion: pain score under 4 at triage
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 4 weeks
data_source: ED triage record (pain score, arrival time) and drug chart/EPMA administration time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a nurse-initiated analgesia patient group direction for suspected renal colic at triage (NSAID unless contraindicated, otherwise paracetamol or opioid), prompted automatically when the triage template flags flank pain with a pain score of 4 or more.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety/pain management meeting; make the patient group direction permanent if it improves time to first analgesia
evidence: The library holds 8 general time-to-analgesia audits and NNA-024 audits surgical treatment timing in renal colic, but no audit targets time to first analgesia in this specific patient group
pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded at triage → include 'no pain score recorded' as its own category rather than excluding these patients
NSAID contraindications (renal impairment, GI bleed history) may not be checked before an audit reviewer assumes non-compliance → record contraindications explicitly
Small numbers in a lower-volume unit → extend the collection period to 6 weeks
Nursing staff may be reluctant to give analgesia before a doctor review → confirm the patient group direction is signed off by the relevant clinical governance committee before cycle 1
Gains fade if the patient group direction is not refreshed on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
pearls: Agree the patient group direction with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting
Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the new prompt
Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop
Keep the pain-score threshold and analgesia options identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from triage and EPMA records
pass: A first dose of NSAID, paracetamol or opioid analgesia is given within 20 minutes of arrival for a patient with a pain score of 4 or more and suspected renal colic

question: What proportion of adults given IV opioid analgesia in the ED have their respiratory rate and sedation score checked within 30 minutes of the dose?
why: No closed-loop audit of post-opioid respiratory monitoring specifically in the ED has been published in the library.

standard.source: Resuscitation Council UK / Royal College of Anaesthetists guidance on opioid safety, summarised in NHS England Patient Safety Alert on opioid medicines (2020) principle
standard.wording: Patients receiving parenteral opioids should have their respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and sedation score monitored regularly following administration to detect early signs of opioid-induced respiratory depression.

population: Inclusion: adults given IV morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl or other parenteral opioid in the ED, over 2 weeks. Exclusion: opioid given immediately before transfer to theatre or critical care with monitoring continued there
sample: 30 consecutive IV opioid doses over 2 weeks
data_source: Drug chart/EPMA administration record and nursing observation chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the EPMA IV opioid administration step to automatically create a 30-minute 'respiratory rate and sedation score due' nursing task on the tracking board, which cannot be dismissed until both are recorded.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting; keep the automatic task permanently if compliance improves and share with the trust medication safety group
evidence: No audit of post-opioid respiratory monitoring in the ED is in the library; the nearest related entries concern general time-to-analgesia in the ED
pitfalls: Observations may be recorded as part of routine hourly obs rather than a specific post-opioid check, making them hard to attribute → record the nearest observation time relative to the dose, not just whether one exists in the hour
Sedation scoring tools vary between departments → agree a single sedation scale before cycle 1
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different times of day
Nursing staff already stretched may see this as extra burden → pair with the automatic EPMA task rather than a manual checklist
Gains fade if the EPMA task is removed in an update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the sedation scoring tool with anaesthetics/critical care outreach before starting, so it is consistent across the hospital
Recruit an ED pharmacist to help design the EPMA task
Use the ED patient safety meeting to close the loop
Keep the 30-minute window and sedation scale identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPMA and observation charts
pass: A respiratory rate and sedation score are both documented within 30 minutes of any IV opioid dose given in the ED

question: What proportion of adults with suspected sepsis who are discharged from the ED after a period of observation have a documented safety-netting plan given to them in writing?
why: No closed-loop audit of written safety-netting advice for ED patients discharged after a sepsis screen has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management, rec 1.10.2 (2025)
standard.wording: Give people being discharged after a suspected sepsis episode (and their family members or carers as appropriate) verbal and written information ... about ... signs and symptoms that should prompt them to seek further medical help.

population: Inclusion: adults assessed for suspected sepsis in the ED, treated and discharged home (not admitted), over 4 weeks. Exclusion: patients admitted to a ward or transferred to another provider
sample: 30 consecutive eligible discharges over 4 weeks
data_source: ED discharge summary/EPR discharge documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'sepsis safety-netting leaflet given' tick box to the ED discharge template, linked to an automatic print of the leaflet whenever a sepsis screening tool has been used during the attendance.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety meeting; keep the automatic print and mandatory tick box permanently if compliance improves
evidence: NNA-074/NNA-075/NNA-076 (sepsis bundle timing in the ED) show this department already audits the sepsis pathway in detail; no audit of discharge safety-netting after a sepsis episode is in the library
pitfalls: Verbal advice may be given but not documented → audit only what is written in the record, and note this limitation when presenting results
Leaflet availability may run out during busy shifts → confirm stock levels with the ED matron before cycle 1
Small numbers if sepsis screening is not consistently coded → cross-check against the sepsis screening tool completion rate
Staff may see this as an extra step in an already complex pathway → automate the print rather than relying on staff to remember
Gains fade if the automatic print is switched off in a system change → recheck after any EPR update
pearls: Use the existing sepsis steering group to design and own the leaflet trigger
Recruit an ED nurse educator to reinforce safety-netting messaging at induction
Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists for other sepsis audits, to close the loop
Keep the definition of 'sepsis screen performed' identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ED discharge record
pass: A written safety-netting leaflet listing red-flag symptoms and when to seek help is documented as given at discharge

question: What proportion of adults presenting to the ED with an acute exacerbation of COPD have their oxygen prescribed with a target saturation range appropriate to their risk of hypercapnia?
why: No closed-loop audit of oxygen target-range prescribing specifically for COPD exacerbations in the ED has been published in the library, although general oxygen-prescribing audits exist.

standard.source: BTS/RCP/RCN emergency oxygen guideline, updated NICE NG115 COPD guideline, rec 1.2.9 (2018, updated 2019)
standard.wording: Use a target oxygen saturation range of 88-92% for patients with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who are at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, until blood gas results are available.

population: Inclusion: adults with a known or newly suspected diagnosis of COPD presenting to the ED with breathlessness who are prescribed supplemental oxygen, over 2 weeks. Exclusion: patients requiring immediate resuscitation before a target range could be set
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 2 weeks
data_source: ED drug chart/EPR oxygen prescription and arterial/venous blood gas record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the oxygen target saturation range a mandatory field on the ED electronic drug chart whenever a COPD diagnosis flag is present, defaulting to 88-92% with an override reason required to change it.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety and respiratory joint meeting; keep the mandatory default field permanently if compliance improves
evidence: Oxygen prescribing with target saturations already has 2 audits in the library; no audit targets the COPD-specific 88-92% range decision at ED presentation, which is the group at highest risk of harm from over-oxygenation
pitfalls: Undiagnosed COPD patients may not be flagged → include 'newly suspected' cases identified from smoking history and examination, not only coded diagnoses
Staff may prescribe 94-98% by habit → make the correct range the system default rather than relying on memory
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across a longer period if COPD presentations are infrequent
Definitions of 'at risk of hypercapnia' can be disputed → agree the criteria (known COPD, previous NIV, known CO2 retention) before cycle 1
Gains fade if the default is changed in a system update → recheck after any EPR change
pearls: Involve the respiratory team in agreeing the target-range default and override reasons
Recruit an ED pharmacist to help build the mandatory field
Use joint ED-respiratory governance to close the loop
Keep the 88-92% threshold and 'at risk' definition identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the drug chart and blood gas record
pass: An oxygen target saturation range of 88-92% is documented on the drug chart/oxygen prescription for a patient with known or suspected hypercapnic risk, before or pending the first blood gas

question: What proportion of adults with a suspected ectopic pregnancy have a formal transvaginal ultrasound or gynaecology review arranged within 24 hours of presenting to the ED?
why: No closed-loop audit of time to definitive imaging or gynaecology review for suspected ectopic pregnancy presenting via the ED has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, rec 1.2.4 (2019, updated 2021)
standard.wording: Refer women and pregnant people to an early pregnancy assessment service if they are more than 6 weeks pregnant, or if the gestation is uncertain and they have pain and/or bleeding, or other complications ... to confirm the location and viability of the pregnancy.

population: Inclusion: women/pregnant people presenting to the ED with a positive pregnancy test and abdominal pain and/or bleeding of uncertain gestation, over 4 weeks. Exclusion: confirmed intrauterine pregnancy already seen by an early pregnancy service before this attendance
sample: 30 consecutive eligible attendances over 4 weeks
data_source: ED clerking record and early pregnancy assessment unit referral/appointment log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a direct electronic referral route from the ED clerking template to the early pregnancy assessment unit, with a weekend/out-of-hours pathway to on-call gynaecology so referrals made overnight are still seen within 24 hours.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the joint ED-gynaecology governance meeting; keep the direct electronic referral route permanently if it improves the 24-hour rate
evidence: No audit of time to early pregnancy assessment from the ED is in the library; the nearest related entries concern general ED diagnostic pathway timing (e.g. CT KUB in renal colic)
pitfalls: Weekend and overnight presentations are the most likely to breach 24 hours → analyse weekday versus weekend/overnight separately
Haemodynamically unstable patients go straight to theatre and should be analysed separately, not counted as a breach → exclude or flag them
Small numbers in a unit with a low volume of early pregnancy attendances → extend the collection period to 6 weeks
Referral may be made but the appointment not actually booked → audit the actual scan/review time, not just referral completion
Gains fade if weekend gynaecology cover is not sustained → confirm the out-of-hours pathway is resourced before scaling up
pearls: Agree the out-of-hours pathway with gynaecology before starting data collection
Recruit the early pregnancy assessment unit lead as a co-owner of the audit
Use the joint ED-gynaecology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the referral criteria and 24-hour definition identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per case from ED and EPAU records
pass: A referral to the early pregnancy assessment service (or a transvaginal ultrasound/gynaecology review if the service is closed) is made and actioned within 24 hours of ED presentation

question: What proportion of adults with suspected acute limb ischaemia in the ED are discussed with the vascular surgery on-call team within 30 minutes of the diagnosis being suspected?
why: No closed-loop audit of time to vascular surgery discussion in suspected acute limb ischaemia has been published in the library.

standard.source: Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland, Quality Improvement Framework for Acute Limb Ischaemia (2020)
standard.wording: Patients with suspected acute limb ischaemia should be discussed with a vascular surgeon immediately, and those with an ischaemic limb should be assessed by a vascular surgeon within 30 minutes of referral.

population: Inclusion: adults presenting to the ED with a clinically documented suspicion of acute limb ischaemia (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold limb), over 6 months. Exclusion: chronic limb ischaemia without an acute change
sample: 15 consecutive eligible presentations over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: ED clerking note (time suspicion first documented) and switchboard/bleep log or EPR referral timestamp for the vascular call
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an 'acute limb ischaemia' one-click referral button to the ED EPR that pages the vascular on-call team directly and time-stamps the call automatically, bypassing switchboard.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the joint ED-vascular surgery governance meeting; keep the direct one-click referral button permanently if it improves the 30-minute rate
evidence: No audit of time to vascular surgery referral in suspected acute limb ischaemia is in the library; the nearest related entries concern trauma call activation and attendance timing for other time-critical surgical referrals
pitfalls: Suspicion is not always explicitly time-stamped in free-text notes → train staff to write the time of suspicion as a discrete entry
Small numbers given the expected low volume of this presentation → collect over 6-12 months or pool across a vascular network
Switchboard/bleep delays may be outside ED control → record whether the delay was in ED referral or in reaching the vascular team
Anticoagulation may be delayed while awaiting vascular advice → audit this as a secondary process measure
Gains fade if the one-click referral button is removed in an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the case-finding method (clerking note text search for limb ischaemia symptoms) with ED and vascular leads before starting
Recruit the vascular surgery on-call rota lead as a co-owner of the audit
Use the joint ED-vascular governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 30-minute definition and referral method identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per case from ED and vascular referral records
pass: The vascular surgery on-call team is contacted (call time documented) within 30 minutes of a clinician first documenting suspected acute limb ischaemia

question: What proportion of adults triaged as category 2 (very urgent) in the ED are seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of triage?
why: No closed-loop audit of time from triage category to first clinician contact for the most urgent non-resuscitation patients has been published in the library.

standard.source: Manchester Triage Group / RCEM Triage position statement, summarised in RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Triage (2017, reviewed)
standard.wording: Patients triaged as 'very urgent' (category 2) should be seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of arrival at triage.

population: Inclusion: all adults triaged as category 2 over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients who deteriorate to resuscitation status before first clinician contact (already captured by resuscitation-room standards)
sample: 40 consecutive category 2 triage episodes over 2 weeks
data_source: ED tracking system triage-complete and first-clinician-seen timestamps
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a category 2 visual flag and 10-minute countdown to the ED tracking board, with a nurse-in-charge escalation if the countdown expires before a clinician has been assigned.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety and flow meeting; keep the countdown flag permanently if it improves the 10-minute rate
evidence: ED triage accuracy already has 5 audits in the library, but none measures time from category 2 triage to first clinician contact, which is the outcome that matters for patient safety
pitfalls: Tracking system timestamps can be inaccurate if staff log in retrospectively → spot-check a sample against direct observation
Occupancy pressure is the main driver of delay and is outside the audit's control → record occupancy as a confounder, not an excuse to exclude cases
Small numbers on quiet shifts → sample across day, evening and night shifts
Staff may feel individually blamed for system-level overcrowding → present results as a department-level flow measure, not a named performance table
Gains fade once escalation fatigue sets in during sustained high occupancy → review escalation triggers at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the triage-category definitions with the ED triage lead before starting
Use the department's existing flow/safety huddle to close the loop
Keep the 10-minute definition and category 2 criteria identical across both cycles
Track occupancy alongside compliance so the effect of flow pressure is visible, not hidden
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ED tracking system
pass: Time from triage completion to first clinician (doctor, ACP or ENP) contact is 10 minutes or less for a category 2 patient

question: What proportion of adults discharged from the ED with a new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation have anticoagulation risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) formally assessed before discharge?
why: No closed-loop audit of anticoagulation risk assessment at first ED presentation of atrial fibrillation has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.1 (2021)
standard.wording: Use the CHA2DS2-VASc score to assess stroke risk in people with any of the following: symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent or permanent atrial fibrillation ... atrial flutter ... a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion back to sinus rhythm.

population: Inclusion: adults with a new ED diagnosis of atrial fibrillation or flutter who are discharged home (not admitted), over 4 weeks. Exclusion: known pre-existing AF already on anticoagulation review by another team
sample: 30 consecutive eligible discharges over 4 weeks
data_source: ED clerking record/EPR discharge summary
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory CHA2DS2-VASc calculator field to the ED discharge template whenever an AF/flutter diagnosis code is entered, which must be completed (with an anticoagulation decision) before the discharge letter can be printed.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED and cardiology joint governance meeting; keep the mandatory calculator field permanently if compliance improves
evidence: No audit of CHA2DS2-VASc assessment at first ED presentation of atrial fibrillation is in the library; NNA-384 (angiography timing in NSTEMI) shows this network already audits other cardiac pathway steps
pitfalls: New AF is sometimes coded under a general 'palpitations' diagnosis → search discharge diagnoses broadly, not just the exact AF code
Score components (hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease history) may be incompletely documented → record 'unable to calculate, missing data' as its own category
Small numbers in a lower-volume unit → extend the collection period to 6 weeks
Clinicians may defer the decision to the GP without a formal score → count 'deferred with reason' as a partial pass only if the score itself is still documented
Gains fade if the mandatory field is bypassed by overriding it → monitor override rates at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the discharge coding search terms with the ED coding/informatics team before starting
Recruit a cardiology liaison clinician to help design the mandatory field and anticoagulation guidance
Use the joint ED-cardiology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the CHA2DS2-VASc calculation method and pass definition identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ED discharge record
pass: A CHA2DS2-VASc score is calculated and documented, with an anticoagulation decision (start, defer to GP/cardiology, or not indicated) recorded before ED discharge

question: When ambulance crews attend a person who has self-harmed but does not need urgent physical care, what proportion have a documented discussion of the person's care/safety plan and this information passed on if not conveyed?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance non-conveyance self-harm care has been published in the library; NNA-088/NNA-145/NNA-146 audit the ED end of the self-harm pathway but not the ambulance non-conveyance decision.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.9 (2022)
standard.wording: When attending a person who has self-harmed but who does not need urgent physical care, ambulance staff and paramedics should: discuss with the person the best way that the ambulance service can help them; follow the person's care plan and safety plan if available; seek advice from mental health professionals, where necessary; record relevant information ... and pass this information to staff if the person is conveyed, or share it with other relevant people involved in the person's ongoing care if the person is not being conveyed.

population: Inclusion: adults attended by ambulance following self-harm who did not need urgent physical care, over 3 months. Exclusion: patients conveyed to hospital for physical treatment of the self-harm injury itself
sample: 20 consecutive eligible non-conveyance episodes over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record self-harm/mental health section
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a structured self-harm non-conveyance section to the ambulance electronic patient record with mandatory fields for care/safety plan check, mental health advice sought, and information sharing, linked to a direct referral route to the crisis/home treatment team.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust mental health lead and the community mental health governance meeting; embed the structured section permanently if it improves documented information-sharing
evidence: NNA-088, NNA-145 and NNA-146 (self-harm risk rating and discharge in the ED) show this pathway is well audited once patients reach hospital; no audit of the ambulance non-conveyance decision itself is in the library
pitfalls: Non-conveyed episodes are not always separately coded from other 'not conveyed' outcomes → agree a coding filter with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Care and safety plans may exist in mental health records the ambulance crew cannot access in real time → record whether the crew had access to the plan, not just whether one existed
Small numbers given how this presentation is coded → extend the collection period to 6 months
Crews may under-document sensitive conversations → keep the audit tool short and focused on the specific NG225 items
Gains fade if the crisis team referral route is not resourced → confirm capacity with the crisis team before scaling up
pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's mental health lead and the local crisis team from the start
Use an existing joint mental health/ambulance governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the coding filter for 'self-harm, not conveyed' identical across both cycles
Track whether alternative services were actually accessed, not just discussed, as a secondary outcome
effort: ~15 min per case from the ambulance electronic patient record
pass: The ambulance record documents that the person's existing care/safety plan was checked and followed (or that none existed), and that relevant information was shared with the person's ongoing care team if not conveyed

question: What proportion of pre-hospital chest decompressions for suspected tension pneumothorax are performed only in patients with documented haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise?
why: No closed-loop audit of appropriateness of pre-hospital chest decompression has been published in the library; unnecessary decompression itself causes harm.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.3.4 (2016)
standard.wording: Only perform chest decompression in a patient with suspected tension pneumothorax if there is haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise.

population: Inclusion: all patients who received a pre-hospital needle or open chest decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax, over 6 months. Exclusion: decompression performed after hospital arrival
sample: 15 consecutive pre-hospital chest decompressions over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance/HEMS/critical care paramedic patient report form
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'indication for decompression: haemodynamic instability / severe respiratory compromise' field to the ambulance/HEMS chest trauma pathway, and reinforce the NG39 threshold in the trauma network's annual pre-hospital training update.
reaudit: Re-audit at 12 months, same sample definition (given expected low case volume)
close_loop: Present at the regional trauma network pre-hospital governance meeting; embed the mandatory field permanently if appropriateness improves
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital chest decompression appropriateness is in the library; ONA-024/ONA-026 show the same trauma network already audits other pre-hospital trauma interventions
pitfalls: Very low case numbers make single-trust audit under-powered → pool data across the regional trauma network
Retrospective documentation may under-record the clinical picture at the time of decision → use direct crew debrief where possible, in addition to the written record
Post-decompression observation for recurrence is a separate but related safety step → record this alongside indication appropriateness
Crews may feel individually scrutinised for a rare, high-stakes decision → present findings in aggregate, with a focus on system learning
Gains fade without regular case-based teaching → use real (anonymised) cases in the annual training update
pearls: Agree with the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead to pool data across the network before starting
Recruit a HEMS/critical care paramedic clinical lead as co-owner of the audit
Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the indication definitions (haemodynamic instability, severe respiratory compromise) identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from the ambulance/HEMS patient report form
pass: The pre-hospital record documents haemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock) or severe respiratory compromise immediately before chest decompression was performed

question: What proportion of adults on warfarin with a head injury and CT-confirmed intracranial haemorrhage receive prothrombin complex concentrate within 1 hour of the scan result?
why: No closed-loop audit of anticoagulation reversal timing in traumatic intracranial haemorrhage has been published in the library; NNA-080 audits the CT-decision step but not reversal once bleeding is confirmed.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.5.13 (2023), cross-referring to NICE's guideline on blood transfusion
standard.wording: For advice on reversing vitamin K antagonists for people with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, see the section on prothrombin complex concentrate in NICE's guideline on blood transfusion.

population: Inclusion: adults taking warfarin or another vitamin K antagonist with a head injury and CT-confirmed intracranial haemorrhage, over 6 months. Exclusion: patients on a DOAC (audited separately) or with a normal CT
sample: 15 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: ED clerking record, CT report timestamp and drug chart/EPMA administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 'warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage' order set in the ED EPR that fires automatically when a CT report containing both 'intracranial haemorrhage' and an anticoagulant flag is filed, pre-selecting weight-based prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K.
reaudit: Re-audit at 12 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the ED and haematology joint governance meeting; embed the automatic order set permanently if time to reversal improves
evidence: NNA-080 (documented CT decision in anticoagulated head injury) shows this trust already audits the earlier step of this pathway; no audit of reversal timing once bleeding is confirmed is in the library
pitfalls: Small numbers given expected low volume of warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage → extend the collection period to 12 months
PCC may be delayed by blood bank turnaround time rather than a clinical decision delay → record the time PCC was requested as well as when it was given
INR results may lag behind the clinical decision to reverse → do not delay treatment purely for INR confirmation, in line with the guideline's intent, and audit accordingly
DOAC-treated patients need a different reversal agent and should not be mixed into this sample → keep the two anticoagulant types in separate audits
Gains fade if the order set is switched off in an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the order set design with haematology and pharmacy before starting
Recruit an ED pharmacist to identify eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid
Use the ED-haematology joint governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the same reversal-timing definition (from CT report to administration) across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from CT, drug chart and blood bank records
pass: Prothrombin complex concentrate is prescribed and administered within 1 hour of the CT report confirming intracranial haemorrhage in a patient taking a vitamin K antagonist

question: What proportion of adults with an ambulance-diagnosed STEMI, when the primary PCI centre is not the nearest hospital, are taken directly to the primary PCI centre rather than the nearest emergency department?
why: No closed-loop audit of direct-to-cath-lab bypass decisions for ambulance-diagnosed STEMI has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes, rec 1.1.6 (2013)
standard.wording: Offer coronary angiography, with follow-on primary PCI if indicated, as the preferred coronary reperfusion strategy for people with acute STEMI, if: presentation is within 12 hours of onset of symptoms and primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given.

population: Inclusion: adults with a pre-hospital 12-lead ECG diagnosis of STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset, where the nearest hospital is not the primary PCI centre, over 6 months. Exclusion: patients presenting more than 12 hours after symptom onset
sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form destination decision and cardiac network call-to-balloon time audit
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a documented bypass-distance threshold with the ambulance trust and cardiac network so any ambulance-diagnosed STEMI within the threshold travel time bypasses the nearest ED automatically, with the cath lab activated directly from the ambulance ECG transmission.
target: ≥90% direct conveyance where within the network's agreed bypass threshold
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the cardiac network primary PCI governance meeting with ambulance trust representation; adopt the bypass threshold as standard ambulance policy if call-to-balloon times improve
evidence: NNA-384 (angiography timing in NSTEMI) shows this network already audits related cardiac pathway timings; no audit of the ambulance bypass decision itself for STEMI is in the library
pitfalls: Rural geography may mean bypass is not always feasible within the 120-minute window → record travel time and distance as confounders
Small numbers in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network
Ambulance ECG transmission failures can force a default to the nearest ED → record technical failures as a separate reason category
Crews may default to the nearest ED out of habit → reinforce the bypass threshold in annual cardiac pathway training
Gains fade if cath lab activation from the ambulance ECG is not reliably actioned → audit cath lab response time alongside conveyance decision
pearls: Agree the bypass-distance threshold jointly with the ambulance trust and cardiac network before starting
Use the existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 12-hour symptom-onset window and destination definitions identical across both cycles
Track call-to-balloon time as the ultimate outcome, alongside the process measure of direct conveyance
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and cardiac network records
pass: The patient is taken directly to the primary PCI centre (bypassing the nearest non-PCI ED), or a documented reason for going to the nearest ED first is recorded (for example, cardiac arrest requiring immediate resuscitation, or the calculated travel time exceeding the network's bypass threshold)

question: What proportion of children assessed by an ambulance crew with a NICE 'red' (high-risk) fever feature are conveyed immediately by emergency ambulance rather than left for a delayed or alternative assessment?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance conveyance decisions for febrile children with red-flag features has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management, rec 1.3.2 (2007)
standard.wording: Children with 'red' features ... should be referred immediately for emergency medical care by the most appropriate means of transport (usually 999 ambulance).

population: Inclusion: children under 5 assessed by an ambulance crew with fever and at least one NICE 'red' feature documented, over 6 months. Exclusion: children with only 'amber' or 'green' features
sample: 20 consecutive eligible children over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record fever/traffic-light assessment section
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build the NICE traffic light system into the ambulance paediatric assessment screen so a 'red' feature triggers a mandatory conveyance recommendation and a paediatric pre-alert prompt, with an override reason required to deviate.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust paediatric lead and the paediatric emergency governance meeting; embed the mandatory prompt permanently if compliance improves
evidence: NNA-078 (observations in febrile children in the ED) shows this pathway is already audited once children reach hospital; no audit of the ambulance conveyance decision for red-flag fever is in the library
pitfalls: Traffic light features may be assessed inconsistently by non-paediatric-trained crews → provide a laminated traffic-light reference card on every vehicle
Small numbers given expected low volume of red-flag paediatric fever calls → extend the collection period to 12 months
Parents may decline conveyance despite advice → record 'declined against advice' as its own category, not a system failure
Ambulance and hospital records may use different fever assessment tools → agree a shared traffic-light tool with the paediatric department
Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual paediatric update
pearls: Agree the traffic-light assessment tool jointly with the paediatric emergency department before starting
Recruit the ambulance trust's paediatric clinical lead as a co-owner of the audit
Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the 'red feature' definition identical to the one used in the ED for continuity across the pathway
effort: ~15 min per case from the ambulance electronic patient record
pass: A child with a documented NICE 'red' fever feature is conveyed by emergency ambulance immediately (not left at home or referred to a delayed pathway), or a documented clinical reason for an alternative pathway is recorded

question: What proportion of people with sudden-onset neurological symptoms assessed by an ambulance crew have a validated FAST (Face Arm Speech Test) screen documented before hypoglycaemia is excluded and a stroke pre-alert decision is made?
why: No closed-loop audit of the completeness of the pre-hospital FAST and hypoglycaemia-exclusion sequence has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, recs 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 (2008)
standard.wording: Use a validated tool, such as FAST (Face Arm Speech Test), outside hospital to screen people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms for a diagnosis of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Exclude hypoglycaemia in people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms as the cause of these symptoms.

population: Inclusion: adults assessed by ambulance for sudden-onset neurological symptoms over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients with an obvious alternative cause identified at scene (for example, a witnessed seizure with full recovery)
sample: 30 consecutive eligible ambulance assessments over 2 weeks
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record neurological assessment section
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make both the FAST score and capillary glucose mandatory fields on the ambulance electronic patient report form before the stroke pre-alert option can be selected, so the sequence cannot be skipped.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust and stroke operational delivery network; keep the mandatory field sequence permanently if completeness improves
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital FAST and hypoglycaemia-exclusion completeness is in the library; NNA-119/NNA-120 show this network already audits the hospital-side stroke/TIA pathway
pitfalls: Capillary glucose may be checked but not documented in the neurological assessment section → search the whole ambulance record, not just the stroke-specific field
FAST scoring can be inconsistently applied by less experienced crews → provide a laminated FAST reference card on every vehicle
Small numbers if stroke-call coding is inconsistent → cross-check against the stroke pre-alert log as well as the neurological assessment field
Crews under time pressure may prioritise conveyance speed over full documentation → keep the mandatory fields quick (tick-box, not free text)
Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual stroke pathway update
pearls: Agree the mandatory field design with the ambulance trust's stroke clinical lead before starting
Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the FAST tool and glucose threshold definitions identical across both cycles
Track pre-alert accuracy (stroke mimics versus confirmed stroke) as a secondary measure of the pathway's overall quality
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ambulance electronic patient record
pass: Both a documented FAST score and a documented capillary blood glucose (excluding hypoglycaemia) are recorded on the ambulance patient report form before the stroke pathway decision is made

question: What proportion of adults with major trauma and active or suspected bleeding who are taking an anticoagulant have a documented decision about reversal made with, or by, a haematologist?
why: No closed-loop audit of haematology involvement in anticoagulation reversal decisions for bleeding trauma patients has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.5.11-1.5.12 (2016)
standard.wording: Do not reverse anticoagulation in patients who do not have active or suspected bleeding. For advice on reversing direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), see the MHRA safety advice on DOACs for a list of reversal agents.

population: Inclusion: adults with major trauma known to be taking an anticoagulant (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) who are admitted via the trauma pathway, over 6 months. Exclusion: patients on antiplatelet monotherapy only
sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Trauma clerking record, haematology consultation note, drug chart/EPMA administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'anticoagulant reversal decision: haematology contacted, agent/reason' field to the trauma team clerking proforma whenever an anticoagulant is flagged in the drug history.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance and haematology joint meeting; keep the mandatory field permanently if compliance improves
evidence: No audit of haematology involvement in trauma anticoagulation reversal decisions is in the library; the anticoagulated head-injury reversal audit in this set covers a related but narrower (intracranial haemorrhage only) population
pitfalls: Anticoagulant use may not be reliably known at first assessment → cross-check with the GP summary care record and pharmacy medicines reconciliation
Small numbers given expected low volume of anticoagulated major trauma → extend the collection period to 12 months
Out-of-hours haematology advice may be by telephone and not always documented → agree a documentation standard for telephone advice before cycle 1

Reversal may be started before haematology is reached in a genuine emergency, which is appropriate → audit for a subsequent haematology discussion, not necessarily a prior one, in the most urgent cases
Gains fade if the mandatory field is not maintained after an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the reversal pathway and documentation standard with haematology before starting
Recruit the trauma coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively
Use the joint trauma-haematology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the definitions of 'active or suspected bleeding' and 'reversal indicated' identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from trauma and haematology records
pass: For a bleeding trauma patient on an anticoagulant, the trauma record documents a reversal decision (agent given, or reversal not indicated) made with haematology input; anticoagulation is not reversed in a patient without active or suspected bleeding

question: What proportion of adults triaged in the ED with a pain score of 7 or more (severe pain) receive their first analgesia within 20 minutes of triage?
why: No closed-loop audit of time to first analgesia specifically for severe (rather than any) pain has been published in the library; the corpus's 8 general time-to-analgesia audits do not isolate the severe-pain group most likely to come to harm from delay.

standard.source: Local standard, based on the pain-severity thresholds used in RCEM's Pain in Children quality improvement programme (2021/22) extended to adults
standard.wording: Patients in severe pain (pain score 7 or more out of 10) should receive their first dose of analgesia within 20 minutes of a pain score being recorded.

population: Inclusion: adults triaged with a documented pain score of 7 or more, over 2 weeks. Exclusion: patients who decline analgesia or for whom analgesia is contraindicated and this is documented
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 2 weeks
data_source: ED triage record (pain score, time) and drug chart/EPMA administration time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a nurse-initiated analgesia protocol at triage for any adult scoring 7 or more, covering oral and intranasal options that do not need a doctor's prescription first.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED pain management/patient safety meeting; make the nurse-initiated protocol permanent if it improves the 20-minute rate
evidence: The library holds 8 general time-to-analgesia audits in the ED, none of which isolates the severe (≥7/10) pain-score subgroup, where delay causes the most harm and complaints
pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded consistently by all triage staff → audit the recording rate itself as a secondary measure
Nurse-initiated analgesia protocols need pharmacy and governance sign-off before use → secure this before cycle 1
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different shift types
Some patients decline analgesia or have a contraindication, which should not count as a breach → record these separately, not as failures
Gains fade if the protocol lapses on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
pearls: Agree the nurse-initiated analgesia protocol with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting
Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the change
Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop
Keep the pain-score threshold (≥7) and time window identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from triage and EPMA records
pass: A first dose of analgesia (any route) is given within 20 minutes of a pain score of 7 or more being recorded at triage

question: What proportion of patients whose ambulance handover is delayed beyond 60 minutes have a full set of vital sign observations recorded by ambulance or ED staff at least every 30 minutes while still in the ambulance or queue?
why: No closed-loop audit of observation frequency during prolonged ambulance handover delay has been published in the library, despite a national review finding severe potential harm in this group.

standard.source: AACE, Delayed Hospital Handovers: Impact Assessment of Patient Harm (November 2021), summarised on the AACE Hospital Handovers webpage (accessed 2026)
standard.wording: Over eight in ten of those whose 'handover' (from ambulance clinician to hospital clinician) was delayed beyond 60 minutes were assessed as having potentially experienced some level of harm; 53% low harm, 23% moderate harm and 9% (one patient in ten) could have been said to have experienced severe harm.

population: Inclusion: all patients whose ambulance-to-ED handover exceeds 60 minutes over a 4-week period. Exclusion: handovers under 60 minutes
sample: 20 consecutive handovers exceeding 60 minutes over 4 weeks (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance observation chart during the wait, cross-checked with the ED tracking system handover time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a joint ambulance-ED 'queue safety officer' role during any period when more than 2 ambulances are waiting, responsible for cycling through queued patients to check and escalate observations every 30 minutes.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the joint ambulance-ED patient safety meeting; make the queue safety officer role permanent during escalation if it improves observation compliance
evidence: This set's ambulance-to-ED handover time audit measures the 15-minute target itself; no audit in the library measures clinical monitoring quality during a delay once it has already happened
pitfalls: Responsibility for observations during a handover delay can be unclear between ambulance and ED staff → agree ownership explicitly before cycle 1
Small numbers if 60-minute-plus delays are rare (a good sign operationally, but limits audit power) → extend the collection period
Ambulance staff may be tied up with other calls during a queue → record which service (ambulance or ED) took each observation
Staff may see this as adding a role during an already unsafe situation → frame it as protecting patients, not adding paperwork
Gains fade once escalation pressure passes and the role is dropped informally → tie the role to a defined occupancy/queue-length trigger, not to memory
pearls: Use the trust's existing ambulance handover delay escalation policy meeting to close the loop
Recruit both an ED matron and an ambulance operations manager as joint audit owners
Keep the 60-minute delay threshold and 30-minute observation interval identical across both cycles
Track NEWS2 escalation events as the safety outcome that matters most, not just the observation count
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance observation and ED tracking records
pass: A full set of vital sign observations is recorded at least every 30 minutes for every patient whose handover exceeds 60 minutes, with escalation to a senior clinician if NEWS2 rises

question: In women on continuous CTG monitoring in labour, what proportion of hourly fetal heart rate assessments had an in-person 'fresh eyes' review by a second clinician documented before the next hourly assessment?
why: Delayed or absent fresh-eyes review of the CTG is a recurring theme in avoidable intrapartum stillbirth and brain injury cases; the corpus holds general intrapartum care and PPH audits [1] but no closed-loop audit of fresh-eyes CTG review timing.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.3.6 (2022)
standard.wording: Obtain an in-person review of every hourly assessment (see recommendation 1.3.5) by another clinician ("fresh eyes") for women on CTG, to be completed before the next assessment takes place.

pass: The hourly CTG assessment has a documented fresh-eyes review (name/role and time) by a second clinician, completed before the next hourly assessment is due
population: Inclusion: all women on continuous CTG monitoring in established labour. Exclusion: births before continuous CTG was started, home births.
sample: 40 consecutive women on continuous CTG monitoring in labour over the last 4 weeks, one CTG episode of at least 3 hours per woman
data_source: Labour ward CTG trace annotations and electronic partogram/labour record

template.note: number of hourly CTG assessments during the labour reviewed
how many had a documented second-clinician review before the next assessment

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a timed 'fresh eyes review due at __:__' prompt to the CTG trace and electronic labour record that is generated automatically at each hourly assessment and must be signed by a second clinician before it can be marked complete.
reaudit: At 12 weeks after the prompt is introduced, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward forum and maternity governance meeting; if compliance improves, embed the CTG fresh-eyes prompt as a fixed field in the electronic labour record build
evidence: [1892] intrapartum care and PPH: before → after (proforma change)
no closed-loop audit of fresh-eyes CTG review timing found in the library
pitfalls: Paper CTG annotations are often illegible or missing a time → agree a single place (trace margin or e-record) and a minimum data set with the labour ward before cycle 1
Small numbers if the unit has few continuous-CTG labours in the sample window → extend the collection period rather than lowering the sample
Staff may see the fresh-eyes prompt as another tick-box → involve labour ward coordinators in designing the prompt and explain the Each Baby Counts rationale
Definition of 'in-person' review may be interpreted loosely (a verbal comment vs a documented review) → fix the definition and a single documentation location before data collection starts
Gains fade once the audit team rotates → make the fresh-eyes field mandatory in the EPR build rather than relying on a poster reminder
pearls: Recruit a labour ward co-ordinator and a supervisor of midwives/PMA as co-investigators so the change has authority on the ward
Agree the exact fresh-eyes documentation field and audit definition with labour ward before cycle 1 starts
Time the audit to include day and night shifts, as fresh-eyes reviews are more often missed at night
Share individual near-miss examples (anonymised) at the labour ward forum to build buy-in before the second cycle
Keep the re-audit sample the same size and season to allow fair comparison
effort: ~30 min per 10 labours from the CTG trace and electronic labour record

question: In women with a low risk of complications having intermittent auscultation in established first stage of labour, what proportion of documented auscultations were performed at least once every 15 minutes?
why: RCEM's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK reviews repeatedly identify failure to follow the recommended frequency and technique of intermittent auscultation as a contributory factor in avoidable harm; no closed-loop audit of intermittent auscultation frequency is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.2.9 (2017, amended 2026)
standard.wording: Offer women with a low risk of complications, fetal heart rate monitoring with intermittent auscultation when in established first stage of labour. Do this as follows: ... carry out intermittent auscultation immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, repeated at least once every 15 minutes, and record it as a single rate.

pass: For a woman on intermittent auscultation in established first stage, the interval between two consecutive documented auscultations does not exceed 15 minutes
population: Inclusion: low-risk women having intermittent auscultation in established first stage of labour. Exclusion: women moved to continuous CTG monitoring during the period reviewed.
sample: 40 consecutive low-risk women having intermittent auscultation in established first stage over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Partogram/electronic labour record auscultation entries
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 15-minute auscultation timer into the electronic partogram that flags amber when 12 minutes have elapsed since the last entry and red at 15 minutes, visible on the ward dashboard.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; if the timer improves compliance, make it a permanent feature of the electronic partogram build
evidence: no closed-loop audit of intermittent auscultation frequency found in the library
pitfalls: Paper partograms with gaps in recording → exclude labours with more than 20% missing entries and note the exclusion rate
Busy labour ward staffing may make 15-minute auscultation genuinely difficult → review staffing ratios alongside the audit, not instead of the process change
Definition of 'established first stage' varies between recorders → agree the definition (4 cm plus regular contractions) with the labour ward before data collection
One midwife's caseload dominating the sample → sample across shifts and midwives
Improvement fading after the audit team moves on → make the electronic timer the permanent default rather than a temporary poster
pearls: Recruit a practice development midwife to co-lead so the change is owned by the ward, not just the audit team
Pilot the electronic timer on one bay before full roll-out to iron out false alarms
Use real (anonymised) examples of delayed auscultation from incident reports to explain the 'why' at launch
Cross-reference with the labour ward's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK action plan so this audit is not seen as a duplicate task
Feed results back to individual midwives confidentially as well as to the team, to support learning
effort: ~25 min per 10 labours from the partogram

question: Once a woman has signs of, or is in confirmed second stage of labour, what proportion of documented intermittent auscultations were performed at least once every 5 minutes?
why: Each Baby Counts identified failure to increase the frequency of intermittent auscultation in second stage as a recurring contributory factor in intrapartum harm; this specific second-stage frequency has not had a closed-loop audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.2.10 (2007, amended 2026)
standard.wording: Once the woman has signs of, or is in confirmed second stage of labour: perform intermittent auscultation immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, repeated at least once every 5 minutes and record it as a single rate.

pass: In second stage, the interval between two consecutive documented auscultations does not exceed 5 minutes
population: Inclusion: women on intermittent auscultation who reach second stage of labour. Exclusion: women converted to continuous CTG before or during second stage.
sample: 40 consecutive women who laboured with intermittent auscultation and reached second stage over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Partogram/electronic labour record and second stage record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a distinct 'second stage' mode to the electronic partogram auscultation timer that shortens the alert interval from 15 to 5 minutes as soon as second stage is confirmed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; embed the second-stage timer mode as a permanent EPR feature if compliance improves
evidence: no closed-loop audit of second-stage intermittent auscultation frequency found in the library
pitfalls: Ambiguity about the exact moment second stage starts → use the documented time of full dilatation or bearing-down urge as the trigger, agreed in advance
Very short second stages give few data points → record the number of auscultations expected as well as achieved
Staff may confuse this with the separate first-stage 15-minute standard → make the EPR mode change explicit and visible
Retrospective note review may miss verbal-only auscultations → accept only documented entries as per protocol
Losing momentum after go-live → include the second-stage timer in new starter induction
pearls: Pair this audit with the first-stage auscultation audit so both cycles share the same data collection visit
Get labour ward coordinator sign-off on the definition of second stage onset before starting
Use huddle boards to display real-time compliance during the embedding phase
Link learning to the unit's Each Baby Counts action plan
Keep sample size and season consistent at re-audit
effort: ~25 min per 10 labours from the partogram

question: In women starting induction of labour, what proportion had a Bishop score and antenatal cardiotocography documented before the first method of induction was started?
why: Assessment before induction confirms the baby is suitable for induction and that the fetal heart rate is normal; the corpus has induction of labour practice audits [general] but no closed-loop audit of pre-induction assessment completeness.

standard.source: NICE NG207 Inducing labour, rec 1.5.1 (2008, amended 2021)
standard.wording: Ensure the position of the baby and the woman's condition are suitable for induction by: abdominally assessing the level and stability of the fetal head in the lower part of the uterus at or near the pelvic brim ... assessing and recording the Bishop score, confirming a normal fetal heart rate pattern using antenatal cardiotocography interpretation, confirming the absence of significant uterine contractions (not Braxton-Hicks) using cardiotocography.

pass: A Bishop score and a CTG confirming a normal fetal heart rate pattern are both documented in the notes before the first induction method (sweep excluded) is administered
population: Inclusion: all women undergoing induction of labour on the delivery suite or induction ward. Exclusion: induction started in extremis (category 1 indication) where immediate delivery supersedes assessment.
sample: 40 consecutive women started on induction of labour over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Induction of labour proforma and CTG trace
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Redesign the induction of labour proforma so the Bishop score box and a mandatory pre-induction CTG result field must both be completed before the first prostaglandin, balloon or amniotomy step can be signed for.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity governance meeting; if compliant, roll the redesigned proforma out across the induction ward and delivery suite
evidence: no closed-loop audit of pre-induction Bishop score and CTG assessment found in the library
pitfalls: Bishop score sometimes recorded narratively rather than as a number → accept only a numeric or component score as compliant
CTG performed but not formally reported before induction starts → require a documented category (normal/suspicious/pathological), not just a trace reference
Staff shortages leading to skipped pre-induction CTG on busy days → escalate persistent gaps to the labour ward matron
Retrospective note-finding may undercount compliance if records are split between paper and EPR → check both systems for each case
Definition drift between cycles (e.g. accepting an antenatal CTG from earlier in the day as 'pre-induction') → fix the definition (within 4 hours of starting) before cycle 1
pearls: Involve the induction ward coordinator in designing the proforma change
Pilot the new proforma for two weeks and fix obvious problems before the full re-audit
Use real anonymised delayed-recognition cases to make the case for the change at launch
Keep the same definition of 'before induction started' across both cycles
Feed back individual near-misses privately as well as team results
effort: ~20 min per 10 inductions from the induction proforma

question: In women having active management of the third stage after a vaginal birth, what proportion received the uterotonic at the correct dose and route (10 units oxytocin IM, 5 units oxytocin IV, or 5 units oxytocin plus 500 micrograms ergometrine IM)?
why: Active management substantially reduces postpartum haemorrhage, but the correct 2023-updated dose and route of oxytocin is not yet embedded everywhere; no closed-loop audit of third-stage uterotonic dose and route accuracy is in the library (carbetocin at caesarean birth is separately audited [NNA-203]).

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.10.11 (2023)
standard.wording: For active management after vaginal birth, administer 10 units of oxytocin (by intramuscular injection), 5 units of oxytocin (by intravenous injection, see recommendation 1.10.12) or 5 units of oxytocin plus 500 micrograms of ergometrine (by intramuscular injection) immediately after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut.

pass: The uterotonic given for active management is one of the three NICE-specified dose/route combinations, given after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut
population: Inclusion: women having a vaginal birth who chose active management of the third stage. Exclusion: physiological management, caesarean births.
sample: 40 consecutive vaginal births with active third-stage management over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Birth register/electronic labour record drug administration entries
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the third-stage drug chart pre-print with the three NICE-approved oxytocin/ergometrine dose-route options only, removing any legacy non-standard options.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward drug safety meeting; if compliant, standardise the pre-print across all birth settings including the midwifery-led unit
evidence: no closed-loop audit of active third-stage uterotonic dose and route accuracy found in the library
pitfalls: Legacy local practice (e.g. syntometrine as default) may persist after guidance changes → communicate the 2023 update explicitly to all grades of staff
Documentation of exact time relative to cord clamping is often absent → add a simple tick box rather than relying on free text
Small numbers if the maternity unit has a low birth rate → extend the collection period
Staff may conflate this with the caesarean carbetocin standard → make clear this audit is for vaginal births only
Improvement fading if the old pre-printed chart re-enters stock → destroy old stock once the new chart is live
pearls: Involve the labour ward pharmacist in redesigning the drug chart
Brief anaesthetic and obstetric staff as well as midwives, since doctors sometimes give the third-stage drug at instrumental births
