Keep the audit result visible on the ED results board so staff see their own performance in real time.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from LIMS and ED pathway timestamps
pass: For every patient on the pathway, the second troponin sample is drawn between 2.5 and 3.5 hours after the first, as timestamped by the laboratory information system.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of samples sent to the laboratory are rejected because the patient identifiers on the sample do not match, or are missing from, the request?
why: No audit of overall sample-labelling rejection rate exists in the library, despite this being the single most common preventable cause of transfusion and other laboratory sample rejection nationally.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final), item viii Primary identifier
standard.wording: The NHS number or in Scotland the Community Health Index (CHI) to be used as the primary identifier.

population: Inclusion: all samples received by the core laboratory (biochemistry, haematology, microbiology) over the sample period. Exclusion: samples from services with a separate, already-audited labelling standard (for example transfusion, audited nationally).
sample: All rejected samples over the last month, plus a denominator of total samples received in the same period, from the LIMS rejection log.
data_source: LIMS sample-rejection log and total accession count.
change: Introduce point-of-collection barcode or electronic positive-patient-identification labelling in the two clinical areas generating the most labelling rejections, so labels are printed and applied at the bedside as a single continuous step.
target: Rejection rate below 1% of samples received
reaudit: At 4 months, same clinical areas.
close_loop: Present at the pathology and nursing/phlebotomy joint governance meeting; expand electronic labelling to further wards if the pilot areas show a sustained fall.
evidence: [7693] transfusion sample mislabelling and wrong blood in tube: rejection rate rose from 2.99% to 4.4% between the 2012 and 2022 national comparative audits despite more sites introducing bedside electronic labelling (23% of sites, up 224%)
pitfalls: Rejection reasons are recorded inconsistently between shifts → agree one coded reason list before cycle 1.
Areas with the highest rejection rates resist being singled out → present rates by ward without individual staff names to keep the focus on the system.
A resampling delay from a rejected sample can itself cause harm (for example delayed antibiotics) → track this delay as a balancing measure.
Electronic labelling pilots stall without dedicated project support → assign a named implementation lead before starting.
Gains fade once new staff are not trained on the labelling process → include it in ward induction.
pearls: Recruit a biomedical scientist and a ward sister from the pilot area together.
Use the national transfusion comparative audit findings [7693] to show this is a recognised, worsening national problem, which helps secure support for change.
Report the resampling delay in hours as a tangible harm measure alongside the rejection rate.
Keep the barcode/electronic labelling pilot data live on a ward dashboard to sustain engagement.
effort: ~15 min per week from the LIMS rejection log
pass: Every sample accepted by the laboratory carries the patient's NHS number (or CHI in Scotland) along with name and date of birth, matching the request form exactly; any mismatch results in rejection and a logged reason.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adult inpatients have the same blood test (full blood count or urea and electrolytes) requested and performed twice within a 24-hour period without a new clinical indication documented?
why: No audit of unnecessary duplicate ward blood test ordering exists in the library; related work shows unnecessary preoperative testing is common and responds well to a simple system change [7076][6456].

standard.source: Local standard, informed by NICE guideline NG45 on routine preoperative tests for elective surgery and Choosing Wisely UK principles on avoiding unnecessary repeat testing
standard.wording: Local standard: a repeat full blood count or urea and electrolytes test within 24 hours of a normal or unchanged previous result should have a documented new clinical indication (for example a change in condition, a new treatment started, or a scheduled monitoring protocol).

population: Inclusion: adult general medical or surgical inpatients with two or more requests for the same FBC or U&E panel within a 24-hour period. Exclusion: patients on a recognised monitoring protocol requiring daily or more frequent testing (e.g. acute kidney injury, electrolyte replacement).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible duplicate-test episodes over the last month, identified from the LIMS by matching patient and test type within 24 hours.
data_source: LIMS request history, medical and nursing notes.
change: Add a soft-stop alert to the electronic ordering system that flags when the same test has been requested within the last 24 hours and asks the ordering clinician to confirm the reason before the request is submitted.
target: ≥85% of repeats with a documented reason (equivalently, ≤15% unexplained duplicate requests)
reaudit: At 3 months, same identification method.
close_loop: Present at the medical directorate quality meeting; if repeats fall, report the laboratory cost and phlebotomy time saved to sustain support for the alert.
evidence: [7076] routine preoperative blood tests for elective breast surgery: education and a poster cut inappropriate tests and produced a 71% reduction in spend
[6456] reducing unnecessary liver function tests on the paediatric intensive care unit (related unnecessary-testing audit, different population)
pitfalls: Genuine monitoring protocols (e.g. daily U&E on IV fluids) are wrongly flagged as unnecessary duplicates → build an explicit exclusion list before cycle 1.
Junior doctors order repeats defensively out of habit → pair the alert with a short teaching session on when repeat testing adds value.
The soft-stop is clicked through without real thought → sample-check a subset of overridden alerts for a genuine reason.
Reducing tests could delay detection of real deterioration → monitor a balancing measure such as unplanned escalations to ensure safety is not compromised.
Savings are hard to attribute without a clear baseline → record baseline test volume and cost before the alert goes live.
pearls: Recruit a biochemistry or haematology lead and a ward-based junior doctor educational supervisor.
Present the laboratory cost per avoided test as a concrete number for the business case.
Use existing LIMS request-pattern reports rather than manual note review to identify duplicate episodes quickly.
Share results with the trust's phlebotomy service, since fewer unnecessary requests reduce patient venepuncture burden too.
effort: ~15 min per 10 duplicate episodes from the LIMS and notes
pass: Where the same test is repeated within 24 hours, the request or notes record a specific new clinical reason (deterioration, new treatment, scheduled protocol); a repeat with no reason documented fails.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of unexpected malignant findings identified by pathology from a specimen taken for a benign or unrelated indication are actively flagged to the requesting clinician by telephone or an equivalent direct alert, in addition to the standard report?
why: No audit specifically of the active flagging step (as opposed to the eventual clinical action) for unexpected malignancy exists in the library; the corpus entry on this topic measures action within 14 days of the report, not whether an active alert was sent at the time of reporting [NNA-264].

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for the communication of radiological reports and fail-safe alert notification (2016)
standard.wording: Local policies of the referring institution will also define the need to send fail-safe alerts, for example, where there is a suspected but unexpected cancer on imaging... Significant, important, unexpected and actionable findings: Cases where the reporting radiologist feels that the findings are important and a fail-safe alert should be added to the normal communication method to ensure that they are acted upon in a timely manner.

population: Inclusion: all pathology and imaging reports over the audit period coded as containing an unexpected malignant finding unrelated to the original clinical question. Exclusion: findings that are the expected subject of the request (e.g. a cancer resection specimen).
sample: All eligible cases over the last 6 months (expect a small number; extend the window if fewer than 20 are found).
data_source: LIMS/RIS unexpected-finding flag, fail-safe communication log.
change: Add a mandatory 'unexpected malignancy - fail-safe alert sent' field, with recipient name, role and time, to the LIMS/RIS reporting template whenever the unexpected-finding code is used.
reaudit: At 6 months, same source.
close_loop: Present at the joint pathology/radiology/MDT governance meeting; keep the mandatory field permanently if it is being reliably completed.
evidence: No audit of the active fail-safe alerting step (distinct from downstream action) for unexpected malignancy exists in the library
pitfalls: Reporters assume the standard report is enough and skip the extra alert → make the extra step explicit and separately auditable.
Small numbers make percentages swing on one case → report a running total across the audit period.
The alert is sent but not documented → count only documented alerts, since undocumented ones cannot be relied on later.
Weekend and out-of-hours cases have a different, less reliable alerting pathway → check this specifically as a sub-group.
Teams push back that this duplicates the MDT listing process → clarify that the alert is the immediate safety net, separate from and faster than the next MDT.
pearls: Recruit both a pathologist and a radiologist, since unexpected malignancy can arise from either specialty.
Cross-check against the MDT tracking list to find any cases that were never alerted at all.
Use this audit as a template for other 'significant, important, unexpected and actionable' findings beyond malignancy.
Report the time from authorisation to alert as well as whether an alert happened, to show speed as well as completeness.
effort: ~20 min per case from LIMS/RIS and communication logs
pass: For every pathology or imaging report containing an unexpected malignant finding unrelated to the requested indication, a fail-safe alert (telephone call, electronic flag or equivalent) is documented as sent, separate from the routine report, on the day of authorisation.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: Of positive blood cultures that grow after a patient has already been discharged from hospital, what proportion are telephoned within 2 hours of the result becoming available to a named clinician in the last team that cared for the patient?
why: No audit of post-discharge positive blood culture communication timeliness exists in the library, even though this is a recognised patient-safety gap distinct from the pre-discharge critical-result pathway.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of biochemistry, haematology, medical microbiology and virology critical requests phoned/actively communicated by laboratory within 2 hours of result being available to the laboratory (includes out of hours)... Local agreements must be in place to cover patient pathways defining critical results and providing clear lines of communication and failsafe systems.

population: Inclusion: all blood cultures that flag positive after the patient's discharge date over the audit period. Exclusion: contaminants agreed as not clinically significant by the reporting microbiologist.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 3 months (expect a small but important number in most trusts).
data_source: Microbiology LIMS positive-culture flag, on-call communication log.
change: Add a 'patient discharged' flag to the microbiology LIMS positive-culture screen that automatically shows the last ward and the agreed emergency contact route (ED results clinician or ward team bleep), so the on-call biomedical scientist does not need to search manually.
reaudit: At 6 months, same source.
close_loop: Present at the microbiology and acute medicine joint governance meeting; keep the automatic flag permanently if the target is met.
evidence: No post-discharge positive blood culture communication audit exists in the library; related work on blood cultures covers pre-discharge use in pyrexial surgical patients [1975]
pitfalls: The patient's GP is contacted instead of a hospital clinician with no documented handover of responsibility → require a named hospital clinician contact as the primary route, with GP notification as a secondary step.
Contact details for the discharging team are out of date → build the flag from the live bed management system, not a static ward list.
Small numbers make a single missed case very visible → use this as a positive, since even one miss should trigger a review.
Weekend discharges create a longer gap before someone reads the flag → check weekday/weekend performance separately.
Staff assume 'it will be picked up at GP follow-up' → make clear the 2-hour standard applies regardless of onward care plans.
pearls: Recruit the microbiology on-call lead and the acute medicine discharge team.
Use the existing critical-result LIMS infrastructure as the base and add the discharge-specific flag on top, rather than building something new.
Report each case as a mini case review at the microbiology governance meeting, given the low numbers and high stakes.
Share results with the ED, since it often becomes the default contact point for discharged patients.
effort: ~15 min per case from LIMS and on-call logs
pass: For each positive blood culture that turns positive after discharge, the microbiology on-call record shows a named clinician contacted by telephone within 2 hours, with the patient's last ward or team and the contact route documented.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of out-of-hours laboratory results requiring urgent clinical action are successfully communicated to primary care before the practice next opens?
why: No audit of out-of-hours critical-result communication specifically to primary care (as opposed to hospital teams) exists in the library.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final), guidance reference: Out-of-hours reporting of laboratory results requiring urgent clinical action to primary care: Advice to pathologists and those that work in laboratory medicine (RCPath, 2010)
standard.wording: Out-of-hours reporting of laboratory results requiring urgent clinical action to primary care: Advice to pathologists and those that work in laboratory medicine, The Royal College of Pathologists, 2010.

population: Inclusion: all GP-requested critical results generated out of hours (evenings, nights, weekends) over the sample period. Exclusion: results on hospital inpatients, audited under the hospital critical-result pathway.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 2-3 months (expect a modest number; extend the window if fewer than 20 are found).
data_source: LIMS out-of-hours critical-result log, GP communication record.
change: Agree a single, published out-of-hours contact route (a named number covering the local out-of-hours GP service) with primary care commissioners, and make it the default option on the LIMS critical-result communication screen for GP-requested tests.
reaudit: At 4 months, same source.
close_loop: Present jointly at the laboratory governance meeting and the primary care/CCG-equivalent quality meeting; keep the agreed contact route live and review it annually.
evidence: No out-of-hours primary care critical-result communication audit exists in the library
pitfalls: GP practice contact numbers on requests are out of date → validate contact details against a current practice directory rather than the request form alone.
Out-of-hours GP services change provider without the laboratory being told → build a review of the contact route into the annual service review.
Small numbers make a single failure look large → report cumulatively over a longer period.
Biomedical scientists are unsure whom to call and default to 'no action' → give a clear escalation script and contact list at each workstation.
Gains fade if the agreed number is not kept up to date after staff turnover → assign ownership to a named laboratory manager.
pearls: Recruit a GP with an interest in patient safety, plus the laboratory out-of-hours lead, as joint authors.
Use this audit to formalise a route that may currently be informal or ad hoc.
Share results at a primary care network or locality meeting, since GPs are the direct beneficiaries.
Keep a simple laminated escalation card at the out-of-hours bench with the current contact numbers.
effort: ~15 min per case from LIMS and communication logs
pass: For every GP-requested result meeting the local critical-result list generated out of hours, the LIMS shows a documented, successful communication route to the GP practice (or the out-of-hours GP service) before the practice's next opening time.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of babies referred after newborn hearing screening actually attend their audiological assessment appointment within 4 weeks of the screening outcome (or by the corrected equivalent age if born prematurely)?
why: No audit of the national newborn hearing screening attendance standard exists in the library; this measures a different step from the appointment-offered standard, since offering an appointment on time does not guarantee attendance.

standard.source: NHS Newborn Hearing Screening Programme, Newborn hearing screening programme standards (NHSP-S05)
standard.wording: NHSP-S05: time from screening outcome to attendance at an audiological assessment appointment. Babies should attend appointments within less than 4 weeks (28 days), or corrected age if born prematurely. Acceptable level: greater than or equal to 90.0%; achievable level: greater than or equal to 95.0%.

population: Inclusion: all babies referred for audiological assessment following newborn hearing screening over the sample period. Exclusion: babies referred through other routes outside the screening programme.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible referrals over the last 3 months, from the audiology booking and attendance system.
data_source: Audiology appointment attendance record, newborn hearing screening programme IT system.
change: Introduce a structured DNA-recovery process: any family who does not attend the first offered appointment is telephoned within 48 hours and offered a new slot within the remaining part of the 28-day window, rather than waiting for the next routine recall letter.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample source.
close_loop: Present at the newborn hearing screening quarterly quality assurance meeting alongside the NHSP-S04 result, and report against the national standard.
evidence: No attendance-specific audit against NHSP-S05 exists in the library; the companion offer-timeliness audit (NHSP-S04) is the nearest related measure
pitfalls: Families who move or change contact details between screening and the appointment are hard to trace, inflating apparent DNA rates → cross-check against the child health information system for a current address before counting a DNA.
Interpreter needs are not flagged at booking, leading to avoidable non-attendance → record whether an interpreter was booked when needed.
Transport or distance to the audiology clinic is a common but unrecorded barrier → add a free-text reason field for non-attendance.
Rebooked appointments outside the 28-day window are still recorded as 'attended' without flagging the delay → capture both dates in the template.
Gains fade if the 48-hour DNA callback is only done when staff have spare capacity → make it a defined task on the audiology admin rota.
pearls: Recruit an audiology administrator who manages DNAs day to day as co-author.
Use health visitor contacts as an additional route to encourage attendance for families who are hard to reach by phone.
Report DNA reasons thematically to target the fix (for example, transport support for families without a car).
Share the combined NHSP-S04/S05 results with the regional newborn hearing screening quality assurance coordinator, since these feed national reporting.
effort: ~10 min per 10 referrals from the audiology system
pass: The audiology system shows attendance at the assessment appointment within 28 days of the screening outcome date, or by the equivalent corrected age.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adults assessed in routine adult hearing aid audiology clinics with sudden or rapid sensorineural hearing loss (a drop of more than 30 dB across at least three adjacent audiometric frequencies within 72 hours, or rapid progressive loss) are referred the same day for urgent medical assessment rather than continued on the routine pathway?
why: No audit exists in the library of whether audiology staff correctly identify and fast-track this specific non-routine presentation using the defined clinical criteria, as distinct from the ENT-side referral-to-treatment time audits already in the corpus.

standard.source: British Academy of Audiology, Guidance on Identifying Non-Routine Cases of Hearing Loss in Adults (April 2015)
standard.wording: Sudden or rapid hearing loss: Either a greater than 30 dB deterioration in sensorineural hearing loss occurring in at least three adjacent audiometric frequencies over 72 hours or less, or rapid onset of hearing loss or rapid deterioration in hearing.

population: Inclusion: all adults assessed in routine adult audiology clinics whose audiogram and history meet the BAA sudden/rapid hearing loss definition over the sample period. Exclusion: patients already under active ENT follow-up for the same episode.
sample: All eligible cases identified over the last 6-12 months (expect a small number; extend the window if fewer than 15 are found), cross-checked against clinic audiograms flagged for a sudden asymmetric or rapid change.
data_source: Audiology clinic record, audiogram comparison with any prior test, referral letter.
change: Add the BAA sudden/rapid hearing loss criteria as a mandatory check to the audiology assessment template, with an automatic same-day referral pathway (a single agreed phone number or e-referral route) triggered whenever the criteria are met.
reaudit: At 6 months, same identification method.
close_loop: Present at the audiology and ENT joint governance meeting; keep the mandatory check and referral pathway live if the target is sustained.
evidence: No audit of audiology-side identification of sudden/rapid hearing loss against this BAA definition exists in the library; related ENT-side pathway audits measure time from referral to steroid treatment once the diagnosis is already made
pitfalls: Audiologists are unfamiliar with the precise BAA numerical definition and under- or over-refer → include worked examples in training before cycle 1.
No prior audiogram exists for comparison, making 'sudden' hard to confirm from a single visit → use the history (rate of symptom onset) as an equally valid trigger per the BAA definition.
Same-day referral pathways differ between weekday and weekend clinics → check both separately.
Small numbers make a single missed case dominate → review each miss individually as a case review, not just a percentage.
The urgent referral pathway exists on paper but the phone number is out of date → test the pathway before cycle 1 begins.
pearls: Recruit a hearing aid audiologist and an ENT consultant together, since the fix crosses both services.
Use existing audiogram comparison software, if available, to flag a sudden drop automatically at the point of testing.
Share the BAA definition as a laminated quick-reference card in each audiology test room.
Track time from same-day referral to first ENT contact as a natural follow-on audit.
effort: ~20 min per identified case from audiology and referral records
pass: Where the audiogram and history meet the BAA definition of sudden or rapid hearing loss, the audiology record shows a same-day referral for urgent medical assessment (ENT or emergency department), not a routine hearing aid pathway appointment.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adults referred to a hearing aid service with confirmed sensorineural hearing loss suitable for amplification are fitted with their first hearing aid within 18 weeks of referral?
why: No audit of hearing aid fitting waiting times exists in the library, even though prolonged waits are a recognised access issue and the routine adult hearing aid pathway is explicitly funded to provide this service.

standard.source: Local standard, informed by the NHS Constitution 18-week referral-to-treatment standard and British Academy of Audiology description of the routine adult hearing aid pathway
standard.wording: Local standard: adults referred into the routine, direct-referral adult hearing aid pathway who are assessed as suitable for amplification should have their first hearing aid fitted within 18 weeks of referral, in line with the NHS referral-to-treatment standard, since (as the British Academy of Audiology notes) 'Routine, direct referral adult care pathways in the UK specifically fund hearing aid fitting'.

population: Inclusion: adults referred to the routine adult hearing aid pathway, assessed and found suitable for amplification, over the sample period. Exclusion: patients identified as non-routine/complex under BAA criteria (audited separately) and those who decline or delay fitting by choice.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients who completed fitting in the last 3 months, from the audiology patient administration system.
data_source: Audiology patient administration system referral and fitting dates.
change: Introduce a 'straight to fit' pathway for straightforward, symmetrical age-related hearing loss, combining assessment and fitting in a single appointment where clinically appropriate, to reduce the number of separate visits driving the wait.
reaudit: At 6 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the audiology service and commissioner quality meeting; if achieved, embed the combined assessment-and-fit appointment as the default booking template.
evidence: No hearing aid fitting waiting-time audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Patients who decline an offered earlier appointment are wrongly counted as breaches → record patient-choice delays separately from service delays.
Hearing aid stock shortages for a particular model cause a spike in delays → track stock-related delays as a distinct reason code.
Complex or non-routine cases referred on to ENT are wrongly included, understating true routine-pathway performance → apply the exclusion consistently.
Waiting list data quality varies between clinics using different booking systems → validate a sample manually where systems differ.
Gains fade once waiting lists grow again after a temporary staffing boost → track the wait as a rolling monthly metric, not a one-off snapshot.
pearls: Recruit the audiology service manager and a senior hearing aid audiologist as co-authors.
Use the 'straight to fit' pathway pilot data to make a business case for wider rollout if it shortens waits without compromising quality.
Report waiting times alongside patient-reported outcome measures (for example hearing aid use at 3 months) to show waits are not just a numbers exercise.
Share results with commissioners, since hearing aid waiting times are often a locally monitored access metric.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from the audiology patient administration system
pass: The audiology record shows the date of first hearing aid fitting within 18 weeks of the original referral date, for patients assessed as routine and suitable for amplification.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of females aged 12 to 55 attending the general (non-obstetric, non-orthopaedic-theatre) radiology department for a CT or fluoroscopic examination have a documented pregnancy status enquiry before the exposure?
why: No audit of pregnancy enquiry for general outpatient and inpatient radiology attendances exists in the library; existing entries cover orthopaedic theatre fluoroscopy and emergency surgical admissions, not the general radiology department pathway.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 11(1)(f)
standard.wording: A person must not carry out an exposure unless... in the case of an individual of childbearing potential, the person has enquired whether that individual is pregnant or breastfeeding, if relevant.

population: Inclusion: all females aged 12-55 attending general radiology (X-ray, CT, fluoroscopy) as outpatients or inpatients over the sample period. Exclusion: obstetric ultrasound and orthopaedic theatre exposures (audited under separate department-specific pathways).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last month, from the RIS.
data_source: RIS pre-exposure checklist, radiographer's exposure record.
change: Add a mandatory pregnancy-status field to the RIS pre-exposure checklist for all females aged 12-55, which the radiographer must complete before the exposure can be recorded as performed.
reaudit: At 3 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the radiology governance meeting; keep the mandatory RIS field permanently if the target is sustained, and include it in the department's written employer's procedures under IR(ME)R regulation 6.
evidence: No general radiology department pregnancy-enquiry audit exists in the library; related work covers orthopaedic theatre fluoroscopy (a proposed audit) and pregnancy testing in emergency surgical admissions [7712][6008]
pitfalls: Reception staff, not radiographers, ask the question and it is not passed on → clarify in the written procedure who is responsible and where it must be recorded.
The question is skipped for 'obviously' post-menopausal-looking patients → apply the age-band policy strictly regardless of appearance.
Urgent inpatient and out-of-hours exposures bypass the outpatient checklist → build the same mandatory field into the inpatient/urgent request workflow.
Patients decline to answer and this is recorded as 'not pregnant' by default → give 'declined to answer' as its own option requiring an escalation to the practitioner.
Gains fade after a RIS upgrade resets the field to optional → re-check after every system change.
pearls: Recruit the radiology superintendent radiographer and radiation protection supervisor together.
Use the RIS audit trail to pull data quickly rather than manual note review.
Cross-check the CT/fluoroscopy subgroup separately from plain film, since the fetal dose stakes differ.
Present this alongside the department's IR(ME)R regulation 7 clinical audit programme so it counts towards the statutory requirement.
effort: ~10 min per 10 attendances from the RIS
pass: A dated entry, made by the radiographer or radiology reception before the exposure, records that the patient was asked whether she is or might be pregnant, with the answer given.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of CT and MRI requests from general medical and surgical wards (excluding fracture clinic, already audited separately) state a specific clinical question that the imaging is expected to answer?
why: No audit of referrer information quality for general ward CT/MRI requests exists in the library; the corpus contains a related audit for fracture clinic X-ray requests only.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 10(5)
standard.wording: The referrer must supply the practitioner with sufficient medical data (such as previous diagnostic information or medical records) relevant to the exposure requested by the referrer to enable the practitioner to decide whether there is a sufficient net benefit as required by regulation 11(1)(b).

population: Inclusion: all CT and MRI requests from general adult medical and surgical inpatient wards over the sample period. Exclusion: fracture clinic and orthopaedic theatre requests (covered elsewhere), emergency department requests (a distinct high-volume pathway).
sample: 40 consecutive requests over the last 2 weeks, from the RIS.
data_source: RIS request record, vetting comments.
change: Make a free-text 'clinical question this scan should answer' field mandatory on the electronic CT/MRI request form, separate from the diagnosis field, so vetting radiologists can justify the request without chasing the ward.
reaudit: At 3 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the radiology and medical/surgical directorate joint governance meeting; keep the mandatory field if it reduces vetting queries.
evidence: No general ward CT/MRI clinical-question audit exists in the library; the corpus's comparable fracture clinic X-ray request audit uses the same IR(ME)R regulation 10(5) standard
pitfalls: Requesters paste the working diagnosis into the clinical question field without a real question → sample-check for genuine, specific questions versus copied diagnoses.
Junior doctors under time pressure default to brief text → pair the mandatory field with a short example bank of good clinical questions.
Vetting practitioners approve requests anyway despite a vague question, masking the true problem → track the proportion of requests returned for more information as a balancing measure.
The field becomes a free-text box that is easy to leave blank if the system allows it → make it a genuine hard stop, not just a labelled box.
Out-of-hours or verbal requests bypass the electronic form → include a parallel requirement for the on-call radiologist to document the clinical question when accepting a verbal request.
pearls: Recruit a vetting radiologist and a ward-based junior doctor educational lead.
Use the RIS audit trail to identify requests quickly rather than manual chart review.
Publish a one-page 'how to write a good imaging request' guide alongside the change.
Track vetting turnaround time as a related outcome measure, since clear requests should be justified faster.
effort: ~10 min per 10 requests from the RIS
pass: The electronic request includes a specific clinical question or working diagnosis (not just a test name), sufficient for the vetting practitioner to make a justification decision without contacting the referrer.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: For nasogastric tubes checked by X-ray because pH testing failed or aspirate could not be obtained, what proportion have documentation confirming the X-ray viewed was the correct, most current image for that patient, how the tube position was interpreted, and the resulting decision on feeding, recorded before any feed or medication was given?
why: No audit of the specific NPSA/2011/PSA002 documentation requirements for X-ray-confirmed nasogastric tube position exists in the library, distinct from the corpus's existing sticker-completion audit which does not test all three documentation elements together against the original alert wording.

standard.source: National Patient Safety Agency, Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2011/PSA002, Reducing the risk of harm caused by misplaced nasogastric feeding tubes in adults, children and infants (10 March 2011)
standard.wording: Documentation of the tube placement checking process includes confirmation that any x-ray viewed was the most current x-ray for the correct patient, how placement was interpreted, and clear instructions as to required actions. Any tubes identified to be in the lung are removed immediately, whether in the x-ray department or clinical area.

population: Inclusion: all adult inpatients whose nasogastric tube position was confirmed by X-ray (as a second-line test after pH testing failed or no aspirate was obtained) over the sample period. Exclusion: tubes confirmed by pH testing alone.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible X-ray-confirmed tube placements over the last 2-3 months, from radiology and ward records.
data_source: NG tube bedside documentation chart, radiology report, ward nursing notes.
change: Redesign the NG tube bedside chart so the three documentation elements (correct/current X-ray confirmed, interpretation, feeding decision) are a single mandatory sequence that must be completed and signed by a competency-assessed individual before the 'feed commenced' box can be ticked.
reaudit: At 3 months, same sample size.
close_loop: Present at the trust patient safety/never events group, since misplaced NG tube feeding remains a Never Event category; keep the redesigned chart as the trust standard if the target is met.
evidence: [2329] closed-loop audit of NGT documentation using a sticker: sticker use 42.1% to 85%, position documented 63.1% to 75%, confirming staff recorded 60.5% to 75% after teaching and posters
[5472] avoiding never events in nasogastric intubation: interpretation errors fell from 7 to 1 and documentation improved by 22% after a mixed intervention
pitfalls: A sticker or chart is used but not fully completed, as shown in the corpus's own re-audit plateauing at 75-85% rather than 100% [2329] → require full completion, not partial, as the pass criterion.
Out-of-hours or agency staff are not trained in the competency framework → include NG tube X-ray interpretation competency in mandatory induction for all temporary staff.
The X-ray report and the bedside chart are completed by different people who do not cross-check each other → require the bedside documenter to state which X-ray (date/time) they reviewed.
Gains plateau rather than reach 100%, as seen in comparable audits [2329] → treat any gap as a live risk requiring a further PDSA cycle, not a finished project.
Feeding is started based on a verbal 'it looks fine' from radiology without full documentation → make the written record, not a verbal assurance, the requirement.
pearls: Recruit a ward sister, a radiographer/radiologist and the trust's patient safety lead together, since the corpus shows a mixed intervention (documentation, training and radiology involvement) works best [5472].
Use the trust's Never Events log as an early-warning cross-check for missed cases.
Reference the free e-learning tool for X-ray interpretation (as recommended in the alert) in staff training.
Report the audit at the same governance forum that reviews Never Events, to keep visibility high.
effort: ~15 min per case from NG tube charts and radiology reports
pass: The notes or NG tube chart record, before any feed or medication is given: confirmation the X-ray viewed was the current image for the correct patient, the interpreted position, and the resulting feeding decision, all signed and timed by a person assessed as competent.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adult CT pulmonary angiogram examinations for suspected pulmonary embolism have a dose-length product at or below the national diagnostic reference level for that examination?
why: No audit of CT pulmonary angiogram dose optimisation against the national diagnostic reference level exists in the library; a comparable audit exists for CT head in suspected stroke, but CTPA is a distinct high-volume examination with its own reference level.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 12(3)(c) (Optimisation); UKHSA National Diagnostic Reference Levels
standard.wording: Regulation 12(3)(c) requires the employer to establish diagnostic reference levels for standard radiodiagnostic examinations and to ensure they are used as part of the optimisation of exposures; UKHSA publishes the National Diagnostic Reference Levels used to benchmark local practice.

population: Inclusion: all adult CTPA examinations performed for suspected pulmonary embolism over the sample period on each scanner. Exclusion: paediatric examinations and CTPA performed for other indications (e.g. pre-procedural planning) where a different protocol may apply.
sample: 20 consecutive examinations per scanner over the last month, from the CT dose-recording system.
data_source: CT scanner dose report (DLP), medical physics expert's dose audit records.
change: Review the CTPA scan protocol on each scanner with the medical physics expert (tube current modulation, scan range, iterative reconstruction settings) and lock the optimised protocol so individual radiographers cannot alter key dose-determining parameters.
target: Median dose-length product at or below the national diagnostic reference level
reaudit: At 6 months, same scanners and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee and imaging governance meeting; if achieved, extend the locked-protocol approach to other high-volume CT examinations.
evidence: No CTPA-specific diagnostic reference level audit exists in the library; a related proposed audit covers CT head dose in suspected stroke against the national diagnostic reference level
pitfalls: Scan range is extended unnecessarily beyond the chest, inflating dose without diagnostic benefit → check scan range against the protocol as a specific data point, not just overall dose.
Obese or very large patients are compared against the same reference level without size adjustment → report by weight band, since diagnostic reference levels are typically set for a standard adult.
A single scanner with an outdated protocol skews the trust-wide average → report per scanner, not just an overall trust figure.
The medical physics expert review takes months to complete → set an interim manual check while the formal review is under way.
Gains fade after a software or protocol upgrade resets settings → re-verify dose data after any scanner software update.
pearls: Recruit the medical physics expert and CT superintendent radiographer as joint leads.
Use the scanner's automatic dose-recording software to pull data quickly rather than manual review of each study.
Compare results across all CT scanners in the department to identify and share best practice from the lowest-dose scanner.
Report dose trends over time on a simple run chart at the radiation protection committee.
effort: ~10 min per 10 examinations from the CT dose-recording system
pass: The median dose-length product for the audited sample of adult CTPA examinations is at or below the current UKHSA national diagnostic reference level for CT pulmonary angiography.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of interventional radiology procedures carried out under fluoroscopic or CT guidance have the total dose-area product or dose-length product for the procedure documented in the patient record?
why: No audit of interventional radiology procedure dose documentation (as distinct from diagnostic CT dose optimisation) exists in the library, despite interventional procedures often delivering the highest doses in a department.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, Schedule 2, paragraph 1(j)
standard.wording: Schedule 2 sets out the data to be recorded for each exposure, including the radiation dose delivered, which for interventional procedures includes the dose-area product or equivalent dose metric for the procedure.

population: Inclusion: all interventional radiology procedures using fluoroscopic or CT guidance over the sample period. Exclusion: diagnostic-only fluoroscopy studies (e.g. barium studies) without an interventional component.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology procedure log.
data_source: Interventional radiology procedure note, RIS/dose-tracking system.
change: Configure the interventional radiology system to automatically populate the total procedure dose into the electronic procedure note at the point the procedure is closed, removing reliance on manual transcription.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology and radiation protection joint governance meeting; keep the automatic dose transfer if the target is met.
evidence: No interventional radiology procedure dose-documentation audit exists in the library; a related proposed audit covers trauma theatre fluoroscopy dose recording in the operation note
pitfalls: Long or complex procedures with multiple fluoroscopy runs have the dose recorded only for the final run, understating the true total → confirm the figure used is the cumulative procedure total, not a single exposure.
Manual transcription from the fluoroscopy unit display to the notes introduces transcription errors → prefer automatic electronic transfer wherever the system allows it.

Skin-dose alert thresholds are confused with the routine dose-documentation requirement → keep this audit focused on documentation completeness, with skin-dose alerts as a separate, higher-threshold safety check.
Complex cases performed by visiting or locum interventionalists are more likely to have incomplete documentation → include this explicitly in visiting-practitioner induction.
Gains fade if the automatic transfer is not tested after an equipment software update → re-verify after any upgrade.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and radiation protection adviser together.
Use this audit to also identify any procedures approaching or exceeding local skin-dose alert thresholds, as a valuable by-product.
Report dose trends by procedure type to support future protocol optimisation work.
Present alongside the department's regulation 13 population dose estimate work, since procedure-level data feeds that wider requirement.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the procedure log
pass: The patient record (procedure note, RIS record or electronic dose report) documents the total dose-area product (fluoroscopy) or dose-length product (CT-guided) for the completed interventional procedure.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of routine antenatal screening samples for hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis and rubella susceptibility are reported, confirmed and electronically available to the requestor within 6 calendar days of the sample being taken?
why: No audit against this specific RCPath antenatal infection screening turnaround key performance indicator exists in the library, despite the direct harm from delayed hepatitis B and HIV results (missed opportunity for timely maternal and neonatal intervention).

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of routine antenatal screening tests for Hepatitis B, HIV, Syphilis, and Rubella susceptibility reported, confirmed, authorised and electronically available to requestor within 6 calendar days from sample being taken... Challenge: 90% by April 2012 increasing to 97% by April 2014.

population: Inclusion: all routine antenatal screening samples for hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis and rubella susceptibility taken at booking over the sample period. Exclusion: samples taken in labour or at late presentation.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible samples over the last 4-6 weeks, from the LIMS antenatal screening worklist.
data_source: LIMS sample-received and result-authorised timestamps, maternity booking record.
change: Route all antenatal booking bloods through a dedicated, prioritised antenatal screening batch on the analyser and serology platform, with an automatic exception report for any sample not authorised within 6 days sent to the lead biomedical scientist and named midwifery screening coordinator.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present jointly at the pathology and maternity screening governance meeting; keep the prioritised batch and exception report permanently if the target is met.
evidence: No audit against this specific antenatal screening turnaround KPI exists in the library
pitfalls: Late bookings and presentation in labour wrongly inflate the denominator → apply the exclusion criteria exactly as the KPI defines them.
Results are authorised on time but not passed to the midwifery team promptly, so the clinical benefit is lost even when the KPI is met → add the communication step as its own template field.
Repeat testing after an equivocal result is counted as a fresh breach → track repeats separately from the initial screen.
Serology platform downtime causes a batch delay affecting many samples at once → note any platform outage dates when interpreting results.
Gains fade once the dedicated batch is deprioritised during staff shortages → make the exception report, not just the batch process, the sustained safety net.
pearls: Recruit the antenatal screening coordinator midwife and a biomedical scientist from serology/virology together.
This maps to the National Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening Programme's own quality requirements, so the data has a second use beyond this audit.
Use the LIMS exception report as a live dashboard rather than a one-off manual pull.
Report separately for each of the four infections, since some (e.g. syphilis serology) may have different processing times than others.
effort: ~10 min per 10 samples from the LIMS antenatal worklist
pass: The LIMS shows the antenatal hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis and rubella result set authorised and available to the requestor within 6 calendar days of the sample being taken, excluding presentation in labour or late presentation.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of practitioners and operators carrying out exposures in the imaging department have an up-to-date training record, held by the employer, showing the dates and nature of the IR(ME)R training they have completed?
why: No audit of employer training-record completeness under IR(ME)R exists in the library, even though this is the specific, named record the enforcing authority may inspect.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 17(4)
standard.wording: The employer must keep and have available for inspection by the relevant enforcing authority an up-to-date record of all relevant training undertaken by all practitioners and operators engaged by the employer to carry out any exposures or any practical aspect of such exposures showing the date or dates on which training qualifying as adequate training was completed and the nature of the training.

population: Inclusion: all staff currently acting as a practitioner or operator under IR(ME)R in the imaging and nuclear medicine departments. Exclusion: staff whose role does not involve carrying out exposures or practical aspects of exposures.
sample: 30 named staff sampled from the current departmental staff list, cross-checked against the training record system.
data_source: Employer's IR(ME)R training record system, staff list.
change: Consolidate all IR(ME)R training evidence into the trust's single electronic learning management system, replacing paper certificates and local spreadsheets, with a standard record template capturing date and nature of training for every practitioner and operator.
reaudit: At 6 months, same staff sample.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee, since this record is a specific statutory duty subject to enforcing authority inspection; keep the consolidated system if the target is met.
evidence: No audit of IR(ME)R employer training-record completeness exists in the library
pitfalls: Training certificates are held by individual staff members rather than centrally by the employer, failing the regulation's requirement → require submission of a copy to the central record as a condition of the training counting.
New starters and locums are not added to the training record promptly → build training-record creation into the pre-employment/induction checklist.
Records show that training happened but not what it covered, failing the 'nature of training' requirement → require a brief description or course title, not just a date.
Staff who have moved role (e.g. from operator to also acting as practitioner) are not flagged for additional training → cross-check role changes against training records annually.
Gains fade after a learning management system migration loses historical records → export and archive records before any system change.
pearls: Recruit the radiation protection supervisor and trust education/learning management system administrator together.
Use this audit to also identify any staff whose training has lapsed and needs urgent renewal.
Report the audit result to the trust's statutory and mandatory training compliance dashboard, since it likely already has a reporting mechanism.
Keep a simple named list of practitioners and operators, updated whenever the rota changes, to make future audits quick.
effort: ~10 min per 10 staff records from the training system
pass: The employer's training record system holds, for each named practitioner and operator, the date and nature of their IR(ME)R training, and the record is available for inspection without needing to be reconstructed from memory or scattered files.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: For planned (non-emergency) interventional radiology procedures, what proportion of patients have their informed consent confirmed at a separate discussion with the radiologist actually performing the procedure, distinct from the initial information-giving discussion?
why: No audit of this specific two-stage consent process for interventional radiology exists in the library; the corpus's extensive consent-documentation topic focuses on written risk completeness on consent forms generally, not this process step unique to radiology.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition
standard.wording: Interventional or invasive radiological procedures require particular attention in obtaining the express consent of the patient. In a planned procedure, the patient should receive information, verbally or in writing, in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and to consult others if they so wish. The patient should have their informed consent confirmed at a separate discussion with the radiologist performing the procedure.

population: Inclusion: all planned (non-emergency) interventional radiology procedures over the sample period. Exclusion: emergency, unplanned procedures where the standard explicitly allows clinical judgement on timing.
sample: 40 consecutive planned procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology booking system.
data_source: Pre-procedure clinic letter or information-giving record, procedure day consent confirmation note.
change: Add a mandatory 'consent confirmed by performing radiologist' field, with date, time and location, to the interventional radiology electronic procedure record, separate from the initial information-giving documentation.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology governance meeting; keep the mandatory field permanently if the target is met.
evidence: The corpus's consent-documentation topic card describes this area as heavily over-audited for generic risk completeness (45 audits) but notes that whether consent starts in clinic rather than on the day is one of the under-explored angles the consultant advice recommends auditing instead
pitfalls: The 'separate discussion' happens in the procedure room immediately before sedation, which the standard specifically discourages → record the physical location, not just that a discussion happened.
Same-day add-on cases blur the distinction between initial information and confirmation → apply the emergency/unplanned exclusion strictly rather than stretching it to cover convenience add-ons.
A generic consent form is signed without evidence of a genuine second discussion → look for narrative evidence of the discussion, not just a signature.

Patients seen only briefly by a different radiologist than the one performing the procedure may not meet the standard's intent → record whether the confirming radiologist was the same person who performed the procedure.
Gains fade once the mandatory field becomes a box ticked without a real discussion → spot-check a sample against patient-reported experience where feasible.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse who runs pre-procedure clinics.
Use existing pre-assessment clinic letters as the source for the 'initial information' half of the audit.
Present findings alongside patient experience feedback on how well-prepared they felt for the procedure.
Keep this as a standing item in the interventional radiology multidisciplinary team meeting, not just a one-off project.
effort: ~15 min per 10 procedures from booking and consent records
pass: The notes record two distinct consent-related contacts: an initial information-giving discussion in advance of the procedure, and a separate confirmation of consent with the performing radiologist, both documented with dates.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of interventional radiology procedures classified locally as complex or carrying significant risk have written consent (a signed consent form), rather than verbal consent alone, documented before the procedure?
why: No audit specifically of the written-versus-verbal consent threshold for complex interventional radiology procedures exists in the library, separate from the general consent-completeness topic already heavily covered for surgical specialties.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition, citing General Medical Council guidance
standard.wording: The General Medical Council (GMC) suggests that written consent should be taken in cases where: the treatment or procedure is complex and involves significant risk and/or side-effects... With planned procedures, consideration should be given to asking the patient to sign a written consent form for those examinations and procedures which are recognised to be more complex to undertake or which potentially carry a more serious risk of complication.

population: Inclusion: all interventional radiology procedures on the department's agreed complex/significant-risk list over the sample period. Exclusion: procedures not on the list, where verbal consent with a documented discussion may be sufficient.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology log.
data_source: Interventional radiology procedure log, consent form archive.
change: Publish an agreed department list of procedures requiring written consent (built from the GMC/RCR criteria) and introduce procedure-specific consent forms for the highest-volume complex procedures, since the corpus shows procedure-specific forms are the fix that reliably works for consent completeness.
reaudit: At 4 months, same list and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology governance meeting; keep the published list and procedure-specific forms if the target is met.
evidence: The corpus's consent-documentation topic card reports that pre-printed or procedure-specific consent forms reach close to 100% completeness of documented risks, compared with teaching alone which gives only partial gains
pitfalls: Staff disagree on which procedures count as 'complex' without a published list → agree and publish the list with radiology leadership before cycle 1.
A generic hospital consent form is used instead of a procedure-specific one, missing procedure-relevant risks → track use of the correct, procedure-specific form as a separate data point.
Verbal consent is documented in detail but no form is signed, technically failing the standard despite good practice → count only signed forms as meeting 'written consent' for this audit.
Emergency conversions from a planned to an urgent procedure blur the consent pathway → record these separately rather than excluding them silently.
Gains plateau below 100% once the list is published but not enforced → build the list into the booking system so a procedure on it cannot be booked without a linked consent form.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse or consent lead as co-authors.
Reuse procedure-specific consent form templates from surgical specialties as a starting point where suitable.
Present the audit alongside the corpus's own consent-documentation learning (procedure-specific forms work; teaching alone does not) to justify the chosen fix.
Track patient understanding of risks as a longer-term follow-on measure once form completeness is achieved.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the consent form archive
pass: For every procedure on the department's locally agreed 'complex/significant risk' list, a signed written consent form is present in the record before the procedure starts.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of interventional radiology procedures have a completed Sign In, Time Out and Sign Out safety checklist, adapted from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist for radiological interventions, on file before, during and after the procedure?
why: No audit of WHO-style checklist completion specifically for interventional radiology procedures exists in the library, distinct from the theatre-based WHO checklist audits already covered for surgical specialties.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: for Radiological Interventions Only (adapted from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist)
standard.wording: The Royal College of Radiologists adapted the checklist of Safe Surgery from the World Health Organization for use in radiological interventions in England and Wales, entitled 'WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: for Radiological Interventions ONLY', with the three phases of Sign In, Team Time Out and Sign Out.

population: Inclusion: all interventional radiology procedures performed in the interventional suite over the sample period. Exclusion: bedside procedures performed outside the interventional suite (audited under a separate ward-based safety process).
sample: 40 consecutive procedures over the last month, from the interventional radiology log.
data_source: Interventional radiology WHO checklist form, procedure log.
change: Designate a named 'checklist champion' for each interventional radiology session, responsible for leading and confirming all three checklist phases out loud, with the checklist itself made a mandatory field in the electronic procedure record rather than a paper form that can be left incomplete.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology and theatre safety governance meeting; keep the checklist champion role and electronic mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: No interventional radiology-specific WHO checklist completion audit exists in the library
pitfalls: The checklist is completed retrospectively rather than in real time, defeating its safety purpose → spot-check timing against the procedure start time where the electronic system logs it.
Staff view the checklist as a barrier for 'quick' procedures and skip it → apply it to all procedures on the interventional list regardless of expected duration.
A paper checklist is easily lost or left blank → prefer an electronic mandatory field that blocks progression to the next step.

The general anaesthetic section, largely irrelevant to most interventional cases, causes staff to disengage with the whole checklist → confirm the department is using the RCR-adapted version, not the unmodified surgical version.
Champions rotate without a clear handover, and the role lapses → build champion allocation into the weekly interventional list planning.
pearls: Recruit an interventional radiology consultant and the lead interventional radiology nurse/radiographer together.
Designate a champion for each list as recommended in published implementation experience with this checklist.
Use a clipboard or fixed location for the checklist so it is always available at the point of use.
Report near-miss catches attributed to the checklist (e.g. wrong side identified at Time Out) as a powerful qualitative measure alongside completion rates.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the checklist archive
pass: All three phases of the checklist (Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out) are completed and filed in the procedure record for the case.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of patients undergoing an intimate radiological examination or procedure (for example transrectal or transvaginal procedures) have express consent and the offer of a chaperone documented before the examination?
why: No audit of chaperone offer and express consent documentation for intimate radiological examinations exists in the library.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition
standard.wording: Intimate examinations require particular attention and understanding to establish trust and mutual confidence between patient and doctor... Express consent, either verbally or in writing, should be obtained for intimate examinations and serious consideration should be given to the need to provide a chaperone.

population: Inclusion: all patients having an intimate radiological examination or procedure (e.g. transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound where performed by radiology) over the sample period. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible examinations over the last 2-3 months, from the department booking system.
data_source: Procedure note, department booking/checklist record.
change: Add a mandatory 'chaperone offered: outcome' field, alongside the express consent field, to the booking or procedure checklist for all examinations coded as intimate, so the step cannot be skipped or forgotten.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the department governance meeting; keep the mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: No chaperone/express-consent documentation audit for intimate radiological examinations exists in the library
pitfalls: Staff assume a chaperone is 'obviously' not needed for certain examinations and skip documenting the offer → require the field to be completed for every examination on the intimate-examination list, with 'not applicable' as an explicit, reasoned option rather than a blank.
Patients decline a chaperone and this is not distinguished from 'not offered' → give both options explicitly in the template.
Locum or visiting staff are unaware which examinations are classified as intimate locally → publish and circulate the local list.
The field exists on paper but not in the electronic system used for most bookings → prioritise adding it to whichever system captures the majority of these examinations.
Gains are not sustained after a staff rotation → include the requirement in departmental induction for new radiographers, sonographers and radiologists.
pearls: Recruit a radiographer or sonographer who regularly performs these examinations as co-author.
Publish a simple, agreed list of which examinations count as 'intimate' locally to reduce ambiguity.
Present alongside patient experience feedback, since chaperone offer is a well-recognised patient dignity marker.
Keep the audit brief and focused, since this is a quick, high-value dignity-of-care check rather than a complex clinical audit.
effort: ~10 min per 10 examinations from booking records
pass: The record shows express consent obtained (verbally or in writing) and documented consideration of a chaperone (offered and accepted, offered and declined, or not applicable with reason) before the examination.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: For planned interventional radiology procedures, what proportion of patients are given written, procedure-specific information in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and consult others if they wish?
why: No audit of the timing and adequacy of written pre-procedure information for interventional radiology exists in the library; the consent-documentation topic card in the corpus focuses on risks recorded on the form itself, not on information given in advance.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition
standard.wording: In a planned procedure, the patient should receive information, verbally or in writing, in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and to consult others if they so wish.

population: Inclusion: all planned (non-emergency) interventional radiology procedures booked at least 48 hours in advance over the sample period. Exclusion: emergency or same-day add-on procedures.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible planned procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology booking system.
data_source: Booking system record of information sent, pre-procedure clinic letter, patient information leaflet log.
change: Create a library of procedure-specific written information leaflets for the department's highest-volume interventional procedures, sent automatically (by post or patient portal) as soon as the procedure is booked, rather than being handed over only on the day.
reaudit: At 4 months, same sample specification.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology governance meeting; keep the automatic leaflet dispatch if the target is met.
evidence: The corpus's consent-documentation topic card notes that written information given to patients before surgery/procedures 'stayed 8-14%' in some audited settings even after a teaching-only intervention, suggesting this step is commonly under-delivered across specialties
pitfalls: A generic hospital leaflet is sent instead of a procedure-specific one, technically meeting a loose definition of 'written information' but not its intent → require the leaflet to name the specific procedure and its specific risks.
Late-booked planned procedures (booked less than 48 hours ahead) are wrongly included and unfairly counted as failures → apply the inclusion criterion strictly.
Patients report not receiving or not reading the leaflet despite a record that one was sent → consider a simple patient-reported cross-check for a subset of cases.
Leaflets are only available in English, disadvantaging patients needing another language or an accessible format → record whether an alternative format was needed and provided.
Gains fade once the automatic dispatch process is not checked after an IT system change → re-verify the automation after any booking system update.
pearls: Recruit a interventional radiology specialist nurse who manages pre-procedure information as co-author.
Start with the two or three highest-volume procedures to build the leaflet library quickly, then expand.
Ask patients directly (a brief survey) whether they felt they had enough information and time to decide, as a complementary patient experience measure.
Share the leaflet library with the pre-assessment or referring team so information can be given even earlier, at the point of referral.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the booking system
pass: The patient record shows written, procedure-specific information was given (posted, emailed or handed over in clinic) at least 24 hours before a planned interventional radiology procedure, excluding same-day emergency or urgent add-on cases.

question: What proportion of adults with a hip fracture have a physiotherapy assessment and are mobilised the day after surgery, unless medically or surgically contraindicated?
why: Early mobilisation after hip fracture reduces chest infection, pressure damage and loss of independence, but delayed first mobilisation is common when therapy staffing does not cover weekends. No closed-loop audit of day-after-surgery physiotherapy mobilisation for hip fracture inpatients has been published in the library; related fragility-fracture physiotherapy timing has been audited [ONA-157] but that audit explicitly excludes hip fracture.

standard.source: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.7.1 (2011)
standard.wording: Offer people a physiotherapy assessment and, unless medically or surgically contraindicated, mobilisation on the day after surgery.

pass: Physiotherapy assessment documented and mobilisation attempted on the calendar day after surgery, or a documented medical/surgical contraindication recorded that day
population: Inclusion: all adults admitted with a hip fracture who had surgery. Exclusion: patients managed non-operatively, patients who died before day 1, patients discharged before day 1
sample: 40 consecutive adults having hip fracture surgery over the last 2-3 months, from the hip fracture register/NHFD extract
data_source: Physiotherapy notes, NHFD/trauma database, nursing observations, EPR mobility entries
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'day-1 physiotherapy assessment and mobilisation attempt: yes/no, reason if no' field to the hip fracture pathway proforma, and extend weekend physiotherapy cover to match the day-of-week distribution of surgery.
reaudit: 8-10 weeks later, same template and sample size, after the weekend cover change
close_loop: Present at the trauma/orthogeriatric MDT meeting and the therapy department governance meeting; if the change works, embed the field permanently in the hip fracture EPR pathway and report day-1 mobilisation rates alongside other NHFD key performance indicators.
evidence: [ONA-157] fragility fractures other than hip: BOAST day-after-surgery physiotherapy standard used as a comparable, unaudited-for-hip-fracture criterion
[ONA-008] hip fracture nerve block within 4 hours: shows the corpus already tracks other NHFD-linked timing indicators for this population
pitfalls: Weekend and bank holiday surgery has no physiotherapy cover → negotiate 7-day therapy rotas with the therapy lead before cycle 1
Contraindications are recorded inconsistently or not at all → add a mandatory free-text reason field so 'not mobilised' always has an explanation
Small numbers if only complete NHFD-linked cases are used → include all operated hip fractures, not just those with full NHFD data
Definitions of 'mobilised' vary between a sit-out and a walk → agree and print one operational definition before data collection starts
Gains fade once weekend cover reverts → make the rota change permanent in the therapy job plan, not a temporary trial
pearls: Recruit a physiotherapy team lead and the orthogeriatrician as joint audit leads so the change survives staff rotation
Agree the operational definition of 'mobilised' (sit to stand, transfer, or walk) with therapy staff before collecting data
Use the existing NHFD extract to identify the sample quickly rather than searching EPR from scratch
Feed results back to individual consultants and therapy shifts, not just as a trust-wide average, to drive local ownership
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from the NHFD extract and physiotherapy notes

question: What proportion of hip fracture inpatients are mobilised at least once a day with regular physiotherapy review throughout their acute stay?
why: A single day-1 assessment does not guarantee ongoing rehabilitation; patients can be assessed once and then left without daily mobilisation, especially over busy weekends. No closed-loop audit of ongoing (beyond day 1) daily mobilisation frequency for hip fracture inpatients has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.7.2 (2011)
standard.wording: Offer people mobilisation at least once a day and ensure regular physiotherapy review.

pass: Documented mobilisation attempt on every day of the acute admission and at least 3 physiotherapy reviews per week until discharge or rehabilitation-ready
population: Inclusion: adults who had hip fracture surgery and remained an inpatient for at least 5 days. Exclusion: patients who died, were transferred out, or were discharged within 4 days
sample: 40 consecutive hip fracture inpatients with a length of stay of 5 days or more over the last 3 months
data_source: Physiotherapy daily entries, nursing mobility charts, EPR therapy task list
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a daily 'mobilised today: yes/no, reason if no' task to the hip fracture ward's electronic therapy list so a missed day is visible on the ward board round, and set a weekend physiotherapy rota matched to the ward's bed numbers.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthogeriatric MDT and therapy governance meeting; embed the daily task list permanently if missed-day rates fall.
evidence: [ONA-157] day-after-surgery physiotherapy for other fragility fractures: comparable single-timepoint indicator, not the ongoing-frequency question asked here
pitfalls: Weekend staffing gaps are the commonest cause of missed days → confirm weekend rotas before starting
Patients who become medically unwell mid-stay may appropriately miss a day → record a reason rather than counting every miss as a failure
Documentation of 'seen but not mobilised' is easy to miss in free-text notes → use a structured daily tick box, not narrative notes, for data extraction
Staff may see this as a workload-driven target rather than a patient outcome → present length-of-stay and discharge-destination data alongside mobilisation rates
Long lengths of stay reduce the eligible sample → extend the collection window if fewer than 40 eligible patients are found in 3 months
