population: Adults with a documented alcohol history meeting the NICE high-risk threshold (men >50, women >35 units/week for several months), identified from alcohol liaison, GP or gastroenterology records over the last 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults meeting the high-risk drinking threshold.
data_source: Alcohol liaison/GP/gastroenterology records for the drinking history; radiology/hepatology system for the transient elastography referral and result.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic transient elastography referral prompt to the alcohol liaison and GP alcohol-history template whenever units/week above the NICE threshold are recorded.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the alcohol care team and hepatology interface meeting; keep the referral prompt if uptake improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks transient elastography offer rates at the specific high-risk drinking threshold defined by NICE
pitfalls: A full, quantified drinking history (units/week and duration) is often missing from records, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum documentation standard before starting.
Some services already scan all heavy drinkers routinely and this may look like a ceiling effect: check local pathway assumptions before assuming a gap exists.
Elastography referred but not attended should be recorded separately from not offered, since these need different fixes (engagement support versus system prompts).
Patients already known to have cirrhosis do not need this specific test again: exclude them from the denominator.
pearls: Use the alcohol care team, where one exists, as the most reliable route to both take a full drinking history and refer for elastography in one contact.
A community-based (rather than hospital-only) scanning service increases uptake for patients reluctant to attend hospital appointments.
Track attendance as well as referral, since engagement is often the bigger barrier in this population.
Feed positive findings into the wider cirrhosis surveillance pathway audited elsewhere in this set.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from alcohol liaison and hepatology records
pass: Transient elastography is offered (referral made, whether or not the patient attends) within 3 months of a documented drinking history meeting the high-risk threshold.

question: What proportion of adults with alcohol-related liver disease, or MASLD with advanced fibrosis, who do not have cirrhosis are retested for cirrhosis at least every 2 years?
why: People at ongoing risk of progressing to cirrhosis need periodic retesting, not a one-off negative result; no audit in the library checks this retesting interval.

standard.wording: Offer retesting for cirrhosis every 2 years for: people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease, people with hepatitis C virus infection who have not shown a sustained virological response to antiviral therapy, people with MASLD and advanced liver fibrosis.

population: Adults with alcohol-related liver disease or MASLD with advanced fibrosis, previously tested for cirrhosis and found not to have it, under follow-up for at least 2 years.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible adults with at least 2 years since their last negative cirrhosis test.
data_source: Hepatology/gastroenterology clinic letters and the elastography/imaging system for test dates.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 2-yearly recall for cirrhosis retesting to the hepatology or GP chronic liver disease register for eligible patients, rather than relying on ad hoc re-referral.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology governance meeting; keep the recall register if retesting adherence improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures 2-yearly cirrhosis retesting adherence in patients at ongoing risk
pitfalls: Patients who stop attending follow-up (including due to ongoing alcohol use) are the group most likely to miss retesting, and also the group at highest risk: flag non-attendance rather than silently excluding these patients.
A retest done for another reason (e.g. incidental imaging) may satisfy the standard even if not labelled as a 'retest': check imaging history broadly, not just labelled follow-up scans.
Local availability of transient elastography devices limits capacity: record whether delay reflects service capacity rather than a process failure.
Patients who progress to cirrhosis between scheduled retests should be picked up by symptoms/blood tests, not solely by the fixed interval: note any such cases separately.
pearls: A chronic liver disease register with an automatic recall function is the most reliable fix; building this once benefits several of the audits in this set.
Community alcohol and liver clinics can help retain patients who might otherwise disengage from hospital follow-up.
Use this audit as an opportunity to build or refine a shared hepatology-primary care register, since retesting often depends on GP-hospital communication.
Report retesting adherence separately by diagnosis group (ArLD vs MASLD vs HCV), since engagement patterns often differ.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and imaging records
pass: A repeat test for cirrhosis (transient elastography or equivalent) is documented within 2 years of the previous negative test in eligible patients.

question: What proportion of adults with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease, still decompensated after best management and 3 months' abstinence, are referred for assessment for liver transplantation?
why: Liver transplant referral criteria for alcohol-related liver disease are specific and time-defined; no audit in the library checks whether eligible patients are actually referred once they meet them.

standard.source: NICE CG100 rec 1.3.2.1 (2010, amended 2017)
standard.wording: Refer patients with decompensated liver disease to be considered for assessment for liver transplantation if they: still have decompensated liver disease after best management and 3 months' abstinence from alcohol and are otherwise suitable candidates for liver transplantation.

population: Adults with alcohol-related decompensated liver disease under hepatology follow-up, documented as abstinent for 3 months or more, and still decompensated, over the last 12-24 months.
sample: All patients meeting these criteria over 12-24 months (typically 10-20 cases in a DGH hepatology service).
data_source: Hepatology clinic letters/EPR for decompensation status, abstinence duration, and the transplant centre referral letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a '3-month abstinence and still decompensated: transplant referral considered' prompt to the hepatology follow-up template, triggered automatically once 3 months of documented abstinence is reached in a decompensated patient.
reaudit: Repeat in 12-24 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology MDT and regional transplant network meeting; keep the follow-up template prompt if referral rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks referral rates for liver transplant assessment against the specific NICE 3-month abstinence criterion
pitfalls: Confirming '3 months' abstinence' reliably (self-report versus biochemical markers) is itself inconsistent between clinicians: agree a documentation standard before starting.
Some patients are correctly not referred due to other contraindications (severe cardiac or psychiatric comorbidity): capture these as valid reasons, not failures.
Numbers will be small; extend the collection period or audit retrospectively over 24 months.
A patient who relapses during the 3-month period restarts the clock under most local pathways: record this clearly rather than treating it as an audit exclusion only.
pearls: A structured alcohol-abstinence tracking field (rather than free text) makes this measurable and repeatable.
Engage the regional transplant centre early to confirm the exact local interpretation of 'suitable candidate' criteria used alongside the NICE recommendation.
Loop in the alcohol liaison or addiction service, since abstinence support is central to whether patients ever reach the 3-month point at all.
Present outcomes of transplant centre assessments (accepted, declined, further tests needed) to close the loop beyond referral alone.
effort: ~20 min per patient from clinic letters
pass: A referral to a liver transplant centre for assessment is made and documented for patients who remain decompensated after best medical management and 3 months' confirmed abstinence, and who have no other clear contraindication.

question: What proportion of adults on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease have a full blood count checked at the locally agreed monitoring interval, even when TPMT activity is normal?
why: Neutropenia can occur on thiopurines despite normal TPMT activity, so ongoing monitoring remains essential; a related paediatric audit found only 24.5% of patients were fully compliant with blood monitoring frequency [2966]. No audit in the library measures this in adult IBD.

standard.wording: Monitor the effects of azathioprine, mercaptopurine and methotrexate as advised in the BNF or BNFC. Consult the monographs of individual drugs for advice on monitoring immunosuppressives. Monitor for neutropenia in people taking azathioprine or mercaptopurine even if they have normal TPMT activity.

population: Adults on ongoing azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease for at least 6 months, identified from the biologics/immunosuppressant prescribing list.
sample: 40 consecutive adults on ongoing azathioprine or mercaptopurine.
data_source: Laboratory system for FBC dates and results; shared-care monitoring record if monitoring is done in primary care.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up a shared-care monitoring template (hospital or GP-run) with an automatic reminder when an FBC becomes overdue for any patient on ongoing thiopurine therapy for IBD.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same list and sample.
close_loop: Present at the IBD and shared-care governance meeting; keep the reminder system if compliance improves.
evidence: [2966] a paediatric azathioprine monitoring audit found only 24.5% of patients fully compliant with the recommended blood monitoring frequency, and proposed a shared-care guideline with a tick-box proforma as the fix
pitfalls: Shared-care monitoring split between GP and hospital can create gaps where each assumes the other is checking: agree and document one named responsible party per patient.
Missed appointments for blood tests are common and should be flagged for active follow-up, not just recorded as a gap.
A late-but-eventually-done blood test still represents a period of unmonitored risk: report both 'ever done' and 'done on time'.
Dose changes reset or alter the expected monitoring frequency; make sure the expected interval used in the audit matches current, not historical, dosing.
pearls: Use the exact structure that worked in a related paediatric audit: a shared-care guideline plus a tick-box monitoring proforma with all parameters listed together [2966].
A laboratory-generated automatic reminder is more durable than relying on either GP or hospital memory alone.
Make the responsible party for monitoring (GP vs hospital) explicit in every new thiopurine-start letter.
Track outcomes of any neutropenia detected, to show the monitoring system actually catches and acts on the risk it exists to prevent.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the laboratory system
pass: A full blood count is checked at the locally agreed interval (typically weekly for the first month, then monthly, per BNF monographs) throughout the audit period, with no gap longer than the agreed interval.

question: What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with coeliac disease have a documented discussion about pneumococcal vaccination?
why: Coeliac disease is associated with functional hyposplenism and increased pneumococcal infection risk. A related audit found overall vaccine uptake in coeliac disease was only 38.6% at baseline, improving to 49.2% with an invitation letter [9569], but no audit checks whether the vaccination discussion itself is documented at diagnosis.

standard.source: NICE NG20 rec 1.6.5 (2015)
standard.wording: Explain to people with coeliac disease and their family members or carers (as appropriate) that the Department of Health's Green Book recommends immunisation against pneumococcus.

population: Adults with a new diagnosis of coeliac disease in the last 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new diagnosis of coeliac disease.
data_source: Gastroenterology clinic letters/EPR and, where available, GP vaccination records.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'pneumococcal vaccination discussed' tick box with a pre-written information line to the coeliac disease diagnosis clinic letter template, sent to both the patient and the GP.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology-primary care interface meeting; keep the clinic letter template field if documentation improves.
evidence: [9569] a coeliac disease vaccine uptake audit found only 38.6% uptake at baseline, improving to 49.2% with a single invitation letter, showing this step needs an active system prompt rather than relying on the diagnosis conversation alone
pitfalls: The discussion may happen verbally at diagnosis but not be written down: this audit measures documentation, and should say so plainly rather than assuming the conversation never happened.
GPs, not gastroenterology, usually administer the vaccine: the audit should track the discussion (specialist's responsibility) separately from vaccine administration (usually primary care's).

Patients already vaccinated for another indication (for example, age-related pneumococcal vaccination) should still have the coeliac-specific discussion recorded, since guidance and eligibility can differ.
A generic coeliac information leaflet mentioning vaccination in passing is not the same as a documented individual discussion: define the standard clearly before starting.
pearls: A single sentence and tick box in the standard diagnosis letter, copied to the GP, is a low-effort fix that also prompts GP action.
Pair the vaccination discussion with the annual review audit above so both draw on the same diagnosis-clinic dataset.
Consider adapting the invitation-letter approach already shown to work in the library [9569] as the mechanism for actually getting patients vaccinated once discussed.
Track vaccine uptake as well as discussion rates at re-audit to confirm discussion translates into action.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass: A documented discussion about pneumococcal vaccination is recorded at, or within 3 months of, the diagnosis of coeliac disease.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with acute alcohol-related hepatitis have a documented nutritional assessment, with nutritional support started if indicated?
why: Malnutrition is near-universal in acute alcoholic hepatitis and affects survival, but no audit in the library checks whether nutritional assessment is systematically done and acted on in this specific group.

standard.wording: Assess the nutritional requirements of people with acute alcohol-related hepatitis. Offer nutritional support if needed and consider using nasogastric tube feeding.

population: Adults admitted with a clinical diagnosis of acute alcohol-related hepatitis in the last 6-12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults admitted with acute alcohol-related hepatitis.
data_source: Admission clerking, nursing nutritional screening records and dietitian referral system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add acute alcohol-related hepatitis as a trigger diagnosis for an automatic same-day dietitian referral and MUST scoring on the hepatology/gastroenterology admission bundle.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology and nutrition and dietetics governance meeting; keep the automatic referral trigger if assessment completeness improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks nutritional assessment completeness specifically in acute alcohol-related hepatitis
pitfalls: General ward MUST scoring may be completed routinely but not specifically prompt dietitian input for this high-risk group: check whether a score is acted on, not just recorded.
Nasogastric feeding can be difficult in patients with encephalopathy or agitation: a documented reason not to feed enterally should count as a valid clinical decision, not a failure.
Weekend admissions may have delayed dietitian input due to staffing: check whether delays cluster there.
Poor oral intake due to nausea or ongoing alcohol withdrawal symptoms needs separate management alongside nutrition, and should be recorded as context.
pearls: An automatic dietitian referral triggered by the diagnosis code removes reliance on the ward team remembering a nutrition-specific step amid other urgent decisions (steroids, infection screen).
Weekend and out-of-hours dietitian cover (or a clear escalation plan) is often the main practical barrier: check this with dietetics before proposing a fix.
Combine data collection with the pre-steroid infection screening audit above, since both draw from the same acute alcoholic hepatitis admission list.
Track nutritional status trends (weight, albumin) through the admission as an outcome measure at re-audit.
effort: ~15 min per case from admission and dietitian records
pass: A nutritional assessment (for example, MUST score or dietitian review) is documented within 48 hours of admission with acute alcohol-related hepatitis, with nutritional support started if indicated.

question: What proportion of adult inpatients have their drug allergy status recorded using one of the three standard categories (drug allergy / none known / unable to ascertain) before their first drug is prescribed?
why: Unclear or missing allergy status is a recurrent cause of prescribing error and delayed antibiotic administration. No closed-loop audit of the specific three-category recording standard has been published in the library, although related allergy-documentation audits exist [1892].

standard.source: NICE CG183 Drug allergy: diagnosis and management, rec 1.2.1 (2014)
standard.wording: Document people's drug allergy status in their medical records using 1 of the following: 'drug allergy' 'none known' 'unable to ascertain' (document it as soon as the information is available).

pass: One of the three standard categories is recorded in the drug chart or EPR allergy field before the first drug is administered
population: Inclusion: 40 consecutive adult medical or surgical admissions. Exclusion: patients transferred from another ward with allergy status already recorded there and unchanged.
sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Drug chart or EPR allergy field, admission clerking note

question: What proportion of adults treated in hospital for suspected anaphylaxis are offered a referral to a specialist allergy service before discharge?
why: Adult referral after anaphylaxis is under-audited in the library; existing entries cover children [see NNA-188] and adrenaline auto-injector supply [see NNA-085], leaving the adult referral step unmeasured.

standard.source: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, rec 1.1.12 (2011, updated 2026, replaces CG134)
standard.wording: After emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis, offer the adult, young person or child a referral to a specialist allergy service (age-appropriate, where possible) consisting of healthcare professionals with the skills and competencies necessary to accurately investigate, diagnose, monitor and provide ongoing management of, and patient education about, anaphylaxis.

pass: A referral to a specialist allergy service is documented as offered (accepted or declined) in the discharge letter
population: Inclusion: adults (16 and over) treated for suspected anaphylaxis in the emergency department or on a ward. Exclusion: patients who die before discharge.

data_source: ED/ward notes, discharge summary, adrenaline administration record used to identify cases

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

reaudit: 6 months later, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the ED or acute medicine governance meeting; embed the mandatory field in the discharge template if the target is met.
evidence: [no closed-loop audit of adult allergy service referral after anaphylaxis has been published in the library]

question: What proportion of adults discharged after emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis receive a brand-specific demonstration of their adrenaline auto-injector before they leave?
why: Prescribing two auto-injectors is separately audited [see NNA-085], but whether the patient is actually shown how to use the specific device they are given is not measured anywhere in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, rec 1.1.14 (2011, updated 2026, replaces CG134)

sample: 30 consecutive discharges over the last 6 months
data_source: ED/ward discharge documentation, patient information leaflet record

question: What proportion of adults treated for anaphylaxis who receive a single dose of adrenaline with a good response are observed for at least 2 hours before discharge, and what proportion needing two or more doses are observed for at least 6 hours?
why: The minimum safe observation period after anaphylaxis has never been separately audited in the library; existing entries focus on tryptase timing [see NNA-084] rather than the length of observation itself.

standard.source: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, recs 1.1.7 and 1.1.8 (2026)
standard.wording: A suitably qualified and experienced healthcare professional should consider discharging the adult, young person or child after 2 hours of observation... if there was a good response (within 5 to 10 minutes) to a single dose of intramuscular (IM) adrenaline... Observe the adult, young person or child for a minimum of 6 hours after resolution of all symptoms if: 2 doses of intramuscular (IM) adrenaline were needed to treat the anaphylaxis or there is a history of biphasic reaction.

pass: Documented observation time meets or exceeds the 2-hour (single good-response dose) or 6-hour (two or more doses, or biphasic history) minimum before discharge
population: Inclusion: adults treated for suspected anaphylaxis with at least one dose of IM adrenaline. Exclusion: patients admitted to a ward or critical care rather than discharged from the assessment area.
sample: 30 consecutive cases over the last 6 months
data_source: ED observations chart, drug chart (adrenaline doses and times), discharge time

standard.wording: Antibody titres for hepatitis B should be checked one to four months after the completion of a primary course of vaccine. Such information allows appropriate decisions to be made concerning post-exposure prophylaxis following known or suspected exposure to the virus.

pass: An anti-HBs antibody titre result is recorded in the occupational health record 1–4 months after the primary vaccine course is completed
population: Inclusion: staff with direct patient contact who completed a primary hepatitis B vaccine course in the last 12 months. Exclusion: staff who declined vaccination.
sample: 40 consecutive staff completing a primary course over the last 12 months
data_source: Occupational health immunisation record

change: Add an automatic recall for antibody titre testing to the occupational health vaccination database, triggered at the point the final primary-course dose is recorded.
reaudit: 6 months after the automatic recall is switched on, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the occupational health service governance meeting; keep the automatic recall if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of hepatitis B antibody titre checking timing in healthcare staff has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Staff move between departments or trusts before the check is due → flag the pending check in a shared occupational health system rather than a single department log
Blood test uptake among busy staff is often poor → offer testing at the workplace or during an existing appointment
Non-responder status is not always acted on → link this audit to a booster/re-testing pathway for non-responders
New starters may complete the course at a previous employer → confirm completion dates carefully before including a case
pearls: Use the occupational health vaccination database's own recall function rather than a manual spreadsheet
Offer drop-in phlebotomy sessions timed to when most staff are due their check
Report responder/non-responder rates separately, since non-responders need a distinct pathway
Recruit the occupational health nurse manager as audit lead, since they already run the vaccination programme
effort: ~10 min per 10 staff records from occupational health system

question: What proportion of healthcare staff identified as non-responders to a primary hepatitis B vaccine course have a documented further management plan (for example a second course or confirmation of non-infection status)?
why: Follow-up of hepatitis B non-responders is a distinct step from the antibody check itself and is not measured anywhere in the library.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B (updated 5 February 2026)
standard.wording: Reinforcing doses should be considered for people in the following categories: ... healthcare and laboratory workers who have not responded to the primary course (see Testing for evidence of immunity after vaccination).

pass: A documented further management plan (repeat course, further testing, or confirmed non-infectious status recorded) exists for each identified non-responder
population: Inclusion: staff identified as non-responders to a primary hepatitis B vaccine course in occupational health records over the last 2 years. Exclusion: staff who have since left employment.
sample: 20 consecutive non-responders identified over the last 2 years (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low case numbers)
data_source: Occupational health immunisation and serology record

close_loop: Present at the occupational health service governance meeting; keep the mandatory pathway if the target is met.

Occupational health records may be split across paper and electronic systems → check both sources before concluding a plan is missing

question: What proportion of staff with a significant occupational needlestick injury from a known hepatitis B surface antigen-positive source, in whom hepatitis B immunoglobulin is indicated, receive it within 24 hours of the first vaccine dose?
why: Needlestick post-exposure prophylaxis timing has no audit in the library; existing entries relate to patient-facing screening rather than staff post-exposure management.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B (updated 5 February 2026)
standard.wording: If HBIG is also indicated, it should be given as soon as possible, ideally at the same time or within 24 hours of the first dose of vaccine, but not after seven days have elapsed since exposure or vaccine.

pass: HBIG, when indicated, is given at the same time as or within 24 hours of the first vaccine dose, and always within 7 days of exposure
population: Inclusion: staff with a significant percutaneous or mucocutaneous exposure to a known HBsAg-positive source over the last 2 years, in whom HBIG was indicated. Exclusion: exposures to a source of unknown or negative HBsAg status.
sample: 20 consecutive eligible exposures over the last 2 years (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low case numbers)
data_source: Occupational health/emergency department needlestick injury record, pharmacy HBIG dispensing log

close_loop: Present at the occupational health/infection control governance meeting; keep the ED stocking arrangement if compliance is maintained.
evidence: [no audit of hepatitis B immunoglobulin timing after occupational needlestick injury has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Out-of-hours exposures are the highest-risk group for delay, since occupational health is usually closed → ensure the ED pathway covers all hours
HBIG needs a same-day source patient hepatitis B test where status is unknown → build rapid testing into the pathway
Small numbers of eligible exposures → extend the sampling period to the last 2–3 years
Staff may delay reporting an injury out of embarrassment or workload pressure → reinforce a no-blame reporting culture
pearls: Base the local pathway directly on the Green Book's own post-exposure timing wording
Agree HBIG stock-holding and rapid access with pharmacy and the ED lead before cycle 1
Recruit the infection control team, who already investigate needlestick incidents, as co-auditors
Track time-to-first-vaccine-dose as a secondary measure, since this drives the 24-hour HBIG window
effort: ~20 min per 10 records from occupational health/ED

question: What proportion of staff with a significant occupational exposure to blood or body fluids (for example a needlestick injury) have documented evidence that advice was sought immediately, either from occupational health, the emergency department or the local Health Protection Team?
why: Timeliness of first-line advice-seeking after a needlestick injury, as distinct from HBIG administration itself, is not currently audited in the library.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B (updated 5 February 2026)
standard.wording: Individuals who sustain such exposures should wash the affected area well with soap and warm water and seek medical advice. Advice about prophylaxis after such incidents should be obtained by telephone from the nearest Emergency Department, NHS 111, or from the local Health Protection Team.

pass: Documented evidence that first aid (washing) was performed and advice was sought on the same day as the exposure

sample: 30 consecutive reported needlestick/splash injuries over the last 6 months

change: Put a laminated needlestick first-response card (wash, seek advice, report) at every clinical area sink and sharps disposal point, with the out-of-hours contact number printed on it.

close_loop: Present at the infection control/occupational health governance meeting; keep the cards in place if compliance is maintained.
evidence: [no audit of same-day advice-seeking after occupational needlestick injury has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Incident reporting systems capture what happened but not always when advice was first sought → cross-check with occupational health call logs
Staff may assume a low-risk source means advice is unnecessary → make advice-seeking mandatory regardless of perceived risk
Night-shift staff may not know who to call → ensure the out-of-hours contact is on the card, not only daytime numbers
Under-reporting remains a barrier even with cards in place → reinforce reporting culture alongside the practical change
pearls: Involve ward and theatre staff in designing the card so the wording is clear and short
Place cards exactly where sharps injuries happen (sinks, sharps bins), not only in notice boards
Use the same incident case list as the HBIG-timing audit to cover the whole needlestick pathway in one data collection round

question: What proportion of new starters with direct patient contact have a pre-employment health assessment that includes a documented review of immunisation needs?
why: Pre-employment occupational health screening is not audited anywhere in the library, despite being the entry point for every subsequent staff immunisation and infection-control safeguard.

standard.wording: All new employees should undergo a pre-employment health assessment, which should include a review of immunisation needs.

population: Inclusion: new starters with direct patient contact in the last 6 months. Exclusion: internal transfers with an existing, current occupational health record.

question: What proportion of healthcare workers directly involved in patient care are offered influenza immunisation on an annual basis?
why: Staff influenza vaccination uptake campaigns are common, but whether every eligible member of staff is actually offered the vaccine (as distinct from uptake rate) is not measured in the library.

standard.wording: Influenza vaccination is therefore recommended for healthcare workers directly involved in patient care, who should be offered influenza immunisation on an annual basis.

change: Use peer vaccinators to visit every clinical area on the roster during the flu campaign, with a named staff-by-staff checklist so no one is missed, rather than relying on staff to attend a central clinic.

close_loop: Present at occupational health and infection prevention governance; keep the peer vaccinator ward-round model if the offer rate improves.

pitfalls: Bank, agency and night staff are often missed by daytime campaigns → schedule peer vaccinator visits across all shifts

Declining staff should have this recorded, not left blank → treat a blank record as 'not offered', not 'declined'
Campaign timing (early in the season) affects the denominator if staff join partway through → clarify the eligible cohort before cycle 1

question: What proportion of patients on maintenance lithium therapy have a lithium blood level checked at least once every 3 months?
why: Lithium monitoring for physical health parameters is not audited in the library, unlike related psychiatric monitoring topics; this is the single highest-harm, highest-volume medicines-safety gap named in the underlying national alert.

standard.source: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009)
standard.wording: one in 10 patients had no documented lithium blood level. (National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) standard: one blood level measurement every three months. Not met for 70 per cent of patients)

pass: At least one lithium level result is recorded in the preceding 3 months
population: Inclusion: adults on established (more than 6 months) maintenance lithium therapy under primary or secondary mental health care. Exclusion: patients newly starting lithium (still in initial titration monitoring).
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the lithium monitoring register over the last 3 months
data_source: Lithium monitoring register (practice or trust), laboratory results system

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 3-month lithium level recall to the lithium monitoring register, with a hard stop on repeat prescribing if the level is overdue, as recommended in the original NPSA alert.
reaudit: 6 months after the recall/hard stop is switched on, same register, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety or mental health pharmacy governance meeting; keep the hard stop if the target is met.
evidence: [no closed-loop audit of the 3-month lithium level monitoring standard has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Patients under shared care between GP and mental health services can fall between the two → agree who owns the recall before cycle 1
Patients who avoid blood tests are hardest to reach → offer a point-of-care or home phlebotomy option where available
A hard stop on prescribing needs pharmacy system changes → involve pharmacy IT from the outset
Register accuracy depends on all lithium patients being correctly coded → check the register against a full drug search before starting
pearls: Base the recall directly on the original NPSA alert's own 3-month standard so the audit maps onto a nationally recognised benchmark
Use the NPSA lithium record book (patient-held) as a low-cost extra safety net alongside the electronic recall
Recruit a mental health pharmacist to lead, since they typically run the lithium register already
Report separately for primary and secondary care patients, since the fix may differ by setting
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from lithium register

question: What proportion of patients on maintenance lithium therapy have renal and thyroid function checked at least once every 6 months?
why: Renal and thyroid monitoring is a distinct national standard from the lithium level itself, and non-compliance with it was even more marked than lithium level monitoring in the original national audit that founded this alert.

standard.source: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009)
standard.wording: one in five patients had no renal function tests documented (NICE standard: assessment every six months. Not met for 46 per cent of patients); one in six patients had no thyroid function tests documented (NICE standard: assessment every six months. Not met for 51 per cent of patients)

pass: Both a renal function test (U&E/eGFR) and a thyroid function test are recorded within the preceding 6 months
population: Inclusion: adults on established maintenance lithium therapy over the last 6 months. Exclusion: patients newly starting lithium (still in initial titration monitoring).
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the lithium monitoring register over the last 6 months
data_source: Lithium monitoring register, laboratory results system

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

change: Add renal and thyroid function to the same automatic 6-month recall used for the lithium level check, as a single combined blood test request, rather than a separate process.
reaudit: 6 months after the combined recall is switched on, same register, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety or mental health pharmacy governance meeting; keep the combined recall if the target is met.
evidence: [no closed-loop audit of 6-month renal and thyroid monitoring on lithium therapy has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Renal and thyroid tests are sometimes requested separately from the lithium level, causing extra venepuncture visits → combine them on one request form
Deteriorating renal function may not trigger a dose review → link abnormal results to a documented lithium dose review action
Test results filed but not reviewed by a prescriber → require a clinician sign-off field, not just a filed result
Register may not distinguish patients newly started from established patients → exclude the first 6 months, which has its own more frequent monitoring schedule

effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from lithium register

question: What proportion of patients starting lithium therapy are given a patient information booklet and a record book to track their lithium blood levels and relevant clinical tests?

question: What proportion of adults with a single acute paracetamol overdose and a plasma-paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line start acetylcysteine within 8 hours of ingestion?

pass: Acetylcysteine is started within 8 hours of the recorded time of ingestion

sample: 30 consecutive eligible presentations over the last 6 months

close_loop: Present at the neurology/radiology joint governance meeting; keep the ring-fenced slot if the target is met.
evidence: [127 nearest related entry: first seizure specialist assessment within 2 weeks of ED referral]
pitfalls: General radiology waiting lists can push epilepsy MRIs beyond 6 weeks → a ring-fenced slot needs radiology capacity agreement, not just a policy statement
Regionally agreed epilepsy MRI protocols may not be locally documented → confirm the protocol exists and is used before starting
Excluded epilepsy syndromes (idiopathic generalised, self-limited with centrotemporal spikes) must be correctly identified to avoid skewing the denominator
Children may need a general anaesthetic for MRI, adding delay → record this as a distinct, expected cause of delay
pearls: Agree the ring-fenced slot numbers with radiology using cycle 1 referral volume data
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse to track referrals and flag approaching deadlines
Use the same case list as the first-seizure clinic audit to build a complete diagnostic pathway picture
Report scan-to-diagnosis-confirmed time as a secondary measure of overall pathway speed
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from radiology/clinic records

question: What proportion of people newly diagnosed with epilepsy have a documented discussion of the impact of their epilepsy on driving at their first specialist appointment?
why: Driving advice at epilepsy diagnosis is a distinct, safety-critical recommendation not currently measured by any audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 2.1.6 (2022)
standard.wording: Discuss the following issues with them during their first appointment: ... impact on daily activities, including driving ... their epilepsy syndrome or seizure types. The discussion may be reiterated at an information and care-planning session with an epilepsy specialist nurse.

pass: The clinic letter for the first appointment documents that driving was discussed
population: Inclusion: people newly diagnosed with epilepsy attending their first specialist appointment over the last 6 months who are of an age to hold or be approaching driving age. Exclusion: children well below driving age at diagnosis (under 15).
sample: 30 consecutive first appointments over the last 6 months
data_source: First epilepsy clinic letter

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'driving discussed, including DVLA notification' field to the first epilepsy appointment clinic letter template.
reaudit: 6 months after the mandatory field is added, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at neurology governance; keep the mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of documented driving discussion at first epilepsy appointment has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Discussion may happen verbally but not be recorded in the letter → require the field to be in the templated letter, not left to free text
Patients below driving age at diagnosis still need future advice → record this as 'deferred, to be discussed before driving age' rather than a straightforward fail
Letters dictated and typed later may lag behind the consultation, delaying documentation → use a same-day templated letter where possible
DVLA rules change periodically → check the letter template references current DVLA guidance at each audit
pearls: Build the driving field into the same templated letter build as the care-plan-copy audit below, so both changes happen together
Provide clinicians with a one-line DVLA notification prompt card to use during the consultation
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often reiterates this discussion at follow-up
Share DVLA's own patient information leaflet at the same appointment to reinforce the discussion
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of people with epilepsy are given a copy of their care plan after their first specialist appointment?
why: Providing patients with a written copy of their agreed care plan is a distinct, checkable recommendation not currently measured by any audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 2.1.7 (2022)
standard.wording: Provide the person with epilepsy, and their family or carers if appropriate, with a copy of their care plan, which includes details of their care and support as discussed and agreed with the person, and their family or carers if appropriate.

pass: Documented evidence that a copy of the care plan was given to the patient (and family/carer if appropriate) after the appointment
population: Inclusion: people with epilepsy attending a first or care-planning specialist appointment over the last 6 months. Exclusion: telephone-only appointments where a plan could not be finalised.
sample: 30 consecutive appointments over the last 6 months
data_source: Clinic letter, care plan copy sent record

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Print the care plan copy automatically at the end of the consultation from the clinic letter template, so it is given at the appointment rather than posted later (or not at all).
reaudit: 6 months after the automatic printing change, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at neurology governance; keep automatic printing if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of care plan copies given to people with epilepsy has been published in the library]
pitfalls: Letters typed and posted after the appointment may never explicitly confirm a copy reached the patient → track 'given at appointment' separately from 'posted later'
Care plans for children may need a version appropriate for the child as well as the parent → check both were considered
Clinic time pressure can make same-visit printing impractical → agree realistic clinic template time with the service before cycle 1
Patients who prefer a digital copy should still be offered one, recorded as an equivalent pass
pearls: Combine this audit's data collection with the driving-discussion audit, since both use the same clinic letters
Ask reception or clinic support staff to print and hand over the plan at check-out, taking pressure off clinicians
Offer an electronic copy via the patient portal as an alternative to a paper copy
Use patient feedback (a short survey) to confirm plans given were actually understood, not just handed over
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of women and girls with epilepsy of childbearing potential have a documented discussion of the risks of their anti-seizure medication in pregnancy within the last 12 months?
why: This measures the broader pregnancy-risk discussion for any anti-seizure medication, distinct from the valproate-specific Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form audits already in the library [see NNA-159, NNA-186, NNA-323].

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.7 (2022)
standard.wording: Discuss with women and girls with epilepsy who are able to have children (including young girls who are likely to need treatment when they are able to have children), and their families or carers if appropriate, the risks to an unborn child of taking antiseizure medications during pregnancy, such as congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental impairments and fetal growth restriction.

pass: A documented discussion of pregnancy risks of anti-seizure medication within the last 12 months in the clinic letter
population: Inclusion: women and girls of childbearing potential (12 and over) with epilepsy under active neurology or paediatric neurology follow-up. Exclusion: women who have had a permanent sterilisation procedure documented.
sample: 30 consecutive women/girls of childbearing potential on the epilepsy clinic caseload
data_source: Epilepsy clinic letters from the last 12 months

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory annual 'pregnancy risk of current anti-seizure medication discussed' field to the epilepsy clinic letter template for all women and girls of childbearing potential.
reaudit: 12 months after the mandatory field is added, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at neurology governance; keep the mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: [159 nearest related entry: two-specialist sign-off for valproate under 55; 323 nearest related entry: Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form for repeat valproate]
pitfalls: This applies to all anti-seizure medications, not only valproate, so existing valproate-specific systems will not fully capture it → build a medication-agnostic field
Young girls not yet needing contraception discussions may still need age-appropriate risk information → include this group explicitly, not just adult women
Discussions at GP-led reviews (rather than specialist clinic) may be missed if only specialist letters are checked → clarify which setting is in scope before cycle 1
Patients seen only by telephone may have shorter, less complete documentation → check both face-to-face and telephone clinic letters
pearls: Use the same clinic caseload list as any existing valproate ARAF audit to avoid duplicating case-finding work
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often leads these discussions in practice
Provide clinicians with a short structured prompt card covering all anti-seizure medications with teratogenic risk, not only valproate
Report findings by medication class to show where risk communication is strongest and weakest
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of people of childbearing potential prescribed an enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medication (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate) have documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness?
why: Interaction advice for enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medications and hormonal contraception is a distinct recommendation from the valproate-specific pregnancy prevention audits already in the library, and is not measured anywhere.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.10 (2022)
standard.wording: Be aware that some antiseizure medications, for example, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and topiramate, can impair the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Refer to the summary of product characteristics (SPC) and BNF or BNF for children for individual drug advice on the interactions between antiseizure medications and contraception.

pass: Documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness and the need for an alternative or additional method
population: Inclusion: people of childbearing potential prescribed carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate for epilepsy, under active follow-up. Exclusion: patients using a copper intrauterine device or another method unaffected by enzyme induction, if already documented.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients on the epilepsy clinic caseload
data_source: Epilepsy clinic letters, GP contraception review records

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a drug-interaction alert to the epilepsy prescribing system that fires when one of the four enzyme-inducing medications is prescribed to a person of childbearing potential, prompting a documented contraception discussion.
reaudit: 6 months after the alert is switched on, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at neurology and sexual health/contraception joint governance; keep the alert if the target is met.
evidence: [324 nearest related entry: topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme highly effective contraception recorded]
pitfalls: This standard covers four specific drugs, not all anti-seizure medications, so the alert must be drug-specific to avoid unnecessary prompts
Contraception method may be managed entirely in primary care and not visible to the neurology clinic → check both GP and specialist records
Non-hormonal or copper IUD users need this explicitly recorded as 'not applicable' rather than being marked as a fail
Topiramate's own separate Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements (already audited) may overlap with this general interaction advice → keep the pass criteria distinct
pearls: Coordinate with the existing topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme audit to avoid double data collection on the same patients
Provide a simple interaction quick-reference card (drug name, effect on contraception, alternative advice) for clinicians
Recruit a contraception/sexual health lead as an occasional co-reviewer for complex cases
Report by individual drug, since carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and topiramate caseloads may differ in size
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures despite treatment are offered an epilepsy specialist nurse session after each emergency department attendance for a seizure?
why: Epilepsy specialist nurse contact after an ED attendance is a specific, checkable recommendation not currently measured by any audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 11.1.3 (2022)
standard.wording: For people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures, offer epilepsy specialist nurse sessions: at least twice a year and after emergency department visits.

pass: An epilepsy specialist nurse contact (session, call or clinic appointment) is documented within 2 weeks of the ED attendance
population: Inclusion: people with known epilepsy and ongoing seizures who attend the ED with a seizure over the last 6 months. Exclusion: ED attendances for a reason unrelated to epilepsy in a person who happens to have the condition.
sample: 30 consecutive epilepsy-related ED attendances over the last 6 months
data_source: ED attendance record, epilepsy specialist nurse contact log

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic epilepsy specialist nurse referral to the ED discharge system, triggered whenever a seizure-related attendance is coded in a patient with known epilepsy.
reaudit: 6 months after the automatic referral is switched on, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint ED/neurology governance meeting; keep the automatic referral if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of epilepsy specialist nurse contact after emergency department attendance has been published in the library]
pitfalls: ED coding may not clearly distinguish a seizure-related attendance from other reasons → cross-check with the triage complaint as well as the diagnosis code
Epilepsy specialist nurse capacity may not match ED attendance volume → agree a realistic response model (call-back, not always a face-to-face session) with the service before cycle 1
Attendances out of hours or at weekends may be harder to flag for follow-up → build the referral into the discharge process itself, not a manual daily list
Patients who decline contact should be recorded as offered but declined, not as non-compliance
pearls: Base the automatic referral trigger on the same seizure-related attendance coding used for existing seizure audits
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse team directly, since they are best placed to say what response is realistic
Track whether ED re-attendance rates change over time as a secondary outcome of better specialist nurse contact
Present this alongside the referral-to-first-seizure-clinic audit for a fuller picture of the epilepsy urgent care pathway
effort: ~15 min per 10 attendances from ED/specialist nurse records

question: What proportion of adults have a corrected serum calcium checked within 12 hours of thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy?
why: Post-operative hypocalcaemia is a common, preventable cause of delayed discharge and re-admission after thyroid and parathyroid surgery, and no closed-loop audit of the timing of the first postoperative calcium check has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Post-operative Hypocalcaemia Guidance
standard.wording: POST THYROIDECTOMY / PARATHYROIDECTOMY CORRECTED CALCIUM LEVELS: Check within 12h postoperatively

pass: Corrected serum calcium result is filed and actioned within 12 hours of the end of surgery
population: Inclusion: all adults undergoing total or completion thyroidectomy, or parathyroidectomy. Exclusion: hemithyroidectomy or thyroid lobectomy only
sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid or parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
data_source: Theatre system for operation type and time, laboratory system for calcium sample time, EPR for the documented action
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 'post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery' order set that auto-requests a corrected calcium for 12 hours post-op and displays the BAETS treatment algorithm next to the result
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size, on the next 40 consecutive operations
close_loop: Present at the endocrine surgery/ENT MDT and departmental audit meeting; embed the order set as the default post-op set if the target is met
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library] related: NNA-069 (post-thyroidectomy observation schedule) shows the same order-set approach improving compliance with a post-thyroid surgery bundle
pitfalls: Sample drawn but result not checked out of hours → build the check into the nursing handover, not just the request
Small numbers at units doing few parathyroidectomies → combine thyroid and parathyroid cases for the denominator
Definition of 'checked' drifts between cycles (requested vs resulted) → fix the definition as 'result available in EPR' before cycle 1
New starters unaware of the algorithm → laminate the algorithm in recovery and on the ward
pearls: Recruit the endocrine surgery clinical nurse specialist to check for missed 12-hour bloods each morning
Agree the exact cut-off time (12h from skin closure, not from admission) before cycle 1 starts
Link the order set to the procedure code so it fires automatically
Keep the same nurse-led calcium round after the surgical trainees rotate
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from theatre system and EPR

question: What proportion of adults undergoing thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy have a documented post-operative laryngoscopy to assess vocal cord movement?
why: Vocal cord palsy is a leading cause of litigation after thyroid and parathyroid surgery, yet the true incidence is only known where laryngoscopy is performed routinely; no audit of compliance with mandatory post-operative laryngoscopy has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
standard.wording: Post-operative laryngoscopy is required as a key quality control measure and should become mandatory.

pass: A fibreoptic or transcutaneous laryngoscopy assessment of vocal cord movement is documented at any point after surgery, up to and including the first outpatient follow-up
population: Inclusion: all adults undergoing thyroid or parathyroid surgery. Exclusion: patients refusing the examination (documented separately)
sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid/parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
data_source: Operation note, ENT/voice clinic letters, EPR results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make a laryngoscopy booking (by the surgical team or ENT) a mandatory step on the electronic discharge checklist for every thyroid/parathyroid operation
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the endocrine surgery MDT and joint ENT/endocrine surgery governance meeting; embed the discharge checklist step if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: No ENT or voice clinic slots available → negotiate a ring-fenced weekly slot before cycle 1
Refusals not distinguished from omissions → add a separate 'declined' field so the denominator is fair
Surgeons doing their own transcutaneous ultrasound assessment not counted → agree what counts as 'laryngoscopy' before starting
Result not filed back into the surgical record → ask ENT to copy the surgical team into every report
pearls: Agree with ENT a same-day or next-day slot before starting the first cycle
Use a transcutaneous laryngeal ultrasound pathway where trained staff exist, to reduce reliance on ENT capacity
Put the laryngoscopy step on the WHO-style discharge checklist so it cannot be missed
Feed back cord palsy rates to the department each year so the mandatory step is not seen as a paperwork exercise
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPR and clinic letters

question: What proportion of adults with a voice change or suspected/confirmed thyroid malignancy have a documented pre-operative laryngoscopy before thyroid or parathyroid surgery?
why: Pre-operative vocal cord assessment changes intraoperative and consent decisions when malignancy or voice change is present; no audit targeting this selective indication (rather than routine laryngoscopy in all patients) has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
standard.wording: Pre-operative laryngoscopy in non-cancer patients with no history of voice change has a low rate of abnormal findings.

pass: A pre-operative laryngoscopy result is documented in the notes before surgery for any patient with a voice change or a cytological/clinical suspicion of malignancy
population: Inclusion: adults listed for thyroid or parathyroid surgery with documented voice change or suspected/confirmed malignancy. Exclusion: benign disease with a normal voice
sample: All patients with voice change or suspected malignancy listed for thyroid/parathyroid surgery over the last 6 months (expect 30-40)
data_source: Pre-assessment clinic letters, MDT proforma, ENT clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'voice change / suspected malignancy → pre-op laryngoscopy booked' field to the thyroid MDT outcome proforma
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT; embed the proforma field if it improves compliance
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Voice change not systematically asked about at clinic → add a standard voice question to the pre-assessment template
Small numbers if malignancy is rare locally → run over 6 months rather than 3
Laryngoscopy done but not documented in the surgical notes → require the ENT report to be filed in the same record
MDT proforma completed retrospectively → complete it in real time at the MDT
pearls: Add the voice question to every thyroid nodule clinic template, not just cancer clinics
Use the MDT coordinator to check the field is complete before the case is listed
Share abnormal pre-op findings with the operating surgeon before consent
Keep a log of pre-op abnormal cords to compare with post-op findings
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from MDT proforma

question: What proportion of adults with structural persistent thyroid cancer after total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine are discussed at the thyroid cancer multidisciplinary team meeting?
why: Persistent structural disease after primary treatment changes management (further surgery, radiotherapy or systemic treatment) and should not be managed outside the MDT; no audit of MDT discussion for this specific group has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.4 (2022)
standard.wording: Discuss at the multidisciplinary team meeting any person who has had a total or completion thyroidectomy and RAI and has evidence of structural persistent disease.

pass: Documented discussion and outcome at the thyroid cancer MDT within 4 weeks of imaging or biochemistry showing structural persistent disease
population: Inclusion: adults with thyroid cancer who have had total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine and subsequent evidence of structural persistent disease. Exclusion: biochemical-only persistence with no structural correlate
sample: All such patients identified over the last 12 months (expect 20-30 in a regional cancer centre)
data_source: MDT database, oncology and endocrine clinic letters, imaging reports
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'structural persistent disease' MDT-list trigger from the radiology reporting system when a report contains that phrase for a coded thyroid cancer patient
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT and cancer services governance meeting; embed the radiology trigger if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Structural persistence identified in a non-cancer clinic and not flagged → educate all clinicians reviewing thyroid cancer follow-up scans
MDT list overloaded, cases delayed → create a fast-track 'persistent disease' slot
Ambiguity over what counts as 'structural' vs biochemical → agree the definition with radiology and oncology before cycle 1
Retrospective identification bias if reliant on memory → use a coded database search
pearls: Ask radiology to use a standard phrase ('structural persistent disease') in reports to enable searching
Give the MDT coordinator a standing search of the radiology system each week
Keep a register of persistent disease cases for continuity when staff rotate
Feed outcomes back to the referring endocrinologist so follow-up plans are updated
effort: ~30 min per month from MDT database and radiology search

question: What proportion of fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples for a thyroid nodule are reported as Thy1 (non-diagnostic/inadequate)?
why: A high non-diagnostic rate delays diagnosis and increases repeat procedures; no audit of local Thy1 rates against the NICE quality trigger has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.2.10 (2022)
standard.wording: Consider rapid on-site evaluation of FNAC adequacy rates to improve the diagnostic yield of samples if the Thy1 (inadequate) rate for the centre or individual healthcare professionals is higher than 15% (when Thy1c is excluded).

pass: Thy1 (excluding Thy1c) rate for the service is 15% or lower over the audit period
population: Inclusion: all thyroid nodule FNAC samples taken over the audit period. Exclusion: repeat FNAC on the same nodule within 4 weeks
sample: All thyroid FNAC samples over the last 6 months (expect 40-60)
data_source: Cytology reporting system, radiology (ultrasound-guided FNAC) records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) of FNAC adequacy for ultrasound-guided thyroid biopsies
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint cytology/radiology/endocrine surgery governance meeting; embed ROSE if the target is met
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: ROSE requires a cytotechnologist or pathologist present at every list → negotiate cover before starting the change
Operator-level data seen as punitive → present anonymised operator codes first, agree feedback approach with the team
Thy1c cases wrongly counted as inadequate → use the coded cytology categories, not free text
Small numbers per individual operator → report at service level first, individual level only with consent
pearls: Agree with cytology in advance which category counts as 'inadequate' for the audit
Use a dedicated ultrasound-guided FNAC list run by trained operators to improve consistency
Share Thy1 rates quarterly at the endocrine surgery/radiology joint meeting
Track repeat-biopsy rate as a secondary outcome
effort: ~20 min per month from cytology reporting system

question: What proportion of patients with T1a/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without radioactive iodine receive the recommended surveillance ultrasound and annual clinical follow-up?
why: Under-surveillance risks missed recurrence in low-risk thyroid cancer managed without RAI; no audit of adherence to the NICE surveillance schedule has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.2 (2022)
standard.wording: Consider an ultrasound at 6 to 12 months initially then annual clinical follow-up for up to 5 years for people with T1a (m) or T1b stage or greater thyroid cancer, who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI.

pass: An ultrasound is booked or performed 6-12 months after surgery and an annual clinical follow-up appointment is booked for each year up to 5 years
population: Inclusion: adults with T1a(m)/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer treated by hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI. Exclusion: patients who received RAI
sample: All such patients treated in the last 18 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Cancer MDT database, radiology booking system, clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'low-risk thyroid cancer surveillance' pathway on the cancer follow-up system that books the 6-12 month ultrasound and annual reviews at the point of MDT outcome
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT; embed the automated pathway if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from surgical clinic → use a single named follow-up pathway owner
Ultrasound slots not protected for surveillance → agree a standing allocation with radiology
Definition of T1a(m) vs T1a ambiguous to non-specialists → confirm staging with the MDT coordinator for each case
Surveillance stopped early without documented reason → require a reason field if follow-up is curtailed before 5 years
pearls: Use the MDT outcome form to auto-generate the follow-up schedule
Give patients a printed follow-up plan at their post-op clinic visit
Audit alongside the cancer MDT's annual outcomes review
Nominate a CNS to track the pathway centrally
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT database

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are not already taking a beta-blocker are offered pharmacological prophylaxis (amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) to reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation?
why: Postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery prolongs stay and increases stroke risk; while restarting a pre-existing beta-blocker is already tracked in the library [NNA-047], no audit has measured whether patients who are not already on a beta-blocker are offered any of the recommended prophylactic options.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.1 (2021)
standard.wording: In people having cardiothoracic surgery: reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation by offering 1 of the following: amiodarone a standard beta‑blocker (that is, a beta-blocker other than sotalol) a rate‑limiting calcium‑channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) do not offer digoxin.

pass: One of amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker is prescribed for AF prophylaxis by the end of the first postoperative day, and digoxin is not used for this purpose
population: Inclusion: adults having elective cardiac surgery who were not on a beta-blocker before admission. Exclusion: patients on a pre-existing beta-blocker (covered by the restart pathway)
sample: 40 consecutive beta-blocker-naive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
data_source: Anaesthetic chart, ICU drug chart, EPMA
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'AF prophylaxis: amiodarone / beta-blocker / calcium-channel blocker (tick one) or contraindicated (reason)' line to the post-cardiac surgery ICU order set
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery/anaesthesia governance meeting; embed the order set default if effective
evidence: [NNA-047] restarting a pre-existing beta-blocker by POD1 improved with a default ICU order-set line; the same approach is proposed here for beta-blocker-naive patients
pitfalls: Digoxin still used from habit → remove it as an option from the order set
Bradycardia or hypotension used as a blanket reason to omit prophylaxis without considering alternatives → require the alternative agent to be considered first
AF occurring after ICU discharge missed by the audit → extend data collection to hospital discharge
Anaesthetists and surgeons prescribing inconsistently → agree a single default order set for both teams
pearls: Build the three options into a single tick-box so an active choice is required
Involve pharmacy in checking interactions before amiodarone loading
Review the order set uptake weekly during the first cycle
Keep the postoperative AF rate as a linked outcome measure
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from ICU drug chart

question: What proportion of patients started on a rhythm-control strategy for new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery have their need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment reassessed at around 6 weeks?
why: Postoperative AF often resolves once the precipitant settles, but antiarrhythmic drugs are frequently continued by default; no audit of the 6-week reassessment has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.6 (2021)
standard.wording: If a rhythm‑control strategy is chosen, reassess the need for antiarrhythmic drug treatment at a suitable time point (usually at around 6 weeks).

pass: A documented reassessment of the need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment occurs between 4 and 8 weeks after starting rhythm control
population: Inclusion: adults started on a rhythm-control strategy for new postoperative AF after cardiac surgery. Exclusion: rate-control strategy chosen
sample: All patients started on rhythm control for postoperative AF in the last 6 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Discharge summary, cardiology/cardiac surgery follow-up clinic letters, GP correspondence

change: Add a mandatory 6-week antiarrhythmic review task to the discharge summary for any patient discharged on antiarrhythmic treatment for postoperative AF
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery follow-up governance meeting; embed the discharge task if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are already taking a statin have it continued after surgery?
why: Unintentional omission of a pre-existing statin at the time of surgery is a recognised, avoidable medicines-reconciliation failure; no audit of statin continuation after cardiac surgery has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.4 (2021)
standard.wording: In people having cardiothoracic surgery who are already on statins, continue this treatment.

pass: A pre-existing statin is represented on the post-operative drug chart by the end of the first postoperative day, or a documented reason for stopping it is recorded
population: Inclusion: adults on a statin before elective cardiac surgery. Exclusion: statin started for the first time postoperatively
sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients known to be on a statin pre-operatively, over the last 4 months
data_source: Medicines reconciliation record, ICU/ward drug chart

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add pre-existing statins to the medicines reconciliation prompt that appears automatically when writing the post-cardiac-surgery drug chart
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery/pharmacy medicines safety meeting; embed the reconciliation prompt if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Statin omitted because the patient is nil by mouth and not represented once feeding resumes → add a re-check step once oral intake restarts
Reconciliation done by a junior doctor without pharmacy cross-check → involve pharmacy in every post-op reconciliation
Statin stopped for a genuine reason (e.g. rhabdomyolysis risk) but not documented → require a reason field
Discharge summary omits the statin even though it was continued in hospital → check the discharge letter as well as the inpatient chart
pearls: Use the electronic medicines reconciliation list as the single source of truth for pre-op medicines
Ask pharmacy to review post-cardiac-surgery drug charts within 24 hours
Flag any statin omission for consultant sign-off
